tiers.name: Pre-algebra
tiers.summary: You can calculate confidently with whole numbers, negatives, fractions, decimals and percents, use powers and square roots, and solve one-variable equations. You can also convert units, find areas, volumes and angles, and summarize data with averages.

modules.title: Integers
modules.summary: Calculate reliably with whole and negative numbers and break numbers into primes to find common factors and multiples.
refs: Patrick–Rusczyk–Boppana, AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 1 (Properties of Arithmetic), ch. 3 (Number Theory)

practice.title: Alcumus adaptive drills on arithmetic and number theory

units.title: Place value and rounding
objectives: Give the value of any digit of a whole number from its place
Write a whole number in expanded form using powers of ten
Round a number to a given place and state the round-half-up rule
Explain why a positional system needs a symbol for zero
refs: Gelfand–Shen, Algebra, §4 (Addition in the positional number system)

units.title: Order of operations and the laws of arithmetic
objectives: Evaluate expressions in the conventional order: grouping, exponents, multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right
Use the commutative and associative laws to regroup a calculation
Explain why 8 ÷ 2 × 4 equals 16, not 1
Insert parentheses so that an expression reaches a target value

units.title: Negative numbers
objectives: Place and compare integers on a number line
Add and subtract signed numbers, including subtracting a negative
Multiply and divide signed numbers using the sign rules
Find the absolute value and the opposite of a number
Explain with the distributive law why a negative times a negative is positive

units.title: Primes and prime factorization
objectives: Apply divisibility tests for 2, 3, 4, 5, 9 and 10
Decide whether a number is prime by trial division up to its square root
Write the prime factorization of a whole number
State that prime factorization is unique (fundamental theorem of arithmetic)
Explain why 1 is neither prime nor composite

units.title: Greatest common divisor and least common multiple
objectives: Compute the GCD and LCM of two numbers from their prime factorizations
Use gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) = a × b to find one from the other
Recognize relatively prime pairs
Solve 'when do two repeating cycles line up again' problems with the LCM

modules.title: Fractions and proportion
modules.summary: Work fluently with fractions, decimals, ratios, rates and percents, including percent change.
refs: AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 4 (Fractions), ch. 6 (Decimals), ch. 7 (Ratios, Conversions, and Rates), ch. 8 (Percents)

practice.title: Alcumus adaptive drills on fractions, ratios and percents

units.title: What a fraction means
objectives: Interpret a/b as parts of a whole, as a division, and as a point on the number line
Generate equivalent fractions and reduce a fraction to simplest form using the GCD
Convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions
Compare two fractions using a common denominator or cross-multiplication

units.title: Fraction arithmetic
objectives: Add and subtract fractions using the least common denominator
Multiply fractions, cancelling common factors first
Divide by a fraction by multiplying by its reciprocal and explain why this works
Calculate with mixed numbers and negative fractions

units.title: Decimals
objectives: Read decimal places as tenths, hundredths and thousandths
Add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals
Convert between fractions and decimals
State when a fraction in lowest terms has a terminating decimal (denominator has only factors 2 and 5)
Convert a repeating decimal to a fraction

units.title: Ratios, rates and proportions
objectives: Write and simplify ratios, including three-way ratios
Compute unit rates to compare prices or speeds
Set up and solve a proportion
Convert units by multiplying by conversion factors equal to 1

units.title: Percent and percent change
objectives: Convert among percents, decimals and fractions
Find a percent of a quantity, and find the whole from a part and a percent
Compute percent increase and decrease with multipliers such as 1.15 and 0.85
Explain why successive percent changes do not simply add
Distinguish a percent change from a percentage-point change

modules.title: Powers and roots
modules.summary: Use exponent rules, square roots, scientific notation and quick estimates to handle very large, very small and irrational quantities.

units.title: Exponent laws
objectives: Evaluate powers and read a^n as repeated multiplication
Apply the product, quotient and power-of-a-power rules
Justify a^0 = 1 and a^(−n) = 1/a^n from the quotient rule
Distinguish −3² = −9 from (−3)² = 9

units.title: Square roots
objectives: Find square roots of perfect squares and place other square roots between consecutive integers
Simplify square roots such as √72 = 6√2
Multiply and divide square roots
Recognize that the square root of a non-square whole number is irrational

units.title: Scientific notation
objectives: Write a number as a × 10^n with 1 ≤ a < 10
Multiply and divide numbers in scientific notation
Compare sizes by orders of magnitude
refs: Gelfand–Shen, Algebra, §17, §19 (big and small numbers around us)

units.title: Estimation and sense of magnitude
objectives: Round to one or two significant figures to estimate a calculation
Make a Fermi estimate by multiplying rough factors
Check whether an answer is reasonable in size and units

modules.title: Expressions and equations
modules.summary: Translate situations into algebraic expressions and solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable.

units.title: Variables and expressions
objectives: Translate a verbal description into an algebraic expression
Evaluate an expression for given values of its variables
Identify the terms, coefficients and constants of an expression
Explain the difference between an expression and an equation

units.title: The distributive law and like terms
objectives: Expand a(b + c) and (a + b)(c + d)
Factor a common factor out of a sum
Combine like terms to simplify an expression
Distribute a minus sign correctly over parentheses

units.title: Linear equations
objectives: Solve ax + b = c and equations with the variable on both sides by doing the same operation to both sides
Clear fractions by multiplying through by a common denominator
Check a solution by substitution
Recognize equations with no solution and equations true for every number

units.title: Linear inequalities
objectives: Solve a linear inequality in one variable
Explain why multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality
Graph a solution set on the number line and write it in interval notation

units.title: Word problems
objectives: Name the unknown and translate a word problem into an equation
Solve distance–rate–time, consecutive-integer, age and mixture problems
Check that an answer makes sense in the original situation

modules.title: Measurement and data
modules.summary: Convert units, compute perimeters, areas, volumes and angles, use the Pythagorean theorem, and summarize data with averages.
refs: AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 10 (Angles), ch. 11 (Perimeter and Area), ch. 12 (Right Triangles and Quadrilaterals), ch. 13 (Data and Statistics)

units.title: Units and unit conversion
objectives: Convert within the metric system using prefixes
Convert between units by chaining conversion factors
Explain why 1 m² = 10,000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³

units.title: Perimeter, area and volume
objectives: Compute perimeter and area of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms and trapezoids
Compute the circumference and area of a circle from its radius
Compute the volume of a box, a prism and a cylinder

units.title: Angles
objectives: Classify angles and use complementary, supplementary and vertical angles
Use the equal angles formed when a transversal crosses parallel lines
Use the triangle angle sum of 180° and the polygon sum (n − 2) × 180°

units.title: The Pythagorean theorem
objectives: State the Pythagorean theorem and find a missing side of a right triangle
Recognize Pythagorean triples such as 3-4-5 and 5-12-13
Use the side ratios of 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles
Use the converse to test whether a triangle is right

units.title: Mean, median and mode
objectives: Compute the mean, median, mode and range of a data set
Explain why an outlier moves the mean more than the median
Choose a suitable average and read simple tables and charts

tiers.name: High school
tiers.summary: You can handle lines, systems, polynomials, quadratics, exponential and logarithmic functions, triangle and circle geometry, trigonometry, vectors, counting, probability and basic statistics. You can also read and write short proofs, including induction, and calculate with complex numbers.

modules.title: Algebra I
modules.summary: Graph and solve linear equations and systems, factor polynomials and solve any quadratic equation.
refs: Rusczyk, AoPS Introduction to Algebra, ch. 5, 8–11, 13–14, 18

practice.title: Alcumus adaptive drills: linear equations, factoring and quadratics

units.title: Lines and slope
objectives: Compute the slope of a line through two points and interpret it as a rate of change
Write the equation of a line in slope-intercept, point-slope and standard form
Use slopes to decide whether two lines are parallel or perpendicular
Graph a line from its equation and read its intercepts

units.title: Systems of linear equations
objectives: Solve a 2×2 linear system by substitution and by elimination
Classify a system as having one, no, or infinitely many solutions and relate this to the graphs
Solve a 3×3 system by successive elimination
Model a word problem with a system of equations

units.title: Linear inequalities and absolute value
objectives: Graph a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane
Find the feasible region of a system of linear inequalities
Rewrite |x − a| < r as an interval and solve absolute-value equations and inequalities

units.title: Polynomial arithmetic and special products
objectives: Add, subtract and multiply polynomials and state the degree of the result
Expand (a + b)², (a − b)², (a + b)(a − b) and (a + b)³ from memory
Read the coefficients of (a + b)^n from Pascal's triangle
Explain why (a + b)² ≠ a² + b²

units.title: Factoring
objectives: Factor out a greatest common factor and factor by grouping
Factor trinomials x² + bx + c and ax² + bx + c
Factor differences of squares and sums and differences of cubes
Use Simon's Favorite Factoring Trick to solve xy + ax + by = c in integers
refs: AoPS Introduction to Algebra §10.2–10.3, ch. 11 (Special Factorizations)

units.title: Quadratic equations and the quadratic formula
objectives: Solve a quadratic equation by factoring, by completing the square and by the quadratic formula
Derive the quadratic formula by completing the square
Use the discriminant to count real roots
Apply Vieta's formulas for the sum and product of the roots
Rewrite a quadratic in vertex form to find its maximum or minimum
refs: AoPS Introduction to Algebra, ch. 13 (Quadratic Equations, Part 2), ch. 14 (Graphing Quadratics), §15.1, §15.4

units.title: Polynomial division, roots and factors
objectives: Divide one polynomial by another with long division
State and apply the remainder theorem and the factor theorem
List candidate rational roots with the rational root theorem and test them
Relate the zeros of a polynomial, their multiplicities and its factors
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Polynomial Functions' (The Remainder and Factor Theorems; Real Zeros of Polynomials)

modules.title: Functions, exponentials, logarithms
modules.summary: Treat functions as objects you can combine, invert, shift and stretch, and use exponential, logarithmic and rational functions to model real situations.
refs: AoPS Introduction to Algebra, ch. 16–17 (Functions; Graphing Functions), ch. 19–20
Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, chapters 'Introduction to Functions', 'Rational Functions', 'Further Topics on Functions', 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

practice.title: Graph each transformation and model in the Desmos graphing calculator
Work the free Stitz–Zeager exercise sets

units.title: Functions and function notation
objectives: Decide whether a rule, table or graph defines a function and state its domain and range
Evaluate and interpret f(x) notation, including f(a + h)
Compute an average rate of change over an interval
Read and evaluate piecewise-defined functions
refs: AoPS Introduction to Algebra §16.1, ch. 17 (Graphing Functions), §20.5

units.title: Composition and inverse functions
objectives: Compute the composite f∘g and find its domain
Decide whether a function is one-to-one and has an inverse
Find an inverse function algebraically and check f(f⁻¹(x)) = x
Obtain the graph of f⁻¹ by reflecting in y = x
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions' (Function Composition; Inverse Functions)

units.title: Transformations of graphs
objectives: Predict the graph of a·f(b(x − h)) + k from the graph of f
Explain why f(x − 2) shifts the graph right, not left
Recognize even and odd functions from formulas and from symmetry of graphs
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Further Topics on Functions' (Transformations of Graphs)

units.title: Exponential functions
objectives: Interpret a^(m/n) as a root of a power and simplify expressions with rational exponents
Model growth and decay with f(t) = a·b^t and find half-lives and doubling times
Compute compound and continuously compounded interest and explain the number e
Contrast linear growth (constant differences) with exponential growth (constant ratios)
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions'

units.title: Logarithms
objectives: Define log_b x as the inverse of b^x and convert between log and exponential form
Apply the product, quotient and power rules for logarithms and the change-of-base formula
Solve exponential and logarithmic equations, checking for extraneous solutions
Read logarithmic scales such as pH and decibels
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions' (Properties of Logarithms; equations and inequalities)

units.title: Rational functions
objectives: Find the domain, intercepts and holes of a rational function
Find vertical and horizontal asymptotes from the degrees and leading coefficients
Solve a rational inequality with a sign chart
Sketch a rational function from its features

units.title: Modeling with functions
objectives: Choose a linear, quadratic or exponential model from a table by checking differences and ratios
Fit a model through two data points and interpret its parameters in context
Describe the modeling cycle: formulate, compute, interpret, validate, report
Restrict a model's domain to values that make sense in the situation
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Exponential and Logarithmic Functions' (Applications)
Common Core State Standards, High School: Modeling

modules.title: Euclidean geometry
modules.summary: Prove and use the classical facts about congruent and similar triangles, circles, areas and volumes, and carry out compass-and-straightedge constructions.
refs: Jacobs, Geometry: Seeing, Doing, Understanding (3rd ed.), ch. 2–15

practice.title: Solve construction puzzles in Euclidea
Build and test constructions and conjectures in GeoGebra Geometry

units.title: Points, lines, angles and first proofs
objectives: Distinguish undefined terms, definitions, postulates and theorems
Write a conditional statement, its converse and its contrapositive
Prove that vertical angles are equal
Use the parallel postulate to prove alternate interior angles are equal and the angle sum of a triangle is 180°
refs: Jacobs, Geometry 3e, ch. 2 (The Nature of Deductive Reasoning), ch. 3 (Lines and Angles), ch. 6 (Parallel Lines)

units.title: Rigid motions and congruence
objectives: Describe translations, reflections and rotations and compose them
Define congruence as matching by a rigid motion
Apply the SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and HL congruence tests
Give a counterexample showing SSA does not guarantee congruence
Prove the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal
refs: Jacobs, Geometry 3e, ch. 4 (Congruence), ch. 6 (AAS and HL), ch. 8 (Transformations)
Kiselev, Planimetry, ch. 1 (congruence tests for triangles)

units.title: Triangle and quadrilateral theorems
objectives: State and use the triangle inequality and the exterior angle theorem
Prove properties of parallelograms, rectangles and rhombuses
Use the midsegment theorem
Locate the centroid, circumcenter and incenter as intersections of medians, perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors
refs: Jacobs, Geometry 3e, ch. 5 (Inequalities), ch. 7 (Quadrilaterals), ch. 13 (The Concurrence Theorems)
Kiselev, Planimetry, ch. 1 (parallelograms and trapezoids), ch. 2 (four concurrency points in a triangle)

units.title: Similarity
objectives: Describe a dilation by its center and scale factor
Prove triangles similar by AA, SAS and SSS similarity
Apply the side-splitter theorem and the angle bisector theorem
Scale lengths by k, areas by k² and volumes by k³
Use the geometric-mean relations in a right triangle with an altitude
refs: Jacobs, Geometry 3e, ch. 10 (Similarity), ch. 11 (The Right Triangle)

units.title: Compass-and-straightedge constructions
objectives: Construct a perpendicular bisector, an angle bisector, a perpendicular from a point and a parallel through a point
Construct an equilateral triangle and a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle
Justify a construction with a congruence argument
State that some constructions, such as trisecting a general angle, are impossible
refs: Kiselev, Planimetry, ch. 1 (basic construction problems), ch. 2 (construction problems)

units.title: Circle theorems
objectives: Use the facts that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius and that equal chords are equidistant from the center
Prove that an inscribed angle is half the central angle on the same arc
Use the angle in a semicircle and the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral
Apply power of a point to intersecting chords, secants and tangents
Compute arc length and sector area from the central angle
refs: Jacobs, Geometry 3e, ch. 12 (Circles), ch. 14 (Regular Polygons and the Circle)

units.title: Area and volume
objectives: Derive area formulas for triangles, trapezoids and regular polygons by decomposition
Compute a triangle's area with Heron's formula
State Cavalieri's principle and use it to explain the volume formulas for pyramids and cones
Compute volumes and surface areas of prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones and spheres
refs: Jacobs, Geometry 3e, ch. 9 (Area), ch. 14, ch. 15 (Geometric Solids)

modules.title: Trigonometry
modules.summary: Use sine, cosine and tangent to measure triangles, model anything that repeats, and transform trigonometric expressions with identities.
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, chapters 'Foundations of Trigonometry', 'Analytical Trigonometry', 'Geometric Applications of Trigonometry'

practice.title: Plot amplitude, period and phase-shift changes of sinusoids in Desmos

units.title: Right-triangle trigonometry
objectives: Define sine, cosine and tangent as ratios of sides of a right triangle and explain via similarity why they depend only on the angle
Give exact values at 30°, 45° and 60°
Solve a right triangle from one side and one angle or from two sides
Solve angle-of-elevation and angle-of-depression problems
refs: Gelfand–Saul, Trigonometry (chapter on trigonometric ratios in a triangle)

units.title: Radians and the unit circle
objectives: Convert between degrees and radians and explain a radian as arc length on the unit circle
Use s = rθ and A = ½r²θ
Define sine and cosine of any angle as coordinates on the unit circle
Use reference angles, quadrant signs and periodicity to evaluate trigonometric functions
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Foundations of Trigonometry' (Radian Measure of Angles; Circular Functions)

units.title: Graphs of trigonometric functions
objectives: Sketch y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x with their periods, zeros and asymptotes
Read amplitude, period, phase shift and midline from y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D
Fit a sinusoid to periodic data such as tides or daylight hours
refs: Gelfand–Saul, Trigonometry (chapter on graphs of trigonometric functions)
Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Foundations of Trigonometry' (Graphs of Sine and Cosine)

units.title: Trigonometric identities
objectives: Derive sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 and the related tangent and secant identity
State and apply the addition formulas for sine, cosine and tangent
Derive the double-angle and half-angle formulas from the addition formulas
Prove a given identity by transforming one side into the other
refs: Gelfand–Saul, Trigonometry (chapters on the addition formulas and trigonometric identities)
Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Analytical Trigonometry' (Pythagorean Identities; More Identities)

units.title: Laws of sines and cosines
objectives: State and apply the law of sines and the law of cosines
Explain why the SSA case can give zero, one or two triangles
Compute the area of a triangle as ½ab sin C
Solve any triangle from three suitable measurements
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Geometric Applications of Trigonometry' (Law of Sines; Law of Cosines)
Gelfand–Saul, Trigonometry (chapter on trigonometric ratios in a triangle)

units.title: Inverse trigonometric functions and equations
objectives: Define arcsin, arccos and arctan on restricted domains and state their ranges
Explain why arcsin(sin x) = x fails outside [−π/2, π/2]
Solve trigonometric equations and write the general solution using periodicity
refs: Gelfand–Saul, Trigonometry (chapter on inverse functions and trigonometric equations)
Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Analytical Trigonometry' (Inverse Circular Functions; Equations and Inequalities)

modules.title: Coordinates and vectors
modules.summary: Describe curves with equations, parameters and polar coordinates, and compute with vectors and small matrices.
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, chapters 'The Conic Sections', 'Systems of Equations and Matrices', 'Geometric Applications of Trigonometry', 'Polar Coordinates and Parametric Equations'

practice.title: Trace conics, polar roses and parametric curves in Desmos

units.title: Distance, midpoints and circles
objectives: Derive the distance formula from the Pythagorean theorem and compute midpoints
Write the equation of a circle and find center and radius by completing the square
Prove a simple geometric fact, such as the diagonals of a parallelogram bisecting each other, with coordinates
refs: Lang, Basic Mathematics, ch. 8 (Coordinates and Geometry)

units.title: Conic sections
objectives: Define the parabola by focus and directrix, the ellipse by a constant sum of distances and the hyperbola by a constant difference
Read vertices, foci and asymptotes from standard-form equations
Identify the type of conic from a second-degree equation without an xy term
refs: Lang, Basic Mathematics, ch. 12 (Some Analytic Geometry)

units.title: Vectors and the dot product
objectives: Represent a vector by components and by magnitude and direction
Add vectors and multiply by scalars, geometrically and in components
Compute a dot product and use it to find the angle between vectors
Project one vector onto another and test for orthogonality
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Geometric Applications of Trigonometry' (Vectors; The Dot Product)
Lang, Basic Mathematics, ch. 9 (Operations on Points)

units.title: Matrices and plane transformations
objectives: Add, scale and multiply matrices and check that AB and BA can differ
Read a 2×2 matrix as a transformation of the plane, such as a rotation, reflection or scaling
Interpret the determinant of a 2×2 matrix as an area factor and compute a 2×2 inverse
Solve a linear system written as Ax = b
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Systems of Equations and Matrices' (Matrix Arithmetic; Matrix Inverses; Determinants and Cramer's Rule)

units.title: Parametric and polar curves
objectives: Describe motion with parametric equations and eliminate the parameter
Convert between polar and rectangular coordinates
Sketch polar curves such as circles, cardioids and roses
Explain why one point has many polar coordinate pairs
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Polar Coordinates and Parametric Equations'

modules.title: Counting, probability, statistics
modules.summary: Count arrangements and selections, compute probabilities and expected values, and summarize, compare and sample data sensibly.
refs: Lehoczky–Rusczyk, AoPS Introduction to Counting & Probability, ch. 1–14

practice.title: Simulate coins, dice and sampling distributions in Seeing Theory
Work the OpenIntro Statistics exercises and labs

units.title: Counting principles
objectives: Apply the addition and multiplication principles
Count by casework and by complementary counting
Count arrangements with factorials and permutations P(n, k)
Avoid double counting when cases overlap
refs: AoPS Intro to Counting & Probability, ch. 1 (Counting Is Arithmetic), ch. 2 (Basic Counting Techniques)

units.title: Combinations and the binomial theorem
objectives: Count selections with C(n, k) and correct for overcounting by dividing
Build Pascal's triangle and prove Pascal's identity by counting
State the binomial theorem and find a given coefficient of (x + y)^n
Count lattice paths and distributions of identical objects
refs: AoPS Intro to Counting & Probability, ch. 3–5, 12–14

units.title: Probability basics
objectives: Compute probabilities with equally likely outcomes by counting
Use complements and the addition rule for overlapping events
Use the multiplication rule for independent events
Compute geometric probabilities with lengths and areas
refs: AoPS Intro to Counting & Probability, ch. 7–8, 10

units.title: Conditional probability
objectives: Compute P(A | B) from a two-way table or a tree diagram
Test independence by comparing P(A | B) with P(A)
Apply Bayes' rule and explain the base-rate fallacy with a medical-test example

units.title: Random variables and expected value
objectives: Describe a random variable by its probability distribution
Compute expected value and use linearity of expectation
Use expected value to compare games and decisions
Recognize the binomial distribution and use its mean np
refs: AoPS Intro to Counting & Probability, ch. 11 (Expected Value)

units.title: Describing data
objectives: Describe a distribution's shape, center and spread from a histogram or box plot
Compute and interpret the standard deviation and interquartile range
Compute z-scores and use the 68–95–99.7 rule for roughly normal data

units.title: Sampling and experiments
objectives: Distinguish a population from a sample and a statistic from a parameter
Identify sources of sampling bias and explain why random sampling helps
Distinguish observational studies from randomized experiments and explain why only experiments support causal claims
Interpret a margin of error as the typical size of sampling variation

units.title: Correlation and regression lines
objectives: Describe a scatterplot by direction, form and strength
Interpret the correlation coefficient r and its limits
Find and interpret the slope of a least-squares line and its residuals
Explain why correlation does not imply causation

modules.title: Bridge to proof
modules.summary: Read and write short proofs, sum sequences and series, calculate with complex numbers, and get an honest first feel for limits.
refs: Lang, Basic Mathematics, Interlude (On Logic and Mathematical Expressions), ch. 1, 3, 15, 16
AoPS Introduction to Algebra, ch. 12 (Complex Numbers), ch. 21 (Sequences & Series)

units.title: Logic and connectives
objectives: Build truth tables for and, or, not, if–then and if-and-only-if
Write the converse and contrapositive of an implication and say which is equivalent to it
Negate statements containing 'and', 'or', 'all' and 'some'
Explain why an implication with a false hypothesis counts as true
refs: Lang, Basic Mathematics, Interlude: On Logic and Mathematical Expressions

units.title: First proof techniques
objectives: Prove simple facts about even and odd integers directly from the definitions
Prove that √2 is irrational by contradiction
Disprove a universal claim with a single counterexample
Explain why checking many examples does not prove a statement
refs: Lang, Basic Mathematics, ch. 1 (Numbers), ch. 3 (Real Numbers)

units.title: Mathematical induction
objectives: State the principle of induction with its base case and inductive step
Prove formulas such as 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 by induction
Prove inequalities such as 2^n > n by induction
Read and write sums in sigma notation
refs: Lang, Basic Mathematics, ch. 16 (Induction and Summations)
Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Sequences and the Binomial Theorem' (Summation Notation; Mathematical Induction)

units.title: Sequences and series
objectives: Find the nth term and partial sums of arithmetic and geometric sequences
State when an infinite geometric series converges and find its sum
Write a repeating decimal as a geometric series and as a fraction
Evaluate telescoping sums
refs: AoPS Introduction to Algebra, ch. 21 (Sequences & Series)

units.title: Complex numbers
objectives: Add, multiply and divide complex numbers using the conjugate
Plot complex numbers and compute modulus and argument
Multiply in polar form by multiplying moduli and adding arguments, and apply De Moivre's formula
Find the nth roots of unity and solve quadratics with negative discriminant
State the fundamental theorem of algebra
refs: AoPS Introduction to Algebra, ch. 12 (Complex Numbers)
Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'Polar Coordinates and Parametric Equations' (Polar Form of Complex Numbers)

units.title: A first look at limits
objectives: Describe the limit of a sequence informally and decide whether simple sequences converge
Estimate a limit of a function from a table or graph and explain that the value at the point does not matter
Explain why 0.999… = 1
Describe the slope of a tangent as the limit of slopes of secant lines and area as the limit of rectangle sums
refs: Stitz–Zeager, Precalculus 4i, ch. 'First Steps into Calculus'

tiers.name: First-year university
tiers.summary: You can write careful proofs about sets, functions and numbers, and you can use single- and multivariable calculus, linear algebra, discrete mathematics and basic differential equations the way a strong first-year mathematics student does.

modules.title: Proofs, logic, sets
modules.summary: Read and write rigorous proofs using quantifiers, contradiction, contrapositive and induction, and reason about relations, functions and the sizes of infinite sets.
refs: Velleman, How to Prove It (3rd ed.), ch. 1–6, 8
Hammack, Book of Proof (3rd ed.), ch. 1–2, 4–12, 14

practice.title: Prove arithmetic facts by induction in the Lean Natural Number Game
Build natural-deduction proofs in The Incredible Proof Machine
Work the free Book of Proof exercises

units.title: Sets and set operations
objectives: Read and write set-builder notation and decide membership and subset claims
Compute unions, intersections, differences and complements, and draw them as Venn diagrams
Compute power sets and Cartesian products and their sizes for finite sets
Distinguish ∈ from ⊆ and ∅ from {∅}

units.title: Propositional logic
objectives: Decide logical equivalence of two formulas with a truth table
Apply De Morgan's laws and the equivalence of P → Q with ¬P ∨ Q
Recognize tautologies and contradictions
State why a conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive but not to its converse

units.title: Quantifiers
objectives: Translate statements with 'for all' and 'there exists' into symbols and back
Negate a statement with nested quantifiers by pushing the negation inward

units.title: Sylow theorems in action
objectives: State the three Sylow theorems and derive n_p ≡ 1 (mod p) and n_p | m for |G| = p^a·m with p ∤ m.

Use the coset action G → S_n of a subgroup of index n to find normal subgroups when |G| ∤ n!.

Explain why S_3 and S_4 are solvable but not nilpotent.
State Burnside's p^a q^b theorem and Hall's theorem on Hall subgroups of solvable groups, and use them in counting arguments.

Show that composition factors do not determine a group: Z_4 and Z_2 × Z_2, or S_3 and Z_6.
Prove that a finite group is solvable iff all its composition factors are cyclic of prime order.
State the Jordan–Hölder theorem for groups with operators and the Krull–Schmidt theorem.

units.title: Simplicity of A_n

Prove that a simple group with a proper subgroup of index n > 1 embeds in A_n, so |G| divides n!/2, and use it to bound subgroup indices.

Prove the weak Nullstellensatz from Zariski's lemma and derive I(V(J)) = √J over an algebraically closed field.
Describe the Zariski topology on kⁿ and on Spec R, and the bijection between radical ideals and affine algebraic sets.
Define Dedekind domains and discrete valuation rings; show Z[√−5] is Dedekind but not a UFD and state unique factorization of ideals.

units.title: Semisimple rings and Artin–Wedderburn
objectives: Define simple and semisimple modules and prove Schur's lemma: the endomorphism ring of a simple module is a division ring.
Prove the equivalent conditions for a ring to be semisimple (every module semisimple; every submodule a direct summand).
State the Artin–Wedderburn theorem R ≅ ∏ M_{n_i}(D_i) and find the factors for C[S_3] ≅ C × C × M_2(C), R[Z_3] ≅ R × C and Q[Z_n] ≅ ∏_{d|n} Q(ζ_d).
Define the Jacobson radical and show F_p[Z_p] ≅ F_p[x]/(x − 1)^p is not semisimple.
Define central simple algebras (M_n(k), Hamilton's quaternions H) and prove Wedderburn's little theorem: finite division rings are fields.

units.title: Rings and modules qual problems
objectives: Compute tensor products, localizations, Hom, Tor and Ext of explicit modules over Z, k[x] and Z/n.
Decide whether given modules are free, projective, injective or flat, with a proof or a counterexample.

Prove standard qual statements: a surjective endomorphism of a finitely generated module is injective; a domain that is finite-dimensional over a field is a field; a Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal primes.

modules.title: Fields and Galois theory
modules.summary: Compute Galois groups of explicit polynomials and use Galois theory to settle questions about field extensions, including infinite and transcendental ones.
refs: Milne, Fields and Galois Theory (v5.10), ch. 1–9
Lang, Algebra (rev. 3rd ed.), ch. V, VI, VIII

practice.title: Look up the transitive groups of degree 4 and 5 in the LMFDB and match each to its discriminant and resolvent test
Work the exercises, which come with solutions, in Milne's Fields and Galois Theory notes

units.title: Separable, inseparable and normal extensions
objectives: Prove f is separable iff gcd(f, f′) = 1, and that irreducible polynomials over perfect fields (characteristic 0, finite fields) are separable.
Show x^p − t is irreducible and inseparable over F_p(t), and define separable degree and purely inseparable extensions.

Prove every field has an algebraic closure, unique up to non-unique isomorphism, and that a finite extension is normal iff it is a splitting field; compute the splitting-field degrees of x³ − 2, x⁴ − 2 and x^p − 1 over Q.
Prove the primitive element theorem for finite separable extensions and show F_p(s, t)/F_p(s^p, t^p) has no primitive element.

units.title: The Galois correspondence in practice
objectives: State the equivalent definitions of a Galois extension and Artin's theorem [L : L^G] = |G| for a finite group G of automorphisms.
Draw the subgroup and subfield lattices of Q(2^{1/4}, i)/Q (group D_8) and Q(√2, √3)/Q, matching normal subgroups with normal subextensions.
Use Dedekind's independence of characters, and compute Gal(KL/K) ≅ Gal(L/K ∩ L) for L Galois.
Find the fixed field of a given subgroup by building invariant elements such as orbit sums and products.

units.title: Finite fields and cyclotomic extensions
objectives: Prove existence and uniqueness of F_{pⁿ}, that its Galois group over F_p is cyclic generated by Frobenius, and that subfields correspond to divisors of n.
Count monic irreducible polynomials of degree n over F_q: (1/n) Σ_{d|n} μ(d) q^{n/d}.
Prove Φ_n is irreducible over Q, that Gal(Q(ζ_n)/Q) ≅ (Z/n)^×, and that Q(ζ_p) contains Q(√p*) with p* = (−1)^{(p−1)/2} p.
Show that for p ∤ n, Φ_n mod p factors into irreducibles whose degree is the order of p in (Z/n)^×.
State the Kronecker–Weber theorem and build an extension of Q with a prescribed finite abelian Galois group.

units.title: Discriminants, cubics and quartics
objectives: Define the discriminant and prove Gal(f) ⊆ A_n iff disc(f) is a square in the base field.
Find the Galois group of an irreducible cubic x³ + px + q from disc = −4p³ − 27q² (x³ − 3x + 1 has disc 81 and group A_3).
Use the resolvent cubic and the discriminant to decide among S_4, A_4, D_8, V_4 and C_4: x⁴ + x + 1 (S_4), x⁴ − 2 (D_8), x⁴ + 4x² + 2 (C_4), x⁴ − 10x² + 1 (V_4).
Recognize the transitive subgroups of S_4 and S_5 by order and cycle types.
keyTerms: Galois group as a permutation group

units.title: Reduction mod p and S_n as a Galois group
objectives: State Dedekind's theorem: if p ∤ disc(f), the factorization of f mod p gives the cycle type of a Frobenius element of Gal(f).
Prove a transitive subgroup of S_p containing a transposition is S_p, so an irreducible polynomial of prime degree p with exactly two nonreal roots has group S_p (x⁵ − 4x + 2, x⁵ − 6x + 3).
Show Gal(x⁵ − x − 1) = S_5 from its factorizations mod 2 and mod 5.
State the Chebotarev density theorem (each cycle type occurs with frequency proportional to its size) and the status of the inverse Galois problem for S_n, A_n and abelian groups.

units.title: Norms, Hilbert 90 and Kummer theory
objectives: Define norm and trace of a finite extension and compute them from minimal polynomials and embeddings.
Prove Hilbert's Theorem 90 for cyclic extensions in its multiplicative and additive forms.
Prove that if μ_n ⊆ K, every cyclic extension of degree n has the form K(a^{1/n}), and [K(a^{1/n}) : K] equals the order of a in K^×/K^{×n}.
State the Kummer correspondence between subgroups of K^×/K^{×n} and abelian extensions of exponent n, and show [Q(√2, √3, √5) : Q] = 8.
Describe Artin–Schreier extensions x^p − x − a in characteristic p.

units.title: Solvability by radicals
objectives: Define radical extensions and prove Galois's theorem: in characteristic 0, f is solvable by radicals iff Gal(f) is solvable.
Show the general polynomial of degree n has Galois group S_n over k(s_1, …, s_n), using the fundamental theorem on symmetric polynomials.
Give an explicit quintic over Q that is not solvable by radicals and explain why every polynomial of degree ≤ 4 is solvable.

units.title: Transcendence bases and degree
objectives: Prove transcendence bases exist and all have the same cardinality (exchange lemma), and that transcendence degree adds in towers.
Show tr.deg_Q C is the cardinality of the continuum and deduce that C has many field automorphisms.
State Lüroth's theorem and compute Aut(k(t)/k) ≅ PGL_2(k).
Decide whether given elements are algebraically independent, e.g., x + y and xy in k(x, y).

units.title: Infinite Galois theory
objectives: Define profinite groups as inverse limits and the Krull topology on Gal(L/K).

State the fundamental theorem for infinite Galois extensions (closed subgroups correspond to intermediate fields) and show the subgroup generated by Frobenius in Gal(F̄_p/F_p) ≅ Ẑ is dense but not closed.
Compute Gal(F̄_p/F_p) ≅ Ẑ, Gal(Q(ζ_{p^∞})/Q) ≅ Z_p^× and Gal(Q^ab/Q) ≅ Ẑ^×.

units.title: Field and Galois theory qual problems
objectives: Find a polynomial over Q with Galois group S_5, A_4, D_8, C_4 or C_3 and prove it.
Compute the Galois group and full subfield lattice of splitting fields such as x⁴ − 2, x⁸ − 1 and (x² − 2)(x² − 3)(x² − 5), over Q and over F_p.
Answer degree and membership questions: [Q(ζ_n, 2^{1/n}) : Q], whether √2 or 2^{1/3} lies in a cyclotomic field.

modules.title: Representations of finite groups
modules.summary: Build character tables, break representations into irreducible pieces, induce from subgroups, and describe the representations of symmetric groups.
refs: Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups, §1–3, §5–7
Fulton–Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course, Part I (Lectures 1–4)

practice.title: Rebuild the character tables of S_4, A_5 and the groups of order 8 and 21, then compare them with GroupNames

units.title: Representations and Maschke's theorem
objectives: Define representations, G-linear maps, subrepresentations and irreducibility, and identify representations with C[G]-modules.
Prove Maschke's theorem by averaging a projection (or an inner product), and show it fails for F_p[Z_p].
Prove Schur's lemma over C (G-endomorphisms of an irreducible are scalars) and deduce that the irreducible representations of abelian groups are 1-dimensional.

units.title: Characters and orthogonality
objectives: Define characters and class functions, and prove χ(1) = dim V and χ(g⁻¹) is the complex conjugate of χ(g).
State and prove the row orthogonality relations and derive the column relations.
Use ⟨χ, χ⟩ = 1 as an irreducibility test and compute multiplicities ⟨χ_V, χ_i⟩.
Prove Σ (dim V_i)² = |G| from the regular representation, and that the number of irreducibles equals the number of conjugacy classes.
Apply the projection formula p_i = (dim V_i/|G|) Σ_g conj(χ_i(g)) g to find isotypic components.

units.title: Building character tables
objectives: Construct the character tables of S_3, D_8, Q_8, A_4, S_4 and A_5 using lifts from G/[G, G], twisting by the sign, permutation characters minus the trivial character, and column orthogonality.
Read off from a table the center, the commutator subgroup, all normal subgroups (as intersections of kernels) and whether G is simple.
Explain why D_8 and Q_8 have identical tables and why A_5's table contains (1 ± √5)/2.

units.title: Duals, tensor products and symmetric powers
objectives: Compute characters of V*, V ⊗ W, Hom(V, W), Sym²V and Λ²V, including χ_{Λ²V}(g) = (χ(g)² − χ(g²))/2 and χ_{Sym²V}(g) = (χ(g)² + χ(g²))/2.
Decompose tensor products such as standard ⊗ standard for S_4, using dim Hom_G(V, W) = ⟨χ_V, χ_W⟩.
Use the Frobenius–Schur indicator to tell real, complex and quaternionic irreducibles apart.

units.title: Induced representations and Frobenius reciprocity
objectives: Define Ind_H^G W = C[G] ⊗_{C[H]} W and compute its character χ(g) = (1/|H|) Σ_{x ∈ G, x⁻¹gx ∈ H} χ_W(x⁻¹gx).
Prove Frobenius reciprocity ⟨Ind χ, ψ⟩_G = ⟨χ, Res ψ⟩_H and use it to decompose induced characters.
Induce from Z_3 ⊂ S_3, from A_4 ⊂ S_4, and from the normal subgroup of order 7 in the nonabelian group of order 21.
State Mackey's irreducibility criterion and describe how irreducibles of S_n restrict to A_n (they stay irreducible or split into two).

units.title: Integrality and Burnside's theorem
objectives: Show character values are algebraic integers and that ω_χ(C) = |C|·χ(g)/χ(1) is an algebraic integer for a conjugacy class C.
Prove that the degree of an irreducible representation divides |G|, and state that it divides [G : Z(G)].
Outline the proof of Burnside's p^a q^b theorem from the lemma that a conjugacy class of prime-power size greater than 1 forces a nontrivial proper normal subgroup.

units.title: Representations of the symmetric group
objectives: Match partitions of n with conjugacy classes and irreducible representations of S_n through Young diagrams and Young symmetrizers (Specht modules).
Compute dimensions with the hook length formula (S_5: 1, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 1) and identify the trivial, sign, standard and Λ^k(standard) representations.
State the branching rule for restriction from S_n to S_{n−1} and Frobenius's character formula.

units.title: Representation theory qual problems
objectives: Compute the character table of a given group of order ≤ 24 and decompose a given permutation, tensor or induced representation.
Prove facts with characters: G is abelian iff every irreducible has degree 1; a nonabelian group of order p³ has p² + p − 1 conjugacy classes.
Find the irreducible representations of the dihedral groups and the character degrees of SL_2(F_3) (1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3) and of the nonabelian group of order 21 (1, 1, 1, 3, 3).

modules.title: Measure and integration
modules.summary: Build measures, integrate using the limit theorems and iterated integrals, and differentiate integrals, measures and functions of bounded variation.
refs: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples (5th ed.), ch. 2

practice.title: Work the Real Analysis (597) problems, which come with solutions, on Michigan's past QR exams
Do the real-analysis half of UCLA's past Analysis qualifying exams

units.title: Outer measures and Carathéodory's construction
objectives: Define σ-algebras, measures and outer measures, and prove continuity from below and from above (with its finiteness condition).
State and prove Carathéodory's theorem: the μ*-measurable sets form a σ-algebra on which μ* is a complete measure.
Extend a premeasure on an algebra to a measure (Carathéodory–Hahn) and prove uniqueness when it is σ-finite.
Construct Lebesgue–Stieltjes measures with μ_F((a, b]) = F(b) − F(a) from increasing right-continuous F, and describe the completion of a measure.

units.title: Lebesgue measure
objectives: Prove outer and inner regularity of Lebesgue measure (approximation by open supersets and by compact or closed subsets).
Show translation invariance, m(cE) = |c|ⁿ m(E), and m(T(E)) = |det T|·m(E) for linear T.
Construct a non-measurable Vitali set and explain the role of the axiom of choice.
Use Cantor sets: the middle-thirds set is uncountable with measure zero, fat Cantor sets are nowhere dense with positive measure, and some Lebesgue measurable sets are not Borel.

units.title: Measurable functions and Littlewood's principles
objectives: Prove that measurable functions are pointwise limits of simple functions (increasing limits when f ≥ 0).
State and prove Egorov's theorem and Lusin's theorem, and show Egorov needs finite measure.
Compare convergence a.e., in measure and in L¹: prove that convergence in measure gives an a.e. convergent subsequence, and use the typewriter sequence to show it does not give a.e. convergence.
Explain why a continuous function composed after a Lebesgue measurable one is measurable, but the other order can fail.

units.title: Monotone and dominated convergence, Fatou
objectives: State and prove the monotone convergence theorem, Fatou's lemma and the dominated convergence theorem, and give sequences showing each hypothesis is needed (n·1_(0,1/n), 1_[n,n+1], moving bumps).
Differentiate under the integral sign and prove continuity of parameter integrals with dominated convergence.
Evaluate limits such as lim ∫_0^n (1 − x/n)ⁿ e^{x/2} dx = 2 and lim ∫_0^1 n f(x)/(1 + n²x²) dx = (π/2) f(0) for continuous f.
State Vitali's convergence theorem (uniform integrability) and prove that a bounded function on [a, b] is Riemann integrable iff it is continuous almost everywhere.

units.title: Product measures and Fubini–Tonelli
objectives: Construct product measures and state Tonelli (nonnegative, σ-finite) and Fubini (integrable) precisely.

Give counterexamples: Lebesgue × counting measure on the diagonal of [0, 1]² (σ-finiteness fails), f(x, y) = (x² − y²)/(x² + y²)² on (0, 1)² (iterated integrals ±π/4), and a double series with unequal iterated sums.
Prove ∫_R e^{−x²} dx = √π and the layer-cake formula ∫ |f|^p dμ = p ∫_0^∞ t^{p−1} μ(|f| > t) dt.
Show convolution of L¹ functions is defined a.e. with ‖f ∗ g‖₁ ≤ ‖f‖₁‖g‖₁, and prove Minkowski's integral inequality.

units.title: Change of variables and regularity of measures
objectives: State the change of variables formula ∫_{G(Ω)} f = ∫_Ω (f ∘ G)·|det DG| for C¹ diffeomorphisms and outline the proof (linear case, then local approximation).
Use polar coordinates ∫_{Rⁿ} f(|x|) dx = σ(S^{n−1}) ∫_0^∞ f(r) r^{n−1} dr to compute the volume of the unit ball and decide integrability of |x|^{−a} near 0 and near ∞.
Prove that finite Borel measures on metric spaces are outer regular by open sets and inner regular by closed sets, and define Radon measures on locally compact Hausdorff spaces.
Use regularity to show C_c is dense in L¹ of a Radon measure.

units.title: Signed measures and Radon–Nikodym
objectives: Prove the Hahn and Jordan decomposition theorems and define the total variation |ν| of signed and complex measures.
Define absolute continuity and mutual singularity, and prove the ε–δ characterization of ν ≪ μ for finite ν.
State and prove the Lebesgue–Radon–Nikodym theorem for σ-finite measures (by the Hahn decomposition, or von Neumann's L² argument).
Show σ-finiteness is needed (counting measure on [0, 1] versus Lebesgue measure) and use the chain rule dν/dλ = (dν/dμ)(dμ/dλ).

units.title: Maximal function and Lebesgue differentiation
objectives: Prove the Vitali covering lemma (finite version) and the weak (1,1) bound m{Mf > α} ≤ (3ⁿ/α)‖f‖₁.
Prove the Lebesgue differentiation theorem and the existence of Lebesgue points, and deduce the Lebesgue density theorem.
Show Mf is not in L¹(Rⁿ) unless f = 0 a.e., because Mf(x) ≥ c/|x|ⁿ for large |x|.
Differentiate measures: dν/dm(x) = lim ν(B(x, r))/m(B(x, r)) a.e., and identify the singular part.

units.title: Bounded variation and absolute continuity
objectives: Define functions of bounded variation and total variation, and prove every BV function is a difference of increasing functions.
State Lebesgue's theorem that monotone (hence BV) functions are differentiable a.e., and prove the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions.
Show the Cantor function is continuous and increasing with F′ = 0 a.e. but is not absolutely continuous, and that x² sin(1/x²) is differentiable but not BV on [−1, 1].
Match normalized BV functions with complex Borel measures on R, with F absolutely continuous exactly when μ_F ≪ m.

units.title: Borel–Cantelli and the law of large numbers
objectives: Set up probability spaces, random variables, expectation and independence of σ-algebras in measure-theoretic language.
Prove both Borel–Cantelli lemmas and apply them, e.g., limsup X_n/log n = 1 a.s. for i.i.d. exponential(1) variables.
Prove the weak law via Chebyshev and the strong law under a finite fourth moment; state the strong law for i.i.d. L¹ variables and Kolmogorov's 0–1 law.
Define conditional expectation E[X | G] as a Radon–Nikodym derivative and prove its basic properties, including the tower property and conditional Jensen.

units.title: Measure and integration qual problems
objectives: Evaluate or bound limits of integrals with monotone convergence, dominated convergence and Fatou, justifying every interchange.
Prove or disprove measure-theoretic statements: if f ∈ L¹ then n·m(|f| > n) → 0; if m(E) > 0 then E − E contains an interval; if f_n → f a.e. and ‖f_n‖₁ → ‖f‖₁ then ‖f_n − f‖₁ → 0.
Solve differentiation and absolute-continuity problems, e.g., show the Lipschitz functions on [a, b] are exactly the integrals of bounded functions.

modules.title: Lᵖ, Fourier analysis, distributions
modules.summary: Work in Lᵖ spaces, use convolution and the Fourier transform, and solve basic linear PDEs with fundamental solutions and Sobolev estimates.

practice.title: Answer the real-analysis standard questions compiled by Princeton graduate students
Do the Lᵖ and Fourier problems on UCLA's past Analysis qualifying exams

units.title: Lᵖ spaces and their inequalities
objectives: Prove Hölder's, Minkowski's and Jensen's inequalities and the completeness of Lᵖ (Riesz–Fischer).
Decide inclusions: on a finite measure space L^q ⊆ Lᵖ for p < q with ‖f‖_p ≤ μ(X)^{1/p − 1/q}‖f‖_q; ℓᵖ ⊆ ℓ^q for p < q; neither inclusion holds on R.
Prove the interpolation inequality ‖f‖_r ≤ ‖f‖_p^θ ‖f‖_q^{1−θ} and lim_{p→∞} ‖f‖_p = ‖f‖_∞ on finite measure spaces.
Show simple functions and C_c are dense in Lᵖ for p < ∞ but not in L^∞, and that Lᵖ(Rⁿ) is separable for p < ∞ while L^∞ is not.

units.title: Duality of Lᵖ
objectives: Prove (Lᵖ)* ≅ L^q for 1 < p < ∞, and (L¹)* ≅ L^∞ for σ-finite measures, using Radon–Nikodym.
Show (L^∞)* is strictly larger than L¹ (Hahn–Banach or Banach limits) and L¹ is not reflexive, while Lᵖ is reflexive for 1 < p < ∞.
Use the norming formula ‖f‖_p = sup{|∫ fg| : ‖g‖_q ≤ 1} to prove inequalities.
State Clarkson's theorem that Lᵖ is uniformly convex for 1 < p < ∞.

units.title: Riesz representation for C_c(X) and C_0(X)
objectives: State the Riesz–Markov theorem: positive linear functionals on C_c(X), X locally compact Hausdorff, are integration against unique Radon measures.
Identify C_0(X)* with the finite signed (or complex) Radon measures normed by total variation.
Work examples: point evaluations δ_x, Riemann integration, and weak* convergence of measures (δ_{1/n} → δ_0, Riemann-sum measures → Lebesgue measure).
Show C[0, 1]* is not separable, and state that its unit ball is weak* compact (Banach–Alaoglu).
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, Appendix C

units.title: Convolution and approximate identities
objectives: Prove Young's inequality ‖f ∗ g‖_r ≤ ‖f‖_p‖g‖_q with 1 + 1/r = 1/p + 1/q, and that f ∗ g is uniformly continuous for f ∈ Lᵖ, g ∈ L^q conjugate (and in C_0 when 1 < p < ∞).
Show ∂^α(f ∗ φ) = f ∗ ∂^α φ for φ ∈ C_c^∞, and use mollifiers to prove C_c^∞ is dense in Lᵖ for p < ∞.
Prove approximate identities converge in Lᵖ and at every Lebesgue point when the kernels have an integrable radially decreasing majorant.
Prove Steinhaus's theorem (E − E contains an interval if m(E) > 0) from the continuity of 1_E ∗ 1_{−E}.

units.title: Fourier transform and Plancherel
objectives: Prove the L¹ Fourier transform maps into C_0 (Riemann–Lebesgue) but not onto, and compute transforms of Gaussians, e^{−|x|}, 1_[−1,1] and the Poisson and Fejér kernels.
Prove inversion on the Schwartz space and Plancherel's theorem extending the transform to a unitary map of L².
Use Fourier series on the circle: the orthonormal basis e^{inx}, Parseval, Fejér's theorem, and the existence of continuous functions with divergent Fourier series.
State and apply Hausdorff–Young, Poisson summation and the Heisenberg uncertainty inequality.

units.title: Weak Lᵖ and interpolation
objectives: Define distribution functions and weak Lᵖ, prove Chebyshev's inequality, and show Lᵖ is strictly smaller than weak Lᵖ (|x|^{−n/p}).
State Marcinkiewicz interpolation and deduce ‖Mf‖_p ≤ C_p‖f‖_p for p > 1 from the weak (1,1) and L^∞ bounds.
State Riesz–Thorin and recover Hausdorff–Young and Young's inequality as corollaries.

units.title: Distributions
objectives: Define test functions, distributions and tempered distributions, and compute distributional derivatives: H′ = δ, (log|x|)′ = p.v. 1/x, and Δ|x|^{2−n} as a multiple of δ.
Extend the Fourier transform to tempered distributions and compute the transforms of δ, 1 and p.v. 1/x (constants depend on the normalization).
State that a distribution supported at one point is a finite combination of derivatives of δ.
Define the convolution of a distribution with a test function and show it is smooth.

units.title: Fundamental solutions, heat equation and Dirichlet problem
objectives: Verify −ΔΦ = δ for Φ(x) = −(1/2π) log|x| (n = 2) and Φ(x) = |x|^{2−n}/(n(n − 2)α(n)) (n ≥ 3, α(n) the volume of the unit ball), and solve −Δu = f by u = Φ ∗ f.
Prove the mean value property and the strong maximum principle for harmonic functions, and uniqueness for the Dirichlet problem.
Solve the heat equation on Rⁿ by convolution with (4πt)^{−n/2} e^{−|x|²/4t} and prove the weak maximum principle for the heat equation on bounded domains.
Write the Poisson kernels of the ball and half-space and d'Alembert's formula, and state the Malgrange–Ehrenpreis theorem.

units.title: Sobolev spaces and embeddings
objectives: Define weak derivatives, W^{k,p}, and H^s(Rⁿ) through (1 + |ξ|²)^{s/2} f̂ ∈ L².
State the Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality (p < n, p* = np/(n − p)) and Morrey's inequality (p > n gives Hölder continuity), and prove H^s(Rⁿ) ⊆ C_0 for s > n/2 with the Fourier transform.
State the Rellich–Kondrachov compactness theorem and the Poincaré inequality on bounded domains.
Show log log(1 + 1/|x|) lies in W^{1,n} of the unit ball but is unbounded (n ≥ 2), and that W^{1,1} of an interval consists of absolutely continuous functions.

units.title: Characteristic functions and the central limit theorem
objectives: Define the characteristic function φ_X(t) = E e^{itX} as the Fourier transform of the distribution, and state Lévy's continuity theorem.
Prove the CLT for i.i.d. variables with finite variance from φ(t) = 1 − σ²t²/2 + o(t²).
Apply the CLT and Chebyshev's inequality to estimate binomial tail probabilities.

units.title: Lᵖ and Fourier qual problems
objectives: Decide Lᵖ inclusions and convergence questions on finite and infinite measure spaces, with proofs or counterexamples.
Compute Fourier transforms, use Plancherel to evaluate integrals such as ∫_R (sin x / x)² dx = π, and justify Fourier-analytic manipulations.
Solve problems on convolutions, distributions and fundamental solutions, e.g., show a tempered distribution u with Δu = 0 is a polynomial.

modules.title: Functional analysis
modules.summary: Use the main theorems about infinite-dimensional normed spaces and their operators, up to the spectral theorem and Fredholm theory, to solve problems.
refs: Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations, ch. 1–3, 5–6
Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis (2nd ed.), ch. I–III, V–VII, IX, XI

practice.title: Do the functional-analysis problems on UCLA's past Analysis qualifying exams

units.title: Normed and Banach spaces
objectives: Verify completeness of ℓᵖ, c_0, C(K) with the sup norm, and B(X, Y) when Y is complete; show C[0, 1] with the L¹ norm is not complete.
Prove that all norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent and that the closed unit ball is compact iff the dimension is finite (Riesz's lemma).
Compute operator norms of multiplication operators, integral operators with bounded kernels and shifts, and describe quotient spaces.
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, ch. III §1–§4

units.title: Hahn–Banach theorems
objectives: State and prove the analytic Hahn–Banach theorem (extension dominated by a sublinear functional) with Zorn's lemma.
Derive the normed corollaries: norming functionals, ‖x‖ = sup_{‖f‖≤1} |f(x)|, separation of points, and distance to a closed subspace.
State the geometric forms (separating an open convex set, or a compact convex set, from a closed convex set) and apply them.
Identify duals (c_0)* = ℓ¹ and (ℓ¹)* = ℓ^∞, show (ℓ^∞)* is larger than ℓ¹, and construct Banach limits.
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, ch. III §6, ch. IV §3

units.title: Baire category: uniform boundedness, open mapping, closed graph
objectives: State the Baire category theorem and prove the uniform boundedness principle, the open mapping theorem and the closed graph theorem.
Show some continuous function has a Fourier series diverging at a point, and that nowhere-differentiable functions form a residual set in C[0, 1].
Prove that two comparable complete norms are equivalent, and the Hellinger–Toeplitz theorem (an everywhere-defined symmetric operator on a Hilbert space is bounded).
Show completeness is essential: on the finitely supported sequences, the functionals x ↦ n·x_n are pointwise bounded but not uniformly bounded.
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, ch. III §12, §14

units.title: Weak topologies and Banach–Alaoglu
objectives: Define the weak and weak* topologies; show weakly convergent sequences are bounded and the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous.
Give examples: e_n ⇀ 0 in ℓ² but not in norm; sin(nx) ⇀ 0 in L²[0, 2π]; in ℓ¹ weakly convergent sequences converge in norm (Schur).
Prove Banach–Alaoglu (the unit ball of X* is weak* compact) and its sequential version for separable X.
Prove Mazur's lemma (closed convex sets are weakly closed) and state Kakutani's theorem (X reflexive iff its unit ball is weakly compact) and Eberlein–Šmulian.
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, ch. V §1–§4

units.title: Hilbert spaces
objectives: Prove the projection theorem onto closed convex sets and the Riesz representation theorem for H*.
Prove Bessel's inequality and Parseval's identity, and show every separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is isometric to ℓ².
Characterize Hilbert-space norms by the parallelogram law and show Lᵖ is not a Hilbert space for p ≠ 2.
State Lax–Milgram and use it to find weak solutions of −u″ + u = f on an interval.
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, ch. I

units.title: Compact operators
objectives: Define compact operators and prove norm limits of finite-rank operators are compact (with the converse on Hilbert space).
Show Hilbert–Schmidt integral operators with L² kernels are compact, and the identity of an infinite-dimensional space is not.
Prove Schauder's theorem (T compact iff T* compact) and that products of compact and bounded operators are compact.
Describe the spectrum of a compact operator (countable, accumulating only at 0, nonzero points are eigenvalues of finite multiplicity) and show the Volterra operator has spectrum {0}.
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, ch. II §4, ch. VI §3

units.title: Spectrum and the spectral theorem
objectives: Define spectrum and resolvent, prove the spectrum is nonempty and compact, and state the spectral radius formula r(T) = lim ‖Tⁿ‖^{1/n}.
Prove self-adjoint operators have real spectrum and ‖T‖ = sup_{‖x‖=1} |⟨Tx, x⟩|.
Prove the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators and the min–max characterization of eigenvalues, and apply them to Sturm–Liouville expansions.

State the spectral theorem for bounded self-adjoint and normal operators (multiplication-operator form, continuous functional calculus), and compute the spectra of M_x on L²[0, 1] (no eigenvalues), the unilateral shift and its adjoint.
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, ch. II §5, ch. VII §3, ch. IX §2

units.title: Fredholm alternative and index
objectives: Prove the Fredholm alternative for I − K with K compact: finite-dimensional kernel, closed range, injective iff surjective, and dim ker(I − K) = dim ker(I − K*).
Apply it to integral equations u(x) − λ∫ k(x, y) u(y) dy = f(x).
Define Fredholm operators and the index, show the unilateral shift has index −1, and state that the index is locally constant and unchanged by compact perturbations.
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, ch. XI §2–§3

units.title: Functional analysis qual problems
objectives: Decide boundedness, compactness and the spectrum of explicit multiplication, shift, diagonal and integral operators on ℓ² and L².
Prove statements with the Baire-category theorems: an infinite-dimensional Banach space has no countable Hamel basis; a linear T: X → Y with f ∘ T continuous for every f ∈ Y* is bounded.
Use weak compactness and Hilbert-space geometry: bounded sequences in reflexive spaces have weakly convergent subsequences; closed convex sets in Hilbert space have unique nearest points.
refs: Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis, ch. II–VII

modules.title: Complex analysis II
modules.summary: Prove and apply the deeper theorems of one complex variable: limits of analytic functions, conformal maps onto the disk, infinite products, Picard's theorems, special functions and first facts about Riemann surfaces.
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I (2nd ed.), ch. VII–XII

practice.title: Work the Complex Analysis (596) problems, which come with solutions, on Michigan's past QR exams
Answer the complex-analysis standard questions compiled by Princeton graduate students

units.title: Normal families and Montel's theorem
objectives: Prove Weierstrass's theorem (locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions are holomorphic and their derivatives converge) and Hurwitz's theorem (limits of zero-free or injective functions are zero-free or injective, or constant).
Prove Montel's theorem (locally bounded families are normal) from Arzelà–Ascoli and the Cauchy estimates.
Define normality of meromorphic families with the spherical metric and state Marty's theorem (normal iff the spherical derivative 2|f′|/(1 + |f|²) is locally bounded).
Decide normality of {zⁿ} on D, on {|z| > 1} (where it tends to ∞) and on a disk meeting the unit circle, and of {nz} on C.
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. VII

units.title: The Riemann mapping theorem
objectives: Prove the Riemann mapping theorem by maximizing |f′(z_0)| over injective maps into D (square-root trick, Montel, Hurwitz), and derive uniqueness from Schwarz's lemma.
Construct explicit conformal maps onto D from half-planes, strips, sectors, slit planes and lunes with Möbius maps, powers, exp, log and the Joukowski map.
State Carathéodory's boundary extension theorem for Jordan domains and the Schwarz–Christoffel formula.
Prove annuli A(r_1, R_1) and A(r_2, R_2) are conformally equivalent iff R_1/r_1 = R_2/r_2, and list Aut(D), Aut(H), Aut(C) and Aut(Ĉ).
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. VII

units.title: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
objectives: Prove the mean value property, the maximum principle and the Poisson integral formula, and solve the Dirichlet problem on the disk for continuous boundary data.
Prove Harnack's inequality and Harnack's principle, and show harmonic conjugates exist on simply connected domains but not for log|z| on an annulus.
Prove the Schwarz reflection principle for harmonic and holomorphic functions.
Define subharmonic functions and outline Perron's method, explaining when the Dirichlet problem is solvable (barriers) and why it fails on the punctured disk.
State and apply the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle on strips and sectors.
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. X

units.title: Infinite products and Weierstrass factorization
objectives: Prove Π(1 + a_n) converges absolutely when Σ|a_n| < ∞, and handle locally uniform convergence of products of holomorphic functions.
Construct entire functions with prescribed zeros from Weierstrass elementary factors E_p, and prove sin πz = πz Π(1 − z²/n²).
Prove Jensen's formula, define order and genus, and state Hadamard's factorization theorem.
Show an entire function of finite order without zeros is e^{polynomial}, and build Blaschke products for zeros in D with Σ(1 − |a_n|) < ∞.
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. VII, XI

units.title: Mittag-Leffler and partial fractions
objectives: Prove Mittag-Leffler's theorem (meromorphic functions with prescribed principal parts) and that every meromorphic function on C is a quotient of entire functions.
Derive π cot πz = 1/z + Σ_{n≥1} 2z/(z² − n²) and π²/sin² πz = Σ_n 1/(z − n)², and deduce Σ 1/n² = π²/6.
State Runge's theorem (rational approximation on compact sets, polynomial approximation when the complement is connected) and use it to build pointwise limits of polynomials that are not continuous.
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. VIII

units.title: Analytic continuation and monodromy
objectives: Define function elements, continuation along a path and germs of analytic functions.
Prove the monodromy theorem (homotopic paths give the same continuation) and deduce that log and square roots of zero-free functions exist on simply connected domains.
Show Σ z^{2ⁿ} has the unit circle as a natural boundary, and state Hadamard's gap theorem.
Build the Riemann surfaces of log z and √z from germs, and describe the continuation of √(z(z − 1)) around 0, around 1 and around both.
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. IX

units.title: Picard's theorems
objectives: State the little Picard theorem (a nonconstant entire function omits at most one value) and the great Picard theorem (near an essential singularity every value but at most one is taken infinitely often).
Outline a proof via Bloch's and Schottky's theorems, or via the modular function and monodromy.
Prove Montel's fundamental normality test (holomorphic functions omitting two fixed values form a normal family) and derive the great Picard theorem from it.
Apply Picard: e^z omits only 0; if f, g are entire with e^f + e^g = 1 then f and g are constant; an entire function avoiding (−∞, 0] is constant.
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. XII

units.title: The Gamma and zeta functions
objectives: Define Γ by Euler's integral, prove Γ(z + 1) = zΓ(z), continue Γ meromorphically with simple poles at −n of residue (−1)ⁿ/n!, and prove 1/Γ(z) = z e^{γz} Π(1 + z/n) e^{−z/n}.
Prove the reflection formula Γ(z)Γ(1 − z) = π/sin πz and Legendre duplication, and compute Γ(1/2) = √π and the Beta integral.
State Stirling's formula and the Bohr–Mollerup theorem.

Prove the Euler product for ζ(s) on Re s > 1, continue ζ to C ∖ {1} with a simple pole of residue 1, state the functional equation and the trivial zeros, compute ζ(2k) with Bernoulli numbers, and state ζ(1 + it) ≠ 0 and its link to the prime number theorem.
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. VII

units.title: Elliptic functions
objectives: Prove the basic theorems for elliptic functions with period lattice Λ: none is holomorphic and nonconstant, residues in a period parallelogram sum to 0, zeros and poles are equal in number, and their sums agree mod Λ.
Define ℘ (using convergence of Σ′|ω|^{−s} for s > 2), find its Laurent expansion, and prove (℘′)² = 4℘³ − g_2℘ − g_3 with g_2 = 60G_4 and g_3 = 140G_6.
Show the elliptic functions form the field C(℘, ℘′) and that C/Λ ≅ C/Λ′ iff Λ′ = αΛ, classified by j(τ) for τ ∈ H modulo SL_2(Z).
Describe the fundamental domain of SL_2(Z) acting on H.

units.title: First facts about Riemann surfaces
objectives: Define Riemann surfaces and holomorphic maps, with Ĉ, complex tori and smooth curves y² = f(x) as examples.
Prove the local normal form z ↦ z^k, that a nonconstant map between compact Riemann surfaces is surjective with a well-defined degree, and that meromorphic functions on Ĉ are rational.
State and apply the Riemann–Hurwitz formula 2g_X − 2 = n(2g_Y − 2) + Σ(e_p − 1), e.g., y² = (x − a_1)⋯(x − a_{2g+2}) has genus g.
State the uniformization theorem (a simply connected Riemann surface is D, C or Ĉ) and the genus (d − 1)(d − 2)/2 of a smooth plane curve of degree d.
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. IX

units.title: Complex analysis qual problems
objectives: Construct explicit conformal maps between given domains and prove nonexistence where it fails (punctured disk versus annulus, C versus D).
Solve problems with normal families, Hurwitz's theorem and Schwarz–Pick, e.g., bound |f′(0)| over a family or count zeros of a limit function.
Evaluate sums and products with Γ, ζ and partial fractions, and answer questions on elliptic functions (no elliptic function has a single simple pole in a period parallelogram).
refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I, ch. VII–XII

tiers.name: Qualifier II: geometry and topology
tiers.summary: You can pass qualifying exams in geometry and topology: compute homology, cohomology and homotopy groups, work with manifolds, differential forms, bundles and connections, and prove the classical theorems linking curvature and topology.

modules.title: Smooth manifolds
modules.summary: Work with manifolds, tangent bundles, submanifolds, flows and Lie groups, and use Sard's theorem and transversality.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2nd ed.), ch. 1–10, 19–21
Guillemin–Pollack, Differential Topology, ch. 1 and Appendix 1
Fulton–Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course, Lectures 7–10

practice.title: Work the smooth-manifolds problems on UCLA's past Geometry/Topology qualifying exams
Do the General and Differential Topology (591) problems on Michigan's past QR exams

units.title: Manifolds and smooth maps
objectives: Define topological and smooth manifolds through atlases and maximal smooth structures, and put smooth structures on Sⁿ, RPⁿ, CPⁿ, the Grassmannians G_k(Rⁿ) and GL_n(R).
Prove smooth partitions of unity exist and use them for bump functions, extension of smooth functions from closed sets, and existence of Riemannian metrics.

Define manifolds with boundary and diffeomorphisms; show the line with two origins is locally Euclidean but not Hausdorff, and state that R has one smooth structure up to diffeomorphism while S⁷ has exotic ones (Milnor).
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 1–2

units.title: Tangent spaces and vector bundles
objectives: Define T_pM as derivations and the differential dF_p, compute dF in coordinates, and show TM is a smooth 2n-manifold.
Define vector bundles by local trivializations and transition functions satisfying the cocycle condition, and build T*M, E*, E ⊕ F, E ⊗ F, Λ^kE and pullbacks.

Show TS¹ and TS³ are trivial (Lie groups are parallelizable), the Möbius line bundle and the tautological line bundle over RPⁿ are nontrivial, and state that TS² is nontrivial (proved later by the hairy ball theorem).
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 3, 10, 11

units.title: Immersions, submersions and submanifolds
objectives: State and apply the constant rank theorem and the local normal forms of immersions and submersions.
Distinguish injective immersions from embeddings (figure eight, dense line on the torus) and prove an injective immersion of a compact manifold is an embedding.
Prove the regular value theorem and show Sⁿ, O(n) and SL_n(R) are embedded submanifolds, with T_I O(n) the skew-symmetric matrices and dim O(n) = n(n − 1)/2.
Show T_p(F⁻¹(c)) = ker dF_p, and state Ehresmann's theorem that a proper surjective submersion is a fiber bundle.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 4–5

units.title: Sard's theorem, transversality and Morse functions
objectives: State Sard's theorem (critical values have measure zero) with a proof idea, and deduce that regular values are dense and that there is no smooth retraction Dⁿ → S^{n−1}.
Define transversality of a map to a submanifold, prove the preimage of a transverse submanifold is a submanifold of the same codimension, and state the parametric transversality theorem.
Define Morse functions, state the Morse lemma, and prove f(x) + a·x is Morse for almost every a.
List the stable properties: local diffeomorphisms, immersions, submersions, transversality, and embeddings of compact manifolds.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 6

units.title: Whitney embedding and tubular neighborhoods
objectives: Prove the easy Whitney theorems (a compact n-manifold embeds in R^{2n+1} and immerses in R^{2n}) with Sard, and state the strong versions R^{2n} and R^{2n−1}.
State Whitney approximation: continuous maps are homotopic to smooth ones, and homotopic smooth maps are smoothly homotopic.
Construct the normal bundle, prove the tubular neighborhood (ε-neighborhood) theorem, and deduce every manifold is a retract of an open subset of R^N.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 6

units.title: Vector fields, flows and Lie derivatives
objectives: Define vector fields as derivations, the Lie bracket [X, Y] and F-related fields, and compute brackets in coordinates.
State the fundamental theorem on flows, prove compactly supported fields are complete, and show x² ∂/∂x on R is not complete.
Prove L_X Y = [X, Y], that flows commute iff [X, Y] = 0, and the canonical form of a vector field near a nonzero point.
Use flows to prove that diffeomorphisms isotopic to the identity act transitively on a connected manifold.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 8–9

units.title: Distributions and the Frobenius theorem
objectives: Define distributions (subbundles of TM), involutivity and integral manifolds, and prove the local Frobenius theorem.
State the global Frobenius theorem (foliations) and the correspondence between Lie subalgebras and connected Lie subgroups.
Show the plane field spanned by ∂_x + y∂_z and ∂_y on R³ is not involutive (a contact structure), while the span of two commuting fields is integrable.
Solve overdetermined systems ∂u/∂x = f(x, y, u), ∂u/∂y = g(x, y, u) using the integrability condition.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 19
J. M. Lee, Manifolds and Differential Geometry, ch. 11

units.title: Matrix Lie groups and the exponential map
objectives: Define Lie groups, left-invariant vector fields and the Lie algebra T_eG, and compute gl_n, sl_n, so(n), u(n) and su(n) with their dimensions.
Prove t ↦ exp(tX) gives the one-parameter subgroups and exp is a local diffeomorphism near 0, and state the closed subgroup theorem.
Decide compactness and connectedness of O(n), SO(n), U(n), SU(n) and SL_n(R), and show SU(2) ≅ S³ double covers SO(3) ≅ RP³.
Show exp: sl_2(R) → SL_2(R) is not surjective (diag(−2, −1/2) is missed), and state that exp is surjective for compact connected groups.
Use the Lie correspondence for simply connected groups, left-invariant (Maurer–Cartan) forms and homogeneous spaces such as Sⁿ = SO(n + 1)/SO(n).
keyTerms: Lie algebra of a Lie group
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 7, 8, 20, 21

units.title: Nilpotent, solvable and semisimple Lie algebras
objectives: Define ideals, the derived and lower central series, and solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras, with upper triangular b_n (solvable) and strictly upper triangular n_n (nilpotent) as models.
State Engel's theorem and Lie's theorem and use them to triangularize.
Define the Killing form, state Cartan's criteria (solvable iff B(g, [g, g]) = 0; semisimple iff B is nondegenerate), and show a semisimple Lie algebra is a sum of simple ideals.
Classify the irreducible representations of sl_2(C) by highest weight: dimension n + 1 with weights n, n − 2, …, −n.

units.title: Smooth manifolds qual problems
objectives: Prove given sets are embedded submanifolds and compute their dimensions and tangent spaces, e.g., n × n real matrices of rank k form a manifold of dimension k(2n − k).
Answer questions on flows, brackets and Frobenius, e.g., find the integral surfaces of a plane field or decide whether two vector fields are simultaneously straightened.
Compute Lie algebras, exponentials and the topology of matrix groups, e.g., π_0 and π_1 of SO(n), U(n) and SL_2(R).
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 4–9, 19–21

modules.title: Differential forms and de Rham
modules.summary: Integrate differential forms, compute de Rham cohomology, and count zeros, fixed points and preimages with degree and intersection numbers.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2nd ed.), ch. 11, 14–17
Bott–Tu, Differential Forms in Algebraic Topology, ch. I (§1–§7)

practice.title: Do the differential-topology and de Rham problems on UCLA's past Geometry/Topology qualifying exams

units.title: Differential forms and the exterior derivative
objectives: Define alternating tensors, the wedge product, k-forms and pullbacks F*, and compute F*ω in coordinates.
Characterize d by d² = 0, the Leibniz rule and naturality F*dω = dF*ω, and translate grad, curl and div on R³ into d.
Prove Cartan's formula L_X = d ι_X + ι_X d and use it to compute Lie derivatives of forms.
State the forms version of Frobenius (ker θ is integrable iff θ ∧ dθ = 0) and show dθ on R² ∖ {0} is closed but not exact.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 11, 14
