units.title: Orientation, integration and Stokes's theorem
objectives: Define orientations by oriented atlases and nowhere-vanishing top forms, and show RPⁿ is orientable iff n is odd.
Define ∫_M ω with partitions of unity and prove Stokes's theorem ∫_M dω = ∫_{∂M} ω with the outward-normal-first boundary orientation.
Recover the theorems of Green, Gauss and classical Stokes, and show a volume form on a closed manifold is not exact.
Integrate on Riemannian manifolds with the volume form and prove the divergence theorem.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 15–16

units.title: De Rham cohomology and the Poincaré lemma
objectives: Define H^k_dR(M), prove functoriality and homotopy invariance with a homotopy operator, and prove the Poincaré lemma for star-shaped domains.
Derive the Mayer–Vietoris sequence for forms and compute H*_dR of Sⁿ, Tⁿ, Rⁿ ∖ {0}, punctured surfaces and RPⁿ (R in degree 0, and in degree n when n is odd).
Show H⁰ counts components, H¹ vanishes on simply connected manifolds, and integration gives H^n_dR(M) ≅ R for M closed, connected and oriented (and 0 if M is nonorientable).
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 17

units.title: Compact supports, Poincaré duality and Künneth
objectives: Define compactly supported cohomology H*_c, compute H*_c(Rⁿ), and derive Mayer–Vietoris for compact supports.
Prove Poincaré duality H^k(M) ≅ (H_c^{n−k}(M))* for oriented manifolds with a finite good cover by the Mayer–Vietoris argument, and prove the Künneth formula the same way.
Define the Poincaré dual of a closed oriented submanifold and state the Thom isomorphism for oriented vector bundles.
Deduce χ(M) = 0 for closed odd-dimensional M, and compare H*_c of the open cylinder (R in degrees 1 and 2) with the open Möbius band (all zero).
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 17

units.title: Degree of smooth maps
objectives: Define the degree of a smooth map between closed oriented n-manifolds by ∫_M F*ω = deg F · ∫_N ω and by signed counts of preimages, and prove they agree and are homotopy invariant.
Compute degrees: z ↦ z^k on S¹, the antipodal map of Sⁿ ((−1)^{n+1}), reflections, and the map of Ĉ = S² given by a rational function (its algebraic degree).
Prove the hairy ball theorem and the fundamental theorem of algebra with degree, and compute linking numbers with the Gauss integral.
Define the mod 2 degree and state the Hopf degree theorem: maps Sⁿ → Sⁿ are classified up to homotopy by degree.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 17

units.title: Intersection numbers and Lefschetz numbers
objectives: Define mod 2 and oriented intersection numbers I(f, Z) for f transverse to Z with dim M + dim Z = dim N, and prove homotopy invariance.
Prove I(Δ, Δ) = χ(M), and define the Lefschetz number L(f) = I(Δ, graph f) with local index sign det(df_x − I) at a nondegenerate fixed point.
Use mod 2 intersection theory to prove the Jordan–Brouwer separation theorem and the Borsuk–Ulam theorem.

units.title: Vector-field indices and Poincaré–Hopf
objectives: Define the index of an isolated zero of a vector field as the degree of v/|v| on a small sphere, and compute indices of sources, sinks, saddles, z^k (index k) and z̄^k (index −k).
State and outline the proof of the Poincaré–Hopf theorem Σ ind = χ(M), and deduce χ(S^{2n}) = 2 and the hairy ball theorem.
Compute χ of surfaces from gradient fields of height functions, and relate it to Morse functions: χ(M) = Σ (−1)^{index} over critical points.

units.title: Forms and de Rham qual problems
objectives: Compute de Rham cohomology of explicit manifolds (complements, products, quotients, surfaces) with Mayer–Vietoris, Künneth and homotopy invariance.
Evaluate integrals of forms with Stokes (e.g., ∫_{S²} x dy ∧ dz = 4π/3) and decide whether explicit closed forms are exact.
Use degree, Lefschetz numbers and Poincaré–Hopf to prove existence of fixed points, zeros of vector fields or solutions of equations.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 16–17

modules.title: Homology
modules.summary: Compute the homology of spaces built from cells, and use it to prove classical fixed-point and separation theorems.
refs: Bredon, Topology and Geometry, ch. IV

practice.title: Do the chapter 2 exercises in Hatcher's freely available Algebraic Topology
Work the Algebraic Topology (592) problems on Michigan's past QR exams

units.title: CW complexes
objectives: Build CW structures by attaching cells, with small structures on Sⁿ, RPⁿ, CPⁿ, T², the genus-g surface (one 0-cell, 2g 1-cells, one 2-cell) and the Klein bottle.
Use the homotopy extension property of CW pairs to show X → X/A is a homotopy equivalence when A is a contractible subcomplex, and X ∪ CA ≃ X/A.
Describe CW structures on products, wedges, suspensions and mapping cylinders, and state the cellular approximation theorem.

units.title: Simplicial and singular homology
objectives: Compute simplicial homology of Δ-complex structures on T², RP² and the Klein bottle.
Define singular chains, ∂² = 0, H_n(X) and reduced homology, and prove H_0 is free on the path components.
Prove homotopy invariance with the prism operator, using that chain-homotopic maps induce equal maps on homology.
Prove H_1(X) ≅ π_1(X)^ab for path-connected X (Hurewicz in degree 1).

units.title: Long exact sequences and excision
objectives: Derive the long exact sequences of a pair and of a triple from short exact sequences of chain complexes, with the explicit connecting map.
State excision, outline its proof by barycentric subdivision, and show H_n(X, A) ≅ H̃_n(X/A) for good pairs.
Compute H̃_k(Sⁿ) and H_k(Dⁿ, S^{n−1}), and prove the Brouwer fixed point theorem and invariance of dimension (R^m ≇ Rⁿ for m ≠ n) with local homology.
State the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms and the equivalence of simplicial and singular homology.
keyTerms: long exact sequence of a pair

units.title: Degree of maps between spheres
objectives: Define the degree of f: Sⁿ → Sⁿ through H_n and prove: reflections have degree −1, the antipodal map has degree (−1)^{n+1}, and a map without fixed points is homotopic to the antipodal map.
Prove the hairy ball theorem (Sⁿ has a nowhere-zero vector field iff n is odd) and that only Z/2 can act freely on S^{2k}.
Compute degrees as sums of local degrees over preimages, and show suspension preserves degree.

units.title: Cellular homology
objectives: Build the cellular chain complex H_n(Xⁿ, X^{n−1}) and compute its boundary maps with the cellular boundary formula (degrees of attach-then-collapse maps).
Compute H_* of CPⁿ, RPⁿ (Z in degree 0, Z/2 in odd degrees below n, Z in degree n if n is odd, else 0), Tⁿ, genus-g surfaces, the Klein bottle, Sⁿ × S^m and lens spaces (Z, Z/m, 0, Z).
Prove χ(X) = Σ (−1)ⁿ (number of n-cells) = Σ (−1)ⁿ rank H_n(X), and construct Moore spaces M(G, n).

units.title: Mayer–Vietoris sequences
objectives: Derive the absolute, reduced and relative Mayer–Vietoris sequences and describe their maps.
Compute homology of spheres, tori, wedges (H̃(X ∨ Y) = H̃(X) ⊕ H̃(Y)), connected sums, the Klein bottle as two Möbius bands, and Sⁿ minus k points.
Prove the suspension isomorphism H̃_{n+1}(SX) ≅ H̃_n(X), and compute H̃_*(Sⁿ ∖ h(S^k)) ≅ H̃_*(S^{n−k−1}) for an embedded sphere.

units.title: Coefficients and Euler characteristic
objectives: Define H_*(X; G) and compute H_*(RPⁿ; Z/2) (Z/2 in every degree 0 to n) and the homology of surfaces with Z/2 and Q coefficients.
Prove χ does not depend on the coefficient field and is multiplicative under finite covers: χ(X̃) = n·χ(X).
Show the closed orientable surface Σ_g covers Σ_h (h ≥ 1) iff g − 1 = n(h − 1) for some n ≥ 1, and that the orientation double cover doubles χ.

units.title: Classical applications of homology
objectives: Prove the Borsuk–Ulam theorem (odd maps Sⁿ → Sⁿ have odd degree, so there is no antipode-preserving map Sⁿ → S^{n−1}) and deduce the ham sandwich theorem.
Prove the Jordan–Brouwer separation theorem and invariance of domain.
Show a commutative division algebra with identity on Rⁿ exists only for n = 1, 2, and prove that any cover of Sⁿ by n + 1 closed sets has a set containing antipodal points (Lusternik–Schnirelmann).

units.title: Simplicial approximation and the Lefschetz fixed point theorem
objectives: State the simplicial approximation theorem and the Lefschetz fixed point theorem for retracts of finite simplicial complexes, with L(f) = Σ (−1)^k tr(f_* on H_k(X; Q)).
Compute L(f): every map RP^{2k} → RP^{2k} has a fixed point; a map of T² with matrix A has L(f) = det(I − A); a map Sⁿ → Sⁿ of degree ≠ (−1)^{n+1} has a fixed point.
Show every map homotopic to the identity of a compact polyhedron with χ ≠ 0 has a fixed point, and note that translation of R has L = 1 but no fixed point (compactness matters).

units.title: Homology qual problems
objectives: Compute the homology of explicit spaces (polygon quotients, CW complexes, complements of circles or knots in S³, products, mapping tori) with full justification.
Prove nonexistence results with homology: no retraction, no embedding, no covering map between given spaces.
Answer fixed-point, degree and Euler-characteristic questions: which surfaces cover which, and which self-maps of Sⁿ, T² or RP^{2k} must have fixed points.

modules.title: Cohomology and homotopy
modules.summary: Use cohomology rings, Poincaré duality and homotopy groups to tell spaces apart, count fixed points and compute with fibrations.
refs: Bredon, Topology and Geometry, ch. V–VII
Bott–Tu, Differential Forms in Algebraic Topology, §8–§10
Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2nd ed.), ch. 18

practice.title: Do the chapter 3 and 4 exercises in Hatcher's Algebraic Topology
Work the algebraic-topology problems on Harvard's past written qualifying exams

units.title: Cohomology and universal coefficients
objectives: Define singular and cellular cohomology H^n(X; G) with the long exact sequence of a pair and Mayer–Vietoris.
State the universal coefficient theorem 0 → Ext(H_{n−1}X, G) → H^n(X; G) → Hom(H_nX, G) → 0 (split, but not naturally) and its homology version with Tor.
Compute H*(RPⁿ; Z), H*(RPⁿ; Z/2), H* of lens spaces and of the Klein bottle, noting that torsion moves up one degree in cohomology.

units.title: Cup products and cohomology rings
objectives: Define the cup product, prove graded commutativity and naturality, and state the Künneth formula H*(X × Y; F) ≅ H*(X; F) ⊗ H*(Y; F) for a field F and spaces of finite type.
Compute H*(Tⁿ; Z) as an exterior algebra, H*(RPⁿ; Z/2) = Z/2[α]/(α^{n+1}), H*(CPⁿ; Z) = Z[α]/(α^{n+1}) and H*(RP^∞; Z/2) = Z/2[α].
Distinguish spaces with rings: S² ∨ S⁴ versus CP², RP³ versus RP² ∨ S³, T² versus S¹ ∨ S¹ ∨ S²; show cup products vanish on suspensions.
Prove Borsuk–Ulam with cup products (no map RPⁿ → RP^m with m < n is nonzero on H¹(−; Z/2)), and state Adams's Hopf invariant one theorem: the spheres that are H-spaces are S⁰, S¹, S³ and S⁷.
refs: Hatcher ch. 4, additional topic 'The Hopf Invariant'

units.title: Poincaré duality
objectives: Define R-orientations through local homology, the fundamental class [M] and the cap product, and state Poincaré duality: capping with [M] gives H^k(M; R) ≅ H_{n−k}(M; R) for closed R-orientable M (every closed M when R = Z/2).
Prove the cup-product pairing is nondegenerate mod torsion (unimodular intersection form) and use it to derive the ring H*(CPⁿ) and χ(M) = 0 for closed odd-dimensional M.
Define the signature of a closed oriented 4k-manifold and state Lefschetz duality and Alexander duality H̃_i(Sⁿ ∖ K) ≅ H̃^{n−i−1}(K).
Show RP^{2k} (odd Euler characteristic) and CP^{2k} (signature 1, using Thom's theorem) are not boundaries of compact manifolds.

units.title: Lefschetz numbers from cohomology rings
objectives: Compute L(f) from the induced ring map: if f*(α) = dα on CPⁿ then L(f) = 1 + d + ⋯ + dⁿ, so every self-map of CP^{2k} has a fixed point.
Interpret L(f) as the intersection of the graph of f with the diagonal (sum of local indices, the Lefschetz–Hopf theorem) and recover χ(M) = L(id) and Poincaré–Hopf.
Give fixed-point-free maps where L(f) = 0: rotations of tori, the antipodal map of S^{2k+1}, and [z_0 : z_1 : …] ↦ [−z̄_1 : z̄_0 : …] on CP^{2k+1}.

units.title: De Rham, Čech and singular cohomology
objectives: Define the integration map from forms to smooth singular cochains and use Stokes's theorem to show it is a chain map.
State and outline the proof of the de Rham theorem H^k_dR(M) ≅ H^k(M; R), as rings, by Mayer–Vietoris induction over good covers.
Set up Čech cohomology of a good cover and the Čech–de Rham double complex, and state singular ≅ Čech ≅ de Rham with real coefficients.
Explain what de Rham cohomology misses (H²(RP²; Z) = Z/2 but H²_dR(RP²) = 0) and which classes have integral periods.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 18

units.title: Higher homotopy groups
objectives: Define πₙ(X, x_0) and relative homotopy groups, prove πₙ is abelian for n ≥ 2, and derive the long exact sequence of a pair.
Use cellular approximation to show π_k(Sⁿ) = 0 for k < n, and prove Whitehead's theorem (a weak equivalence of CW complexes is a homotopy equivalence).
Show πₙ(X̃) ≅ πₙ(X) for n ≥ 2 for a covering space (so πₙ(S¹) = 0 and πₙ(RP^m) ≅ πₙ(S^m) for n ≥ 2), and that Whitehead fails beyond CW complexes (the Warsaw circle).
State the Freudenthal suspension theorem and the values πₙ(Sⁿ) = Z, π_3(S²) = Z and π_{n+1}(Sⁿ) = Z/2 for n ≥ 3.

units.title: Fiber bundles, fibrations and their exact sequence
objectives: Define fiber bundles and Serre fibrations, prove the homotopy lifting property for bundles, and derive the exact sequence ⋯ → πₙ(F) → πₙ(E) → πₙ(B) → π_{n−1}(F) → ⋯.
Apply it to the Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S² (π_2(S²) = Z and πₙ(S³) ≅ πₙ(S²) for n ≥ 3), to S¹ → S^∞ → CP^∞, and to the path–loop fibration (πₙ(ΩX) ≅ π_{n+1}(X)).
Use SO(n) → SO(n + 1) → Sⁿ and U(n) → U(n + 1) → S^{2n+1} to compute π_1(SO(n)) = Z/2 for n ≥ 3 and π_1(U(n)) = Z.
Show S² and S³ × CP^∞ have isomorphic homotopy groups but are not homotopy equivalent, and state the Leray–Hirsch theorem and the Serre spectral sequence.
keyTerms: long exact sequence of a fibration
refs: Hatcher ch. 4, additional topic 'Cohomology of Fiber Bundles'

units.title: Hurewicz theorem and Eilenberg–MacLane spaces
objectives: State the Hurewicz theorem (if X is (n − 1)-connected with n ≥ 2, then H̃_i(X) = 0 for i < n and πₙ(X) ≅ Hₙ(X)) and its relative version.
Deduce: a simply connected CW complex with trivial reduced homology is contractible; a simply connected closed 3-manifold is a homotopy sphere; πₙ(Sⁿ) ≅ Z.
Construct Eilenberg–MacLane spaces K(G, n), show uniqueness up to homotopy, recognize S¹, RP^∞, CP^∞ and closed surfaces other than S² and RP² as examples, and state Hⁿ(X; G) ≅ [X, K(G, n)].
Describe Postnikov towers and obstruction theory in outline.

units.title: Cohomology and homotopy qual problems
objectives: Compute cohomology rings of explicit spaces (products, wedges, projective spaces, surfaces, connected sums) and use them to rule out homotopy equivalences, retractions and maps of nonzero degree.
Use Poincaré duality and universal coefficients to fill in the homology of a closed manifold from partial data, e.g., the torsion of H_2 of a closed orientable 4-manifold equals the torsion of H_1.
Compute low-dimensional homotopy groups with covering spaces and fibrations, e.g., π_2(S¹ ∨ S²) ≅ Z[t, t⁻¹] and π_3(S² × RP³) ≅ Z ⊕ Z.

modules.title: Bundles and connections
modules.summary: Describe principal and associated bundles, differentiate sections with connections, and use curvature and holonomy to decide when a bundle is flat.
refs: Taubes, Differential Geometry: Bundles, Connections, Metrics and Curvature, ch. 10–14
J. M. Lee, Manifolds and Differential Geometry (GSM 107), ch. 6, 12
Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds (2nd ed.), ch. 10

practice.title: Work the differential-geometry problems on Harvard's past written qualifying exams

units.title: Fiber bundles and principal bundles
objectives: Define fiber bundles with structure group, principal G-bundles (free right action with local triviality) and their transition functions g_αβ with the cocycle condition.
Give examples: the frame bundle of a vector bundle, the Hopf bundle S³ → S² as a principal U(1)-bundle, S^{2n+1} → CPⁿ, and G → G/H as a principal H-bundle.
Prove a principal bundle is trivial iff it has a global section, and classify principal U(1)-bundles over S² by an integer through clutching maps S¹ → U(1).
Describe pullbacks and reductions of structure group (a metric reduces GL_n to O(n); an orientation reduces it to GL_n⁺).
refs: J. M. Lee, Manifolds and Differential Geometry, ch. 6

units.title: Associated bundles and bundle metrics
objectives: Construct P ×_G F and P ×_ρ V for a representation ρ, and show rank-n vector bundles correspond to principal GL_n-bundles.
Identify sections of P ×_ρ V with ρ-equivariant maps P → V.
Build line bundles on S² = CP¹ from characters of U(1) on the Hopf bundle (the tautological bundle; TS² corresponds to O(2)), and prove every vector bundle has a metric.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, ch. 10

units.title: Covariant derivatives and connections
objectives: Define a covariant derivative ∇ on a vector bundle (Leibniz rule), write ∇ = d + A in a local frame, and derive the gauge transformation A ↦ g⁻¹Ag + g⁻¹dg.
Show connections exist (partition of unity), form an affine space over Ω¹(End E), and induce connections on E*, E ⊗ F, Hom(E, F) and pullbacks.

Define principal connections as Lie-algebra-valued 1-forms ω with R_g*ω = Ad(g⁻¹)ω and ω(ξ^#) = ξ (equivalently, invariant horizontal distributions), and match them with covariant derivatives on associated bundles.
Define metric-compatible connections and show they exist.
refs: J. M. Lee, Manifolds and Differential Geometry, ch. 12

units.title: Curvature of connections
objectives: Define the curvature F_∇ = ∇² as an End(E)-valued 2-form, derive F = dA + A ∧ A and F ↦ g⁻¹Fg, and prove the Bianchi identity d_∇F = 0.
Write the curvature Ω = dω + ½[ω ∧ ω] of a principal connection and interpret it as the obstruction to integrability of the horizontal distribution.
Compute the curvature of the standard U(1) connection on the Hopf bundle and show (i/2π)∫_{S²} F = ±1, the sign fixed by convention.
refs: J. M. Lee, Manifolds and Differential Geometry, ch. 12

units.title: Parallel transport, holonomy and flat connections
objectives: Define parallel transport along curves as the solution of a linear ODE, the holonomy group Hol_p(∇) and the restricted holonomy group.
Show transport around a small loop spanning a parallelogram is I − F(X, Y)·(area) + o(area), and state the Ambrose–Singer theorem.
Prove a connection is flat iff the bundle has local parallel frames, and that flat G-bundles over a connected M correspond to homomorphisms π_1(M) → G up to conjugacy.
Compute holonomy for the Möbius line bundle (−1), flat U(1)-bundles over T² (Hom(Z², U(1))), and TS² with the connection induced from R³ (rotation by the enclosed area).

units.title: Chern–Weil theory in brief
objectives: Show tr(F^k) and det(I + (i/2π)F) are closed forms whose cohomology classes do not depend on the connection.
Define the first Chern class c_1(L) = [(i/2π)F] of a complex line bundle and compute ∫_{S²} c_1 = −1 for the tautological bundle (with the usual convention).
State the Gauss–Bonnet–Chern theorem relating the Euler class (Pfaffian of the curvature) to χ(M).

units.title: Bundles and connections qual problems
objectives: Compute connection and curvature forms of explicit connections (trivial bundles, the Hopf bundle, line bundles over surfaces) and check gauge covariance.
Decide flatness and compute holonomy of given connections, and classify flat bundles over tori and surfaces through representations of π_1.
Prove standard facts: a bundle over a contractible base is trivial; a line bundle with a flat connection of trivial holonomy is trivial.
refs: J. M. Lee, Manifolds and Differential Geometry, ch. 6, 12

modules.title: Riemannian geometry
modules.summary: Compute with metrics, geodesics and curvature, and prove the classical theorems that link curvature to topology.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds (2nd ed.), ch. 2–12

practice.title: Read Princeton generals reports with Riemannian geometry as a special topic and answer their questions aloud
Work the differential-geometry problems on Harvard's past written qualifying exams

units.title: Riemannian metrics and the Levi-Civita connection
objectives: Define Riemannian metrics, isometries and local isometries, and write the round sphere, flat tori and hyperbolic space in the upper half-space, Poincaré ball and hyperboloid models.
Prove the fundamental theorem: there is a unique torsion-free metric connection, given by the Koszul formula, with Γ^k_ij = ½ g^{kl}(∂_i g_jl + ∂_j g_il − ∂_l g_ij).
Show parallel transport is an isometry and that the Levi-Civita connection of a submanifold of R^N is the tangential projection of the ambient derivative.
Compute Christoffel symbols for polar coordinates, surfaces of revolution and the hyperbolic plane.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, ch. 2–5

units.title: Geodesics and the exponential map
objectives: Derive the geodesic equation, prove local existence and uniqueness, and find the geodesics of Sⁿ (great circles), Rⁿ and the hyperbolic plane (vertical lines and semicircles orthogonal to the boundary).
Define the exponential map and normal coordinates (g_ij(p) = δ_ij and Γ^k_ij(p) = 0), and prove the Gauss lemma.
Prove that geodesics locally minimize length and that the Riemannian distance induces the manifold topology, and state the existence of convex neighborhoods.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, ch. 5–6

units.title: Curvature tensors
objectives: Define R(X, Y)Z, prove its symmetries and the first and second Bianchi identities, and show sectional curvature determines R.
Define Ricci and scalar curvature and Einstein metrics, and compute the curvatures of Sⁿ (K = 1), Hⁿ (K = −1), flat tori and S² × S² (where mixed planes have K = 0).
Use the constant-curvature formula R(X, Y)Z = K(⟨Y, Z⟩X − ⟨X, Z⟩Y) and, in dimension 2, the conformal change formula: g̃ = e^{2u}g gives K̃ = e^{−2u}(K − Δu).
Define the second fundamental form, prove the Gauss equation and deduce Gauss's Theorema Egregium.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, ch. 7–8

units.title: Completeness and the Hopf–Rinow theorem
objectives: State and prove the Hopf–Rinow theorem (metric completeness, geodesic completeness and compactness of closed bounded sets are equivalent, and then any two points are joined by a minimizing geodesic).
Show compact and homogeneous Riemannian manifolds are complete, and that Riemannian covers of complete manifolds are complete.
Give incomplete examples (R² ∖ {0}, the open disk with the Euclidean metric), show minimizing geodesics need not be unique, and define the cut locus (the antipodal point on Sⁿ).
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, ch. 6

units.title: Jacobi fields and conjugate points
objectives: Derive the Jacobi equation D_t²J + R(J, γ′)γ′ = 0 from geodesic variations and solve it in constant curvature K (normal Jacobi fields proportional to sin(√K t)/√K, t, or sinh(√−K t)/√−K).
Define conjugate points and prove d(exp_p) is singular exactly at conjugate points (at distance π on the unit sphere; never when K ≤ 0).
Derive the first and second variation formulas, define the index form, and prove a geodesic stops minimizing after its first conjugate point.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, ch. 10

units.title: Positive curvature: Bonnet–Myers and Synge
objectives: Prove Bonnet–Myers: a complete manifold with Ric ≥ (n − 1)k > 0 has diameter ≤ π/√k, so it is compact with finite fundamental group.

Prove Synge's theorem (compact, even-dimensional, orientable, K > 0 implies simply connected; odd-dimensional with K > 0 implies orientable) by second variation along a closed geodesic, and state Weinstein's fixed-point theorem behind it.
Apply them: S¹ × S² and Tⁿ admit no metric of positive Ricci curvature; RP^{2n} shows orientability is needed in Synge; the paraboloid shows the uniform positive bound is needed in Myers.
State Cheng's maximal diameter theorem as the rigidity case.
keyTerms: closed geodesic in a free homotopy class
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, ch. 11–12

units.title: Nonpositive curvature and comparison theorems
objectives: Prove Cartan–Hadamard: for complete M with K ≤ 0, exp_p: T_pM → M is a covering map, so the universal cover is diffeomorphic to Rⁿ and π_k(M) = 0 for k ≥ 2.
Deduce that π_1 of a compact manifold with K ≤ 0 is torsion-free (via Cartan's fixed point theorem, stated) and that S² × S¹ and RPⁿ (n ≥ 2) admit no metric with K ≤ 0.
State Preissman's theorem (compact with K < 0: abelian subgroups of π_1 are cyclic) and deduce T² × N admits no metric with K < 0 for compact N.
State the Rauch comparison theorem, Bishop–Gromov volume comparison and Toponogov's theorem.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, ch. 11–12

units.title: Space forms and Gauss–Bonnet
objectives: Prove Cartan's theorem that curvature determines the metric locally, and show a simply connected complete manifold of constant curvature is Sⁿ, Rⁿ or Hⁿ up to scale.
Describe space forms as quotients M̃/Γ by free, properly discontinuous isometry groups: lens spaces, flat tori (Bieberbach's theorem, stated) and hyperbolic surfaces of genus ≥ 2.
State and apply the Gauss–Bonnet theorem ∫_M K dA + ∫_{∂M} k_g ds + Σ exterior angles = 2πχ(M), and compute Isom(Sⁿ) = O(n + 1) and Isom⁺(H²) = PSL_2(R).
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, ch. 3, 9, 12

units.title: Riemannian geometry qual problems
objectives: Compute Christoffel symbols, geodesics and sectional curvatures of explicit metrics (warped products, surfaces of revolution, left-invariant metrics on S³ or the Heisenberg group).
Decide which manifolds admit metrics with K > 0, K ≤ 0, Ric > 0 or K ≡ 0 using Bonnet–Myers, Synge, Cartan–Hadamard, Preissman and Gauss–Bonnet.

Prove standard facts: a local isometry from a complete connected manifold to a connected manifold is a covering map; an isometry of a connected manifold that fixes a point and has identity differential there is the identity.
refs: Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, ch. 5–12

tiers.name: Advanced graduate I
tiers.summary: You can work with the algebra behind modern number theory and geometry: ideals and rings, shapes cut out by polynomial equations, number fields and the counting of primes, elliptic curves and modular forms, and the symmetry algebras of Lie theory. This is the algebra half of a typical PhD qualifying exam.

modules.title: Commutative algebra
modules.summary: Work with ideals, fractions, dimension and completion in the rings that underlie algebraic geometry and number theory.
refs: Atiyah–Macdonald, Introduction to Commutative Algebra, ch. 1–11
Eisenbud, Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry (GTM 150), ch. 1–13 and 17–19

practice.title: Macaulay2: compute radicals, primary decompositions, dimensions and Hilbert series of ideals

units.title: Localization, local rings and Spec
objectives: Construct the localization S⁻¹M and prove that localization is exact.
State and apply Nakayama's lemma to finitely generated modules over local rings.
Describe Spec ℤ, Spec k[x] and Spec ℤ[x] with their Zariski topologies, including generic points.
Prove that the nilradical is the intersection of all prime ideals and the Jacobson radical the intersection of maximal ideals.
Show that a module is zero if and only if all its localizations at maximal ideals are zero.
refs: Atiyah–Macdonald, ch. 1 (Rings and Ideals) and ch. 3 (Rings and Modules of Fractions)

units.title: Noetherian rings and the Nullstellensatz
objectives: Prove the Hilbert basis theorem.
State Zariski's lemma and derive the weak Nullstellensatz from it.
Deduce the strong Nullstellensatz with the Rabinowitsch trick.
Describe the bijection between radical ideals of k[x₁,…,xₙ] and affine algebraic sets over an algebraically closed field k.
Show that an Artinian ring is Noetherian of dimension 0 and a finite product of Artin local rings.
refs: Atiyah–Macdonald, ch. 6 (Chain Conditions), ch. 7 (Noetherian Rings) and ch. 8 (Artin Rings)
Eisenbud, ch. 4 (Integral Dependence and the Nullstellensatz)

units.title: Primary decomposition and associated primes
objectives: Define primary ideals and show that a power of a prime ideal need not be primary.
Prove the Lasker–Noether theorem: every ideal of a Noetherian ring has a primary decomposition.
State the first and second uniqueness theorems for minimal primary decompositions.
Compute a minimal primary decomposition of (x², xy) in k[x, y] and identify its embedded prime.
Show that the zero divisors on a finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring form the union of its associated primes.
refs: Eisenbud, ch. 3 (Associated Primes and Primary Decomposition)

units.title: Integral extensions, going-up and going-down
objectives: Show that the integral elements over a ring form a subring, using the finite-module criterion.
State and prove lying over and going-up for integral extensions.
State going-down with its hypotheses (normal base, domain extension) and give a counterexample when normality fails.
State Noether normalization and use it to compute the dimension of an affine domain.
Compute the integral closure of ℤ in ℚ(√d) and of k[x, y]/(y² − x³) in its fraction field.
refs: Eisenbud, ch. 4 and ch. 13 (The Dimension of Affine Rings)

units.title: Krull dimension and the principal ideal theorem
objectives: Compute the Krull dimension and the heights of primes in ℤ, k[x₁,…,xₙ], k[[x]] and their localizations.
State Krull's principal ideal theorem and its generalization: a prime minimal over n generators has height at most n.
State the dimension theorem for Noetherian local rings: dimension equals the degree of the Hilbert–Samuel polynomial equals the least size of a system of parameters.
State dim A[x] = dim A + 1 for Noetherian A and describe Nagata's Noetherian ring of infinite dimension.
Show that the dimension of an affine domain equals the transcendence degree of its fraction field.
refs: Eisenbud, ch. 8–10 and ch. 12 (Dimension and Hilbert–Samuel Polynomials)

units.title: Discrete valuation rings and Dedekind domains
objectives: Prove the equivalent characterizations of a DVR among one-dimensional Noetherian local domains.
Define Dedekind domains and prove that nonzero ideals factor uniquely into primes.
Show that fractional ideals form a group and define the ideal class group.
Show that ℤ[√−5] is a Dedekind domain but not a unique factorization domain.
Explain why k[x, y]/(y² − x³) is not a Dedekind domain.
refs: Atiyah–Macdonald, ch. 9 (Discrete Valuation Rings and Dedekind Domains)

units.title: Completion, Artin–Rees and Hensel's lemma
objectives: Construct the I-adic completion as an inverse limit and identify ℤₚ and k[[x]] as completions.
State the Artin–Rees lemma and use it to prove that completion is exact and flat on finitely generated modules over a Noetherian ring.
State the Krull intersection theorem.
State Hensel's lemma and use it to lift roots, for example to find √2 in ℤ₇.
State Cohen's structure theorem for complete regular local rings containing a field.
refs: Eisenbud, ch. 5 (Filtrations and the Artin–Rees Lemma) and ch. 7 (Completions and Hensel's Lemma)

units.title: Regular local rings, depth and Cohen–Macaulay rings
objectives: Define regular local rings by dim A = dim m/m² and compute the Zariski cotangent space of k[x, y]/(y² − x³) at the origin.
Define regular sequences and depth, and state that a regular local ring is Cohen–Macaulay.
Show that a regular local ring is a domain and state the Auslander–Buchsbaum theorem that it is a unique factorization domain.
State Serre's criterion: a Noetherian local ring is regular if and only if it has finite global dimension.
Show that two planes meeting in a point of 𝔸⁴ give a ring that is not Cohen–Macaulay.
refs: Eisenbud, ch. 17 (Regular Sequences and the Koszul Complex), ch. 18 (Depth, Codimension, and Cohen–Macaulay Rings) and ch. 19 (Homological Theory of Regular Local Rings)

modules.title: Category theory and homological algebra
modules.summary: Use the language of categories and the machinery of derived functors and spectral sequences to compute algebraic invariants.
refs: Riehl, Category Theory in Context, ch. 1–4
Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, ch. 1–6 and 10
Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician (2nd ed.), ch. I–V and VIII

units.title: Categories, functors and natural transformations
objectives: Define categories, functors, natural transformations and equivalences of categories, with examples (Set, Grp, Top, Vect, a poset, a group as a one-object category).
Decide whether a construction is functorial; for example, show that taking the center of a group is not a functor.
Show that V → V** is a natural isomorphism on finite-dimensional spaces while V ≅ V* is not natural.
State that a functor is an equivalence if and only if it is fully faithful and essentially surjective.
refs: Mac Lane, ch. I (Categories, Functors, and Natural Transformations)

units.title: Universal properties, representability and Yoneda
objectives: State and prove the Yoneda lemma.
Deduce that the Yoneda embedding is fully faithful and that a representing object is unique up to unique isomorphism.
Express products, tensor products and free groups as representing objects of suitable functors.
Give a functor that is not representable, such as the covariant power-set functor on Set.
refs: Riehl, ch. 2 (Universal Properties, Representability, and the Yoneda Lemma)
Mac Lane, ch. III (Universals and Limits)

units.title: Limits, colimits and adjunctions
objectives: Compute products, equalizers, pullbacks, pushouts and inverse limits in Set, Grp and Top.
Define adjunctions by a natural hom-set bijection and by unit and counit, and recognise free ⊣ forgetful, tensor ⊣ hom and abelianization ⊣ inclusion.
Prove that right adjoints preserve limits and left adjoints preserve colimits.
State the general adjoint functor theorem and give a functor with no left adjoint.
refs: Riehl, ch. 3 (Limits and Colimits) and ch. 4 (Adjunctions)
Mac Lane, ch. IV (Adjoints) and ch. V (Limits)

units.title: Additive and abelian categories, exactness
objectives: Define additive and abelian categories; check that R-modules and sheaves of abelian groups form abelian categories while filtered vector spaces do not.
Define left and right exact functors and show that Hom is left exact and ⊗ is right exact.
State the snake lemma and derive the long exact homology sequence of a short exact sequence of complexes.
State the Freyd–Mitchell embedding theorem and explain what it justifies about diagram chases.
Define projective and injective objects and show that ℚ/ℤ is injective in abelian groups.
refs: Weibel, ch. 1 (Chain Complexes) and App. A (Category Theory Language)

units.title: Derived functors, Ext and Tor
objectives: Construct right derived functors from injective resolutions and show they do not depend on the resolution.
Compute Tor^ℤ(ℤ/m, ℤ/n) and Ext¹_ℤ(ℤ/n, ℤ).
Interpret Ext¹ as equivalence classes of extensions and state the balancing of Tor and Ext.
Define projective and global dimension and state Hilbert's syzygy theorem.
Explain how the Koszul resolution proves Serre's theorem that regular local rings have finite global dimension.
refs: Weibel, ch. 2 (Derived Functors), ch. 3 (Tor and Ext) and ch. 4 (Homological Dimension)

units.title: Spectral sequences
objectives: Define a spectral sequence, its pages and differentials, and what it means to converge.
Construct the spectral sequences of a filtered complex and of a double complex.
State the Grothendieck spectral sequence for a composite of derived functors.
Solve extension problems on the E∞ page in small examples.
Derive a long exact sequence from a spectral sequence with two nonzero rows or columns.
refs: Hatcher, Spectral Sequences (online), ch. 1 (The Serre Spectral Sequence)

units.title: Group cohomology
objectives: Define Hⁿ(G, M) as Extⁿ over ℤ[G] and compute it with the bar resolution.
Interpret H¹ as crossed homomorphisms modulo principal ones and H² as classes of group extensions.
Compute the cohomology of a finite cyclic group with its periodic resolution.
State Hilbert's Theorem 90 in cohomological form and the inflation–restriction exact sequence.
State the Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence.
refs: Brown, Cohomology of Groups, ch. III–IV (Homology and Cohomology with Coefficients; Low Dimensional Cohomology and Group Extensions)

units.title: Derived and triangulated categories
objectives: Define the homotopy category K(A) and the derived category D(A) as the localization at quasi-isomorphisms.
State the axioms of a triangulated category and recognise distinguished triangles from mapping cones.
Define total derived functors RF and LF, state R(G∘F) ≅ RG∘RF under acyclicity hypotheses, and explain them as Kan extensions along the localization.
Compute Hom in D(A) from A to B[n] as Extⁿ(A, B).
Explain why D(A) is not abelian.
refs: Riehl, ch. 6 (All Concepts are Kan Extensions)

modules.title: Varieties and curves
modules.summary: Describe the shapes cut out by polynomial equations and compute their dimension, degree, singular points and genus.
refs: Shafarevich, Basic Algebraic Geometry 1 (3rd ed.), ch. 1–3
Harris, Algebraic Geometry: A First Course, Lectures 1–20

practice.title: Macaulay2: compute Hilbert polynomials, singular loci and genera of projective curves

units.title: Affine and projective varieties
objectives: Define affine and projective varieties, the Zariski topology and homogeneous ideals.
Use the projective Nullstellensatz to match projective varieties with homogeneous radical ideals not containing the irrelevant ideal.
Decompose an algebraic set into irreducible components.
Compute the projective closure of an affine curve and its points at infinity.
Write equations for the twisted cubic, the Veronese and Segre embeddings and the Plücker embedding of a Grassmannian.
refs: Harris, Lectures 1–2, 5 and 6 (Affine and Projective Varieties; Regular Functions and Maps; Ideals of Varieties and the Nullstellensatz; Grassmannians)

units.title: Regular functions, morphisms and rational maps
objectives: Define regular functions, morphisms and coordinate rings, and prove the anti-equivalence between affine varieties and finitely generated reduced k-algebras.
Define rational maps and birational equivalence, and show that the image of a projective variety under a morphism is closed.
Parametrize a smooth conic and show it is isomorphic to ℙ¹.
Show that the Cremona transformation is birational but not defined everywhere.
Prove that a rational map from a smooth curve to projective space extends to a morphism.
refs: Harris, Lectures 2 and 7 (Regular Functions and Maps; Rational Functions and Rational Maps)

units.title: Dimension, degree and the Hilbert polynomial
objectives: Define dimension by transcendence degree and by chains of irreducible subvarieties and show the two agree.
State the dimension of an intersection with a hypersurface and the theorem on the dimension of fibres.
Define the Hilbert function and Hilbert polynomial and read off dimension, degree and arithmetic genus from it.
Compute the Hilbert polynomial of a plane curve of degree d (dt + 1 − (d−1)(d−2)/2) and of the twisted cubic (3t + 1).
State Bézout's theorem for plane curves with intersection multiplicities.
refs: Harris, Lectures 11–13 (Dimension; More Dimension Computations; Hilbert Polynomials) and 18 (Degree)

units.title: Tangent spaces, smoothness and singularities
objectives: Define the Zariski tangent space and smooth points via the Jacobian criterion.
Show that the smooth points of a variety form a dense open subset.
Identify smoothness at a point with regularity of the local ring.
Compute the singular points and tangent cones of the node, the cusp and the tacnode.
State Bertini's theorem and deduce that a general hypersurface of degree d is smooth.
refs: Harris, Lectures 14 (Smoothness and Tangent Spaces) and 20 (Singular Points and Tangent Cones)

units.title: Blow-ups and resolving singularities of curves
objectives: Construct the blow-up of 𝔸ⁿ at a point by equations and identify the exceptional divisor with ℙⁿ⁻¹.
Compute strict transforms of the node and the cusp and show that one blow-up resolves the node.
State that curve singularities are resolved by finitely many blow-ups or by normalization, and state Hironaka's theorem in characteristic 0.
Use blow-ups to resolve the indeterminacy of a rational map ℙ² ⇢ ℙ¹.
State that a birational map between smooth projective surfaces factors into blow-ups and blow-downs.
refs: Shafarevich, ch. 2 §4 (The Structure of Birational Maps) and ch. 4 §3 (Birational Maps of Surfaces)
Harris, Lecture 7 (Rational Functions and Rational Maps)

units.title: Divisors and linear systems on curves
objectives: Define Weil divisors, principal divisors, degree and the divisor class group of a smooth projective curve.
Show that a nonconstant rational function on a smooth projective curve has as many zeros as poles.
Define L(D) and complete linear systems and relate base-point-free linear systems to maps to projective space.
Compute Pic(ℙ¹) ≅ ℤ and show that a smooth plane cubic is not isomorphic to ℙ¹.
Define the canonical divisor using differential forms.
refs: Shafarevich, ch. 3 §1–§2 (Divisors; Divisors on Curves) and §5 (Differential Forms)

units.title: Riemann–Roch for curves and its consequences
objectives: State Riemann–Roch, ℓ(D) − ℓ(K − D) = deg D + 1 − g, and deduce deg K = 2g − 2 and ℓ(K) = g.
Prove that a curve of genus 0 is ℙ¹ and that a genus-1 curve with a rational point is a plane cubic.
Show that a divisor of degree at least 2g + 1 is very ample and use this to embed curves.
Show that every curve of genus 2 is hyperelliptic.
Describe the canonical map and state that it is an embedding exactly for non-hyperelliptic curves.
refs: Shafarevich, ch. 3 §7 (The Riemann–Roch Theorem on Curves)

units.title: Riemann–Hurwitz and the genus of curves
objectives: State the Riemann–Hurwitz formula 2g(X) − 2 = n(2g(Y) − 2) + Σ(e_P − 1) for tamely ramified maps.
Compute the genus of a smooth plane curve of degree d and of the hyperelliptic curve y² = f(x).
Show that a curve admits no nonconstant map to a curve of larger genus, and in particular none from ℙ¹ to an elliptic curve.
State Lüroth's theorem.
Explain how wild ramification in characteristic p changes the formula, using an Artin–Schreier cover.

modules.title: Schemes and cohomology
modules.summary: Use schemes, sheaves and their cohomology to state and apply the main finiteness and duality theorems of algebraic geometry.
refs: Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, ch. II §1–§8 and ch. III §1–§10, §12
Vakil, The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry (Princeton UP, 2025), ch. 2–25 and 29

practice.title: Macaulay2: compute sheaf cohomology of coherent sheaves on projective space

units.title: Presheaves, sheaves and sheafification
objectives: Define presheaves, sheaves (identity and gluing axioms) and stalks.
Construct the sheafification of a presheaf and state its universal property.
Show that sheaves of abelian groups form an abelian category in which exactness is checked on stalks.
Give an example where the image presheaf is not a sheaf, using the exponential sequence on ℂ*.
Define pushforward f_* and inverse image f⁻¹ and state that they are adjoint.

units.title: Spec and affine schemes
objectives: Construct the structure sheaf on Spec A with sections A_f over D(f) and stalks A_p.
Define locally ringed spaces and schemes.
Show that morphisms X → Spec A correspond to ring maps A → O(X).
Describe the points of Spec ℤ[x] and 𝔸²_k, including generic points.
Explain non-reduced schemes such as Spec k[ε]/(ε²) and their role as tangent vectors.
refs: Vakil, ch. 3–4 (Toward Affine Schemes; The Structure Sheaf, and the Definition of Schemes in General)

units.title: Gluing, Proj and first properties of schemes
objectives: Glue schemes to construct ℙⁿ_A and the line with doubled origin.
Construct Proj S for a graded ring S.
Define reduced, integral, Noetherian, and finite-type schemes and morphisms.
State that varieties over an algebraically closed field correspond to integral separated schemes of finite type.
Compute fibre products and the fibres of Spec ℤ[i] → Spec ℤ.
refs: Vakil, ch. 5 (Some Properties of Schemes) and ch. 10 (Fibered Products of Schemes, and Base Change)

units.title: Separated, proper and finite morphisms
objectives: Define separated morphisms through the diagonal and show that the line with doubled origin is not separated.
State the valuative criteria of separatedness and properness.
State that projective morphisms are proper and explain the idea of the proof.
Define finite and affine morphisms and show that finite morphisms are proper.
State that there are proper varieties that are not projective and state Chow's lemma.
refs: Vakil, ch. 11 (Separated and Proper Morphisms, and (Finally!) Varieties)

units.title: Quasi-coherent sheaves
objectives: Define O_X-modules and the sheaf M~ attached to an A-module M.
Show that M ↦ M~ is an equivalence between A-modules and quasi-coherent sheaves on Spec A.
Define coherent and locally free sheaves, ideal sheaves and closed subschemes.
Construct O(n) on ℙⁿ and compute its global sections.
Define pullback and pushforward of quasi-coherent sheaves and the sheaf attached to a graded module on Proj.
refs: Vakil, ch. 6 and ch. 14 (quasicoherent and coherent sheaves)

units.title: Line bundles, divisors and maps to projective space
objectives: Define invertible sheaves and Pic X and identify Pic X with classes of Cartier divisors.
Relate Weil and Cartier divisors on normal, locally factorial schemes.
Compute Pic(ℙⁿ) ≅ ℤ and the Picard group ℤ² of a smooth quadric surface.
State that maps X → ℙⁿ correspond to line bundles with n + 1 generating sections.
Define ample and very ample line bundles and state Serre's characterization of ampleness.
keyTerms: linear system and maps to ℙⁿ
refs: Vakil, ch. 15–16 (Line Bundles, Maps to Projective Space, and Divisors)

units.title: Flat, smooth and étale morphisms
objectives: Define flat morphisms and explain flatness as continuity of fibres, including constancy of the Hilbert polynomial in projective flat families.
Show that the blow-up of a point is not flat and that flat limits can acquire embedded points.
Define the sheaf of relative differentials and smooth morphisms via the Jacobian criterion.
Define étale and unramified morphisms and show that Spec ℤ[i] → Spec ℤ is étale away from 2.
State generic smoothness in characteristic 0.

units.title: Sheaf cohomology and Čech cohomology
objectives: Define Hⁱ(X, F) as derived functors of global sections and show flasque sheaves are acyclic.
State Serre's vanishing on affine schemes and Grothendieck's vanishing above the dimension.
Compute cohomology with the Čech complex of an affine cover of a separated scheme, using Leray's theorem.
Use long exact sequences of sheaves to compute cohomology of a point or a hypersurface.
Define the Euler characteristic χ(F) and show it is additive on short exact sequences.
refs: Hartshorne, §III.1–§III.4 (Derived Functors; Cohomology of Sheaves; Cohomology of a Noetherian Affine Scheme; Čech Cohomology)
Vakil, ch. 18 (Čech Cohomology of Quasicoherent Sheaves) and ch. 23 (Derived Functors)

units.title: Cohomology of projective space and finiteness
objectives: Compute Hⁱ(ℙⁿ, O(d)) for all i and d with the Čech complex.
State finite-dimensionality of the cohomology of coherent sheaves on projective schemes and Serre's vanishing for F(m) with m large.
Show that χ(F(m)) is a polynomial in m equal to the Hilbert polynomial.
Compute the arithmetic genus of a plane curve as h¹(O_C).
Derive χ(L) = deg L + 1 − g for line bundles on a curve.
refs: Vakil, ch. 18 (Čech Cohomology of Quasicoherent Sheaves)

units.title: Serre duality, base change and applications
objectives: State Serre duality Hⁱ(X, F) ≅ Hⁿ⁻ⁱ(X, F^∨ ⊗ ω_X)^∨ for smooth projective X and compute ω of ℙⁿ as O(−n − 1).
Derive Riemann–Roch for curves from χ and Serre duality.
Compute the canonical sheaf of a degree-d hypersurface in ℙⁿ by adjunction: O(d − n − 1).
State the semicontinuity and cohomology-and-base-change theorems for flat proper families, using higher direct images.
State Kodaira vanishing in characteristic 0 and that it can fail in characteristic p.
refs: Hartshorne, §III.7 (The Serre Duality Theorem), §III.8 (Higher Direct Images of Sheaves) and §III.12 (The Semicontinuity Theorem)
Vakil, ch. 25 (Cohomology and Base Change Theorems) and ch. 29 (Proof of Serre Duality)

modules.title: Algebraic number theory
modules.summary: Factor primes in number fields, compute class groups and units, work with p-adic numbers, and state the main theorems of class field theory.
refs: Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, ch. I–II and V–VI
Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, ch. II–IV
Milne, Class Field Theory (course notes, v4.03), ch. V

practice.title: PARI/GP: compute rings of integers, class groups, units and prime factorizations in number fields
LMFDB: browse number fields by degree, discriminant and class group

units.title: Number fields and rings of integers
objectives: Define number fields and their rings of integers, and show that O_K is a free ℤ-module of rank [K : ℚ].
Compute O_K for quadratic fields (ℤ[√d] or ℤ[(1+√d)/2]) and for ℚ(ζ_p).
Define trace, norm and discriminant and compute the discriminant of a quadratic field.
Show that O_K is a Dedekind domain.
State Dedekind's example of a cubic field whose ring of integers is not ℤ[α] for any α.
refs: Marcus, ch. 2 (Number Fields and Number Rings)
Neukirch, ch. I §1–§2 (The Gaussian Integers; Integrality)

units.title: Prime factorization of ideals and splitting of primes
objectives: State unique factorization of ideals in O_K and the fundamental identity Σ eᵢfᵢ = n.
Apply the Kummer–Dedekind theorem to factor pO_K by factoring a minimal polynomial modulo p.
Decide how p splits in ℚ(√d) using the Legendre symbol.
Show that p ramifies in K exactly when p divides the discriminant of K.
Factor 2, 3 and 5 in ℤ[√−5] and show that (2, 1 + √−5) is not principal.
refs: Marcus, ch. 3 (Prime Decomposition in Number Rings)
Neukirch, ch. I §3 (Ideals) and §8 (Extensions of Dedekind Domains)

units.title: Minkowski theory and finiteness of the class group
objectives: State Minkowski's convex body theorem and describe O_K as a lattice of covolume 2^(−r₂)√|d_K| in ℝ^(r₁) × ℂ^(r₂).
Derive the Minkowski bound (n!/nⁿ)(4/π)^(r₂)√|d_K| and prove that the class number is finite.
Compute the class group of ℚ(√−5) and show that ℚ(√−163) has class number 1.
Deduce Minkowski's theorem that |d_K| > 1 for every number field K ≠ ℚ.
refs: Neukirch, ch. I §4–§6 (Lattices; Minkowski Theory; The Class Number)
Marcus, ch. 5 (The Ideal Class Group and the Unit Group)

units.title: Dirichlet's unit theorem and the class number formula
objectives: State Dirichlet's unit theorem O_K^× ≅ μ_K × ℤ^(r₁+r₂−1).
Sketch the proof through the logarithmic embedding and Minkowski's theorem.
Find the fundamental units of ℚ(√2) and ℚ(√3) and relate units of real quadratic fields to Pell's equation.
Define the regulator and state the analytic class number formula for the residue of the Dedekind zeta function at s = 1.
refs: Marcus, ch. 5 and ch. 7 (The Dedekind Zeta Function and the Class Number Formula)

units.title: Cyclotomic fields and quadratic reciprocity
objectives: Compute the ring of integers ℤ[ζₙ] and the splitting of a prime p ∤ n in ℚ(ζₙ), with residue degree the order of p mod n.
Prove quadratic reciprocity from the quadratic subfield of ℚ(ζ_p).
State Kummer's theorem on Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes and the role of the class number of ℚ(ζ_p).
refs: Marcus, ch. 1 (A Special Case of Fermat's Conjecture) and ch. 4

units.title: Decomposition and inertia groups; Frobenius
objectives: Define decomposition and inertia groups for a Galois extension and show D/I ≅ Gal of the residue field extension.
Define the Frobenius element and Artin symbol and compute them in cyclotomic and quadratic fields.
Show that efg = n in a Galois extension.
State the Chebotarev density theorem and deduce that infinitely many primes split completely.
Compute decomposition groups in the splitting field of x³ − 2.
refs: Marcus, ch. 4 (Galois Theory Applied to Prime Decomposition) and ch. 8

units.title: p-adic numbers and local fields
objectives: Construct ℚ_p as a completion of ℚ and ℤ_p as an inverse limit of ℤ/pⁿ.
State Ostrowski's theorem classifying absolute values on ℚ and prove the product formula.
Apply Hensel's lemma to decide which elements are squares in ℚ_p and describe ℚ_p^×/(ℚ_p^×)².
Define local fields and classify them as finite extensions of ℚ_p or 𝔽_q((t)).
Describe the Teichmüller lift of roots of unity.
refs: Neukirch, ch. II §1–§5 (The p-adic Numbers; The p-adic Absolute Value; Valuations; Completions; Local Fields)
Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, ch. II (p-adic fields)

units.title: Extensions of local fields and the local–global principle
objectives: Show that unramified extensions of ℚ_p correspond to extensions of 𝔽_p and form a cyclic tower.
Describe totally ramified extensions with Eisenstein polynomials, and tame ramification.
Relate global and local: show K ⊗ ℚ_p ≅ ∏ K_P over the primes P above p.
State the Hasse–Minkowski theorem for quadratic forms and give Selmer's cubic 3x³ + 4y³ + 5z³ = 0 as a failure of the Hasse principle.
Define the higher ramification groups and the Hilbert symbol.
refs: Neukirch, ch. II §6–§10 (Henselian Fields; Unramified and Tamely Ramified Extensions; Extensions of Valuations; Galois Theory of Valuations; Higher Ramification Groups)
Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, ch. III–IV (Hilbert symbol; Quadratic forms over ℚ_p and over ℚ)

units.title: Adeles and ideles
objectives: Define the adele ring A_K as a restricted product over all places, and the idele group.
Show that K is discrete and cocompact in A_K and that the norm-one idele class group is compact.
Recover the class group as a quotient of the idele class group and derive finiteness of h_K and the unit theorem from compactness.
Explain the role of the idele class group C_K in class field theory.
keyTerms: compactness of the norm-one idele classes
refs: Neukirch, ch. VI §1–§2 (Ideles and Idele Classes; Ideles in Field Extensions)
Cassels–Fröhlich (eds.), Algebraic Number Theory, ch. VII (Tate, Global Class Field Theory)

units.title: Class field theory: the statements
objectives: State local class field theory: K^×/N(L^×) ≅ Gal(L/K) for finite abelian L/K, and the existence theorem.
State global Artin reciprocity in idelic form and in terms of ray class groups and conductors.
Define the Hilbert class field and state its properties (maximal unramified abelian extension, Galois group ≅ Cl_K).
State the Kronecker–Weber theorem as the case K = ℚ.
Explain quadratic reciprocity as the simplest instance of Artin reciprocity.
refs: Neukirch, ch. V §1 (The Local Reciprocity Law) and ch. VI §5–§7 (The Global Reciprocity Law; Global Class Fields; The Ideal-Theoretic Version of Class Field Theory)
Milne, Class Field Theory (course notes), ch. V (Global Class Field Theory: Statements)
Cassels–Fröhlich (eds.), ch. VI (Serre, Local Class Field Theory)

modules.title: Analytic number theory
modules.summary: Use complex analysis to count primes, including primes in arithmetic progressions, and understand what sieve methods can and cannot do.
refs: Iwaniec–Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, ch. 1–7, 10 and 17

practice.title: LMFDB: browse L-functions with their functional equations and first zeros

units.title: Dirichlet characters and L-functions
objectives: Define Dirichlet characters, primitive characters and conductors, and prove the orthogonality relations.
Define L(s, χ) with its Euler product and continue it analytically for nonprincipal χ.
Compute Gauss sums and show |τ(χ)| = √q for primitive χ mod q.
State the functional equation of L(s, χ) and the Pólya–Vinogradov inequality for character sums.
refs: Davenport, ch. 2 (Gauss' Sum), ch. 4 (Primes in Arithmetic Progression: The General Modulus), ch. 5 (Primitive Characters), ch. 9 (The Functional Equation of the L Functions) and ch. 23 (The Pólya–Vinogradov Inequality)

units.title: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions
objectives: Prove Dirichlet's theorem from the nonvanishing of L(1, χ).
Prove L(1, χ) ≠ 0 for complex χ and explain why real characters are the hard case.
State Dirichlet's class number formula relating L(1, χ_d) to the class number of binary quadratic forms of discriminant d < 0.
Define Dirichlet density and compare it with natural density.
refs: Davenport, ch. 1 (Primes in Arithmetic Progression), ch. 4 and ch. 6 (Dirichlet's Class Number Formula)
Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, ch. VI (The theorem on arithmetic progressions)

units.title: The Riemann zeta function and its zeros
objectives: Prove the analytic continuation and functional equation of ζ(s) with the theta function.
Define the completed zeta function ξ(s) and state its Hadamard product.
State the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula N(T) = (T/2π) log(T/2πe) + O(log T).
State the Riemann hypothesis and its equivalent form ψ(x) = x + O(x^(1/2+ε)), and distinguish trivial from nontrivial zeros.
State Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture for the spacing of zeros.
refs: Davenport, ch. 8 (Riemann's Memoir), ch. 12 (The Infinite Products for ξ(s) and ξ(s,χ)) and ch. 15 (The Number N(T))
Iwaniec–Kowalski, ch. 5 (Classical Analytic Theory of L-functions) and ch. 25 (The Spacing of Zeros of the Riemann Zeta-Function)

units.title: The prime number theorem and the zero-free region
objectives: Prove ζ(1 + it) ≠ 0 using the 3–4–1 inequality.
State the de la Vallée Poussin zero-free region σ > 1 − c/log|t| and derive the prime number theorem with error x·exp(−c√log x).
Explain the equivalence of the prime number theorem with ψ(x) ~ x and with nonvanishing of ζ on Re s = 1 (Wiener–Ikehara).
State the Vinogradov–Korobov zero-free region and the resulting error term.
refs: Davenport, ch. 13 (A Zero-Free Region for ζ(s)) and ch. 18 (The Prime Number Theorem)
Iwaniec–Kowalski, ch. 2 (Elementary Theory of Prime Numbers)

units.title: The explicit formula
objectives: Derive the explicit formula ψ(x) = x − Σ_ρ x^ρ/ρ − log 2π − ½ log(1 − x⁻²) with Perron's formula and contour shifting.
Use the truncated explicit formula to show that the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to ψ(x) = x + O(√x log² x).
Explain how zeros make prime counts oscillate (Chebyshev's bias; Littlewood's sign changes of π(x) − li(x)).
State Weil's explicit formula as a duality between primes and zeros.
refs: Davenport, ch. 17 (The Explicit Formula for ψ(x)) and ch. 19 (The Explicit Formula for ψ(x,χ))

units.title: Primes in progressions: Siegel–Walfisz and exceptional zeros
objectives: State the zero-free region for L(s, χ) and the possible exceptional (Siegel) zero of a real character.
State Siegel's theorem L(1, χ) ≫_ε q^(−ε) and explain why its constant is ineffective, with Gauss's class number problem as a consequence.
State the Siegel–Walfisz theorem and its range of uniformity in the modulus.
State the generalized Riemann hypothesis and Linnik's theorem on the least prime in a progression.
refs: Davenport, ch. 14 (Zero-Free Regions for L(s,χ)) and ch. 20–22 (The Prime Number Theorem for Arithmetic Progressions; Siegel's Theorem)
Iwaniec–Kowalski, ch. 17–18 and ch. 22–23 (Primes in Arithmetic Progressions; The Least Prime; Imaginary Quadratic Fields; Effective Bounds for the Class Number)

units.title: The large sieve and Bombieri–Vinogradov
objectives: State the analytic large sieve inequality and its arithmetic form.
Derive a Brun–Titchmarsh upper bound for primes in a progression.
State the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem as the generalized Riemann hypothesis on average, with level of distribution 1/2.
State the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture and explain level of distribution θ.
Explain how Zhang and Maynard–Tao used the distribution of primes to prove bounded gaps between primes.
refs: Davenport, ch. 27 (The Large Sieve) and ch. 28 (Bombieri's Theorem)
Iwaniec–Kowalski, ch. 7 (Bilinear Forms and the Large Sieve)
Zhang, Bounded gaps between primes, Annals of Math. 179 (2014); Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Annals of Math. 181 (2015)

units.title: Sieve methods and their limits
objectives: Set up the sifting function S(A, P, z) and derive the Eratosthenes–Legendre identity.
Prove an upper bound with Brun's sieve or Selberg's Λ² sieve and apply it to twin primes: π₂(x) ≪ x/(log x)².
Explain the parity problem and why sieves alone cannot detect primes.
State Chen's theorem and Vinogradov's three-primes theorem via the circle method and Vaughan's identity.
refs: Iwaniec–Kowalski, ch. 6 (Elementary Sieve Methods), ch. 13 (Sums over Primes) and ch. 19–20 (The Goldbach Problem; The Circle Method)
Davenport, ch. 24–26 (Further Prime Number Sums; An Exponential Sum Formed with Primes; Sums of Three Primes)

modules.title: Elliptic curves and modular forms
modules.summary: Compute with elliptic curves over finite, local and global fields and connect them to modular forms and their L-functions.
refs: Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves (2nd ed.), ch. III–X and App. C
Diamond–Shurman, A First Course in Modular Forms, ch. 1–5 and 8–9
Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, ch. VII

practice.title: LMFDB: look up elliptic curves over ℚ (rank, torsion, conductor, L-function) and their matching modular forms
PARI/GP: count points mod p, compute a_p, heights and torsion of elliptic curves

units.title: Weierstrass equations and the group law
objectives: Use Riemann–Roch to put a genus-one curve with a rational point in Weierstrass form.
Define the chord–tangent group law and prove it agrees with the group structure of Pic⁰, which gives associativity.
Compute the discriminant and j-invariant and classify curves over an algebraically closed field by j.
Add points explicitly on a curve such as y² = x³ − 2 and find its 2-torsion.
Define isogenies, the dual isogeny and the multiplication-by-m map of degree m².
refs: Silverman, ch. III (The Geometry of Elliptic Curves)
Shafarevich, Basic Algebraic Geometry 1, ch. 3 §3 (The Plane Cubic)

units.title: Elliptic curves over ℂ and lattices
objectives: Construct the Weierstrass ℘-function of a lattice Λ and the isomorphism ℂ/Λ ≅ E(ℂ).
State the uniformization theorem for elliptic curves over ℂ.
Show E[m](ℂ) ≅ (ℤ/m)² and describe endomorphism rings: ℤ or an order in an imaginary quadratic field (complex multiplication).
Show that homothety classes of lattices are parametrized by SL₂(ℤ)∖ℍ.
refs: Silverman, ch. VI (Elliptic Curves over ℂ) and App. C §11 (Complex Multiplication)
Diamond–Shurman, ch. 1 (Modular Forms, Elliptic Curves, and Modular Curves)

units.title: Elliptic curves over finite and local fields
objectives: State the Hasse bound |#E(𝔽_q) − q − 1| ≤ 2√q and explain the proof through the degree of 1 − Frobenius.
Count points on small curves by hand and compute the trace of Frobenius a_p.
Define good, multiplicative and additive reduction and minimal Weierstrass equations.
Use the formal group to show that the reduction map is injective on prime-to-p torsion.
State the Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich criterion and define supersingular curves.
keyTerms: zeta function of E over 𝔽_q
refs: Silverman, ch. IV (The Formal Group of an Elliptic Curve), ch. V (Elliptic Curves over Finite Fields) and ch. VII (Elliptic Curves over Local Fields)

units.title: The Mordell–Weil theorem
objectives: Prove the weak Mordell–Weil theorem with Kummer theory and the finiteness of class groups and unit groups.
Define naive and canonical heights and state the descent theorem.
State Mordell–Weil, E(K) ≅ E(K)_tors ⊕ ℤ^r, Mazur's torsion theorem over ℚ, the Nagell–Lutz theorem and Siegel's theorem on integral points.
Perform a 2-descent on y² = x³ − x to show its rank is 0.
Define the Selmer and Tate–Shafarevich groups and explain how Ш obstructs descent.
refs: Silverman, ch. VIII (Elliptic Curves over Global Fields), ch. IX (Integral Points) and ch. X (Computing the Mordell–Weil Group)

units.title: Modular forms for SL₂(ℤ)
objectives: Define modular forms and cusp forms of weight k for SL₂(ℤ) and their q-expansions.
Describe the fundamental domain and the generators S and T of SL₂(ℤ).
Prove the valence (k/12) formula and deduce dim M_k and M = ℂ[E₄, E₆].
Compute E₄, E₆, Δ = q∏(1 − qⁿ)²⁴ and the j-function.
Use dim M₈ = 1 to derive a convolution identity between σ₇ and σ₃.
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, ch. VII (Modular forms)
Diamond–Shurman, ch. 1, ch. 3 (Dimension Formulas) and ch. 4 (Eisenstein Series)

units.title: Hecke operators and L-functions of modular forms
objectives: Define the Hecke operators T_n on M_k and compute their effect on q-expansions.
Show that the Hecke operators commute and are self-adjoint for the Petersson inner product, so S_k has a basis of normalized eigenforms.
Derive the multiplicativity of Ramanujan's τ(n) and the Euler product of L(f, s).
State the functional equation of L(f, s) and Deligne's bound |a_p| ≤ 2p^((k−1)/2).
Define Γ₀(N), the level and newforms.
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, ch. VII

units.title: The modularity theorem and Fermat's Last Theorem
objectives: State the modularity theorem in its equivalent forms: matching a_p with a weight-2 newform of level N_E, a modular parametrization X₀(N) → E, and L(E, s) = L(f, s).
Describe the Eichler–Shimura construction of an elliptic curve from a rational weight-2 newform.
Describe the ℓ-adic Tate module and Galois representation of E.
Outline the chain Frey curve + Ribet's level lowering + modularity ⇒ Fermat's Last Theorem.
State what Wiles (semistable curves) and Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor (all curves over ℚ) proved.
refs: Diamond–Shurman, ch. 8 (The Eichler–Shimura Relation and L-functions) and ch. 9 (Galois Representations)
Wiles, Modular elliptic curves and Fermat's Last Theorem, Annals of Math. 141 (1995)
Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor, On the modularity of elliptic curves over ℚ, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 14 (2001)

units.title: L-functions of elliptic curves and Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer
objectives: Define L(E, s) as an Euler product over primes and explain how modularity gives its analytic continuation.
State the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture: the order of vanishing at s = 1 equals the rank, and the strong form with Ш, the regulator, Tamagawa numbers and torsion.
State what is proved: analytic rank at most 1 implies the rank part of BSD and finiteness of Ш (Gross–Zagier and Kolyvagin).
State the parity conjecture via the root number, and the Sato–Tate theorem for the distribution of a_p.
Explain the congruent number problem and Tunnell's criterion, which is conditional on BSD.
refs: Silverman, App. C §16 (L-Series) and §21 (Variation of a_p and the Sato–Tate Conjecture)
Clay Mathematics Institute, Millennium Prize Problems: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture (official problem description)

modules.title: Lie groups and Lie algebras
modules.summary: Classify semisimple Lie algebras by root systems and describe their representations and those of compact Lie groups.
refs: Humphreys, Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory, §1–§24
Fulton–Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course, Lectures 7–26 and App. C–E
Hall, Lie Groups, Lie Algebras, and Representations (2nd ed.), ch. 1–5, 11–12 and App. D
Bröcker–tom Dieck, Representations of Compact Lie Groups, ch. III–VI

practice.title: SageMath thematic tutorial 'Lie Methods and Related Combinatorics': root systems, Weyl characters and branching rules

units.title: Lie groups, Lie algebras and the exponential map
objectives: Define a Lie group and its Lie algebra through left-invariant vector fields or one-parameter subgroups.
Compute the Lie algebras of SO(n), SU(n), SL_n(ℝ) and Sp(2n).
State the correspondence between connected Lie subgroups and Lie subalgebras, and between simply connected Lie groups and Lie algebras.
Show that exp: sl₂(ℝ) → SL₂(ℝ) is not surjective.
Describe SU(2) → SO(3) as a double cover and deduce π₁(SO(3)) ≅ ℤ/2.
refs: Hall, Lie Groups, Lie Algebras, and Representations (2nd ed.), ch. 1–3 and 5 (Matrix Lie Groups; The Matrix Exponential; Lie Algebras; The Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff Formula)
Fulton–Harris, Lectures 7–8 (Lie Groups; Lie Algebras and Lie Groups)

units.title: Solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras: Engel and Lie
objectives: Define the derived and lower central series, solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras, and the radical.
State Engel's theorem and explain its proof by induction on dimension.
State Lie's theorem (a solvable algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 acts by upper triangular matrices) and explain its proof.
Show that Lie's theorem fails over ℝ (rotations of the plane) and in characteristic p.
State the Levi decomposition and Ado's theorem.
refs: Humphreys, §3 (Solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras), §3.3 (Proof of Engel's Theorem) and §4.1 (Lie's Theorem)
Fulton–Harris, Lecture 9 (Initial Classification of Lie Algebras) and App. E (Ado's and Levi's Theorems)

units.title: The Killing form, Cartan's criteria and complete reducibility
objectives: Define the Killing form and compute it for sl₂.
State Cartan's criteria for solvability and for semisimplicity (nondegenerate Killing form).
Prove that a semisimple Lie algebra is a direct sum of simple ideals and that all its derivations are inner.
State Weyl's complete reducibility theorem and explain the role of the Casimir element and Whitehead's lemma.
State the abstract Jordan decomposition in a semisimple Lie algebra.

units.title: Representations of sl₂
objectives: Classify the finite-dimensional irreducible sl₂-modules V(n) by highest weight, with weights n, n − 2, …, −n.
Compute the action of e, f, h on a weight basis and the eigenvalue of the Casimir element.
Decompose V(m) ⊗ V(n) by the Clebsch–Gordan rule.
Identify V(n) with Symⁿℂ² and explain which representations descend from SU(2) to SO(3).

units.title: Cartan subalgebras and the root space decomposition
objectives: Define maximal toral (Cartan) subalgebras and the root space decomposition g = h ⊕ ⨁ g_α.
Prove that root spaces are one-dimensional and that each root gives an sl₂-triple.
Compute the roots of sl_n (eᵢ − eⱼ), so_2n and sp_2n.
Show that the roots span h* and satisfy the integrality ⟨β, α^∨⟩ ∈ ℤ.
State the conjugacy of Cartan subalgebras.
keyTerms: roots of the classical Lie algebras
refs: Humphreys, §8 (Root space decomposition) and §15–§16 (Cartan subalgebras; Conjugacy theorems)
Fulton–Harris, Lecture 14 (The General Set-up) and App. D (Cartan Subalgebras)

units.title: Root systems, Weyl groups and Dynkin diagrams
objectives: State the axioms of a root system and classify the rank-2 systems A₁ × A₁, A₂, B₂ and G₂.
Define simple and positive roots and the Weyl group, and show that the Weyl group acts simply transitively on Weyl chambers.
Define the Cartan matrix and Dynkin diagram and state the classification A_n, B_n, C_n, D_n, E₆, E₇, E₈, F₄, G₂.
State Serre's theorem that each Dynkin diagram comes from a unique simple Lie algebra.
Compute the order of the Weyl group of A_n and the number of positive roots.
refs: Humphreys, §9–§11 (Axiomatics; Simple roots and Weyl group; Classification) and §18 (Generators and relations)
Fulton–Harris, Lectures 21–22 (The Classification of Complex Simple Lie Algebras; g₂ and Other Exceptional Lie Algebras)

units.title: Weights and highest-weight modules
objectives: Define integral, dominant and fundamental weights and the weight lattice.
Construct Verma modules and their irreducible quotients L(λ), using the universal enveloping algebra and the PBW theorem.
State the theorem of the highest weight: finite-dimensional irreducibles correspond to dominant integral weights.
Draw the weight diagrams of the standard, adjoint and Sym² representations of sl₃.
refs: Humphreys, §13 (Abstract theory of weights), §17 (Universal enveloping algebras), §20–§21 (Weights and maximal vectors; Finite dimensional modules)

units.title: The Weyl character and dimension formulas
objectives: State the Weyl character formula as an alternating sum over the Weyl group divided by the Weyl denominator.
Derive the Weyl dimension formula ∏_{α>0} ⟨λ + ρ, α⟩/⟨ρ, α⟩ and compute dimensions of sl₃ irreducibles.
State Freudenthal's multiplicity formula and Kostant's partition-function formula.
Check the character formula on sl₂, where it gives the characters of V(n).
refs: Bröcker–tom Dieck, ch. VI §1 (The Weyl Character Formula)

units.title: Compact Lie groups and maximal tori
objectives: State the maximal torus theorem (maximal tori are conjugate and cover the group) and define the Weyl group N(T)/T.
State Weyl's integration formula and use it to derive the Weyl character formula for compact groups.
Relate complex semisimple Lie algebras to compact real forms through the unitary trick.
Compute the maximal torus and Weyl group of U(n) and of SO(3), and describe Spin(n) as the universal cover of SO(n).
refs: Hall, ch. 11 (Compact Lie Groups and Maximal Tori) and ch. 12 (The Compact Group Approach to Representation Theory)
Bröcker–tom Dieck, ch. IV (The Maximal Torus of a Compact Lie Group)
Fulton–Harris, Lectures 20 and 26 (Spin Representations; Real Lie Algebras and Lie Groups)

units.title: The Peter–Weyl theorem
objectives: Show that finite-dimensional representations of a compact group are unitarizable and completely reducible by averaging over Haar measure.
State the Peter–Weyl theorem L²(G) ≅ ⨁ V_π ⊗ V_π* and the density of matrix coefficients.
Deduce that every compact Lie group is a matrix group and that characters form an orthonormal basis of class functions.
Recover Fourier series from G = S¹ and spherical harmonics from G = SO(3).
refs: Bröcker–tom Dieck, ch. III §3 (The Theorem of Peter and Weyl)
Hall, App. D (Peter–Weyl Theorem and Completeness of Characters)
Folland, A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis (2nd ed.), §5.2 (The Peter–Weyl Theorem)

tiers.name: Advanced graduate II
tiers.summary: You can handle the analysis, probability, topology and geometry half of a qualifying exam: random processes and stochastic calculus, partial differential equations, Fourier and operator theory, invariants of vector bundles, complex, symplectic and low-dimensional geometry, dynamics, and graduate combinatorics, logic and optimization.

modules.title: Probability theory
modules.summary: Prove limit theorems with martingales and characteristic functions, and compute with Brownian motion and Itô's formula.
refs: Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples (5th ed.), ch. 3, 4 and 7
Le Gall, Brownian Motion, Martingales, and Stochastic Calculus (GTM 274), ch. 1–8
Øksendal, Stochastic Differential Equations (6th ed.), ch. 3–5 and 7–8

units.title: Conditional expectation
objectives: Define E[X | G] through the Radon–Nikodym theorem and as an L² projection, and prove existence and almost-sure uniqueness.
Apply the tower property, taking out what is known, and conditional Jensen.
Compute E[X | σ(Y)] for a discrete partition and for a jointly Gaussian pair.
Show that conditional expectation is a contraction on Lᵖ.
Give dependent X, Y with E[X | Y] = E[X].

units.title: Martingales and the convergence theorems
objectives: Define filtrations, adapted processes, martingales, sub- and supermartingales and stopping times.
Prove the upcrossing inequality and the almost-sure convergence of L¹-bounded martingales.
State Doob's maximal inequality and Lᵖ convergence for p > 1.
Give an L¹-bounded martingale that does not converge in L¹ (double or nothing).
Apply martingale convergence to Pólya's urn and to Galton–Watson branching processes.
refs: Durrett, §4.2 (Martingales, Almost Sure Convergence) and §4.4 (Doob's Inequality, Convergence in Lp, p > 1)
Williams, ch. 10–12 (Martingales; The Convergence Theorem; Martingales bounded in ℒ²)

units.title: Uniform integrability and optional stopping
objectives: Define uniform integrability and show that a.s. convergence plus uniform integrability is equivalent to L¹ convergence.
Characterize uniformly integrable martingales as closed martingales E[X | F_n] and state Lévy's upward theorem.
State the optional stopping theorem with its hypotheses and use it to compute gambler's-ruin probabilities and expected hitting times.
Show that optional stopping fails for simple random walk stopped on hitting 1.
Prove Kolmogorov's 0–1 law from Lévy's theorem.
refs: Durrett, §4.6 (Uniform Integrability, Convergence in L1), §4.7 (Backwards Martingales) and §4.8 (Optional Stopping Theorems)

units.title: Characteristic functions and central limit theorems
objectives: Define characteristic functions and state the inversion formula and Lévy's continuity theorem.
Prove the central limit theorem for i.i.d. variables with finite variance by expanding the characteristic function.
State the Lindeberg–Feller theorem and verify Lindeberg's condition in an example.
Explain tightness and Prokhorov's theorem in proofs of weak convergence.
Show that the CLT fails for Cauchy variables and identify the stable limit.
refs: Williams, ch. 16–18 (Basic Properties of CFs; Weak Convergence; The Central Limit Theorem)

units.title: Brownian motion: construction and path properties
objectives: Define Brownian motion as a Gaussian process and construct it (Lévy–Ciesielski, or Kolmogorov extension with the continuity criterion).
Prove scaling and time inversion and state the strong Markov property.
Use the reflection principle to compute P(max_{s≤t} B_s ≥ a) = 2P(B_t ≥ a).
Show that paths have quadratic variation t and are almost surely nowhere differentiable.
State Donsker's invariance principle.
refs: Durrett, §7.1 (Definition and Construction) and ch. 8 (Applications to Random Walk)
Le Gall, ch. 1–2 (Gaussian Variables and Gaussian Processes; Brownian Motion)

units.title: Continuous martingales and semimartingales
objectives: Define continuous local martingales, localizing sequences, quadratic variation ⟨M⟩ and semimartingales.
Show that B_t² − t and exp(θB_t − θ²t/2) are martingales and use them to compute exit times and exit probabilities.
State the Doob–Meyer decomposition.
Give a local martingale that is not a true martingale (the inverse of a three-dimensional Bessel process).
refs: Le Gall, ch. 3–4 (Filtrations and Martingales; Continuous Semimartingales)
Karatzas–Shreve, Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus, ch. 1 (Martingales, Stopping Times, and Filtrations)

units.title: The Itô integral and Itô's formula
objectives: Construct the Itô integral for simple and then square-integrable adapted integrands via the Itô isometry.
State Itô's formula and use it to compute ∫B dB = (B_t² − t)/2 and d(e^(B_t)).
State Lévy's characterization of Brownian motion and the martingale representation theorem.
State Girsanov's theorem and use it to remove a constant drift.
Compare the Itô and Stratonovich integrals.
refs: Øksendal, ch. 3–4 (Itô Integrals; The Itô Formula and the Martingale Representation Theorem)

units.title: Stochastic differential equations and PDE
objectives: State existence and uniqueness of strong solutions of SDEs with Lipschitz coefficients.
Solve the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation and geometric Brownian motion explicitly.
Define the generator of a diffusion and derive Dynkin's formula.
State the Feynman–Kac formula and solve the Dirichlet problem with exit distributions (harmonic measure).
