Derive the Black–Scholes PDE as an application of Itô's formula.
refs: Øksendal, ch. 5 (Stochastic Differential Equations), ch. 7–9 (Diffusions; Other Topics in Diffusion Theory; Applications to Boundary Value Problems) and ch. 12 (Application to Mathematical Finance)
Le Gall, ch. 7 (Brownian Motion and Partial Differential Equations) and ch. 8 (Stochastic Differential Equations)

modules.title: PDE
modules.summary: Solve linear and nonlinear partial differential equations in the weak sense and prove existence, uniqueness and regularity of solutions.
refs: Evans, Partial Differential Equations (2nd ed.), ch. 5–12

units.title: Weak derivatives and Sobolev spaces
objectives: Define weak derivatives and W^(k,p)(U) and show it is a Banach space (a Hilbert space for p = 2).
State the Meyers–Serrin density theorem and the extension theorem.
Define the trace operator and describe W₀^(1,p) as the kernel of the trace.
Characterize Hˢ(ℝⁿ) through the Fourier transform.
Decide when |x|^(−α) lies in W^(1,p) of the unit ball (α < (n − p)/p).

units.title: Sobolev inequalities and compactness
objectives: State the Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality with p* = np/(n − p) and show by scaling that no other exponent is possible.
State Morrey's inequality and the Hölder embedding for p > n.
State the Rellich–Kondrachov compactness theorem and the Poincaré inequality.
Show that log log(1/|x|) lies in W^(1,n) of a small ball but is unbounded.

units.title: Weak solutions and the Lax–Milgram theorem
objectives: Define uniformly elliptic operators in divergence form and the weak formulation B[u, v] = (f, v).
State and prove the Lax–Milgram theorem.
Derive the energy estimate and Gårding's inequality and prove existence for −Δu + cu = f with Dirichlet data.
State the Fredholm alternative for elliptic operators.
Treat the Neumann problem and its compatibility condition ∫f = 0.
refs: Brenner–Scott, The Mathematical Theory of Finite Element Methods (3rd ed.), ch. 2 (Variational Formulation of Elliptic Boundary Value Problems)

units.title: Elliptic regularity, maximum principles and eigenvalues
objectives: State interior H² regularity and higher regularity, and explain the difference-quotient proof.
State boundary regularity and smoothness up to the boundary.
State the weak and strong maximum principles and Hopf's lemma.
Show that the Dirichlet Laplacian has discrete spectrum with a positive simple principal eigenvalue given by the Rayleigh quotient.
State the De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theorem for equations with merely bounded measurable coefficients.

units.title: Parabolic and hyperbolic equations: energy methods
objectives: Define weak solutions of second-order parabolic equations in L²(0, T; H₀¹) and prove existence with Galerkin approximations and energy estimates.
Prove uniqueness with the energy identity and Gronwall's inequality.
Prove conservation of energy and finite speed of propagation for the wave equation.
State the Hille–Yosida theorem and solve the heat equation with a contraction semigroup.
keyTerms: weak solution of the heat equation

units.title: The calculus of variations
objectives: Derive the Euler–Lagrange equation and the second variation of an integral functional.
Prove existence of minimizers by the direct method: coercivity plus weak lower semicontinuity from convexity in the gradient.
Give an example where no minimizer exists because convexity fails.
State Noether's theorem linking symmetries to conservation laws.
State Hilbert's 19th problem and its solution by De Giorgi and Nash.

units.title: Nonlinear methods: fixed points, monotonicity and critical points
objectives: State the Banach, Schauder and Schaefer fixed point theorems and apply one to a semilinear elliptic problem.
Use monotone operators (Minty–Browder) for quasilinear equations.
Apply the method of sub- and supersolutions.
State the mountain pass theorem with the Palais–Smale condition and apply it to −Δu = |u|^(p−1)u for 1 < p < (n + 2)/(n − 2).
Use Pohozaev's identity to show nonexistence at the critical exponent on star-shaped domains.
refs: Evans, ch. 9 (Nonvariational Techniques) and ch. 8 (The Calculus of Variations)

units.title: Nonlinear evolution: conservation laws, Hamilton–Jacobi and Navier–Stokes
objectives: Show that shocks form for Burgers' equation and define entropy solutions and the Rankine–Hugoniot condition.
Define viscosity solutions of Hamilton–Jacobi equations and state their uniqueness.
State Leray's existence of global weak solutions to the 3D Navier–Stokes equations with the energy inequality, and the open regularity problem.
Explain scaling criticality and why 3D Navier–Stokes is supercritical for its energy.
State local well-posedness for a semilinear wave or Schrödinger equation.
refs: Evans, ch. 10 (Hamilton–Jacobi Equations), ch. 11 (Systems of Conservation Laws) and ch. 12 (Nonlinear Wave Equations)
Clay Mathematics Institute, Millennium Prize Problems: Navier–Stokes Equation (official problem description)

modules.title: Harmonic analysis
modules.summary: Bound operators built from the Fourier transform, from interpolation and singular integrals up to the restriction and Kakeya problems.
refs: Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis (3rd ed.), ch. 1–2 and 5–6
Grafakos, Modern Fourier Analysis (3rd ed.), ch. 2–3 and 5
Demeter, Fourier Restriction, Decoupling, and Applications, ch. 1, 5 and 9–13
Folland, A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis (2nd ed.), ch. 2 and 4

units.title: Interpolation and maximal functions
objectives: State Riesz–Thorin (via the three lines lemma) and Marcinkiewicz interpolation (via distribution functions).
Derive the Hausdorff–Young and Young convolution inequalities by interpolation.
Prove the weak (1,1) bound for the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function with the Vitali covering lemma and deduce the Lebesgue differentiation theorem.
Show that the maximal function is not bounded on L¹, and state Carleson's theorem on a.e. convergence of Fourier series of L² functions.
refs: Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, §1.3 (Interpolation) and ch. 2 (Maximal Functions, Fourier Transform, and Distributions)

units.title: Singular integrals and Calderón–Zygmund theory
objectives: Define the Hilbert and Riesz transforms and compute their Fourier multipliers.
Prove the Calderón–Zygmund decomposition and use it to show weak (1,1) bounds for Calderón–Zygmund operators.
State Lᵖ boundedness for 1 < p < ∞ and show failure at p = 1 and p = ∞.
State the Mikhlin multiplier theorem and apply it to bound second derivatives by the Laplacian in Lᵖ.
State the T(1) theorem and the role of A_p weights.
refs: Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, §5.3 (The Calderón–Zygmund Decomposition and Singular Integrals)
Duoandikoetxea, ch. 3–5 (The Hilbert Transform; Singular Integrals (I) and (II)), ch. 7 (Weighted Inequalities) and ch. 9 (The T1 Theorem)

units.title: Littlewood–Paley theory and function spaces
objectives: Define smooth Littlewood–Paley projections and the square function, and prove ‖Sf‖_p ≈ ‖f‖_p for 1 < p < ∞.
Characterize Sobolev and Besov norms through dyadic frequency pieces.
State the Marcinkiewicz multiplier theorem and Bernstein's inequality.
Explain how paraproducts and wavelet bases are used in nonlinear estimates.
refs: Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, ch. 6 (Littlewood–Paley Theory and Multipliers)
Grafakos, Modern Fourier Analysis, ch. 1 (Smoothness and Function Spaces)

units.title: The Hardy space H¹ and BMO
objectives: Define BMO and show that log|x| is in BMO but not in L^∞.
State the John–Nirenberg inequality.
Define H¹ by atoms and by maximal functions, and show that Calderón–Zygmund operators map H¹ to L¹ and L^∞ to BMO.
State Fefferman's duality theorem (H¹)* = BMO and use H¹ and BMO as endpoints for interpolation.
refs: Grafakos, Modern Fourier Analysis, §2.1 (Hardy Spaces), §3.1 (Functions of Bounded Mean Oscillation) and §3.2 (Duality between H¹ and BMO)

units.title: Oscillatory integrals, restriction, Kakeya and decoupling
objectives: State the stationary phase principle and van der Corput's lemma, and compute the decay |ξ|^(−(n−1)/2) of the Fourier transform of surface measure on the sphere.
State the Stein–Tomas restriction theorem and the restriction conjecture.
Define Kakeya sets, describe Besicovitch's construction of measure-zero Kakeya sets, and state the Kakeya conjecture and its maximal-function form.
Explain Fefferman's ball multiplier theorem as a link between Kakeya sets and Fourier multipliers.
State the Bourgain–Demeter decoupling theorem and its use in proving Vinogradov's mean value theorem.
refs: Grafakos, Modern Fourier Analysis, ch. 5 (Boundedness and Convergence of Fourier Integrals)
Demeter, ch. 1 (Linear Restriction Theory), ch. 5 (Kakeya and Square Function Estimates) and ch. 9–11 (decoupling)
Bourgain–Demeter–Guth, Proof of the main conjecture in Vinogradov's mean value theorem for degrees higher than three, Annals of Math. 184 (2016)

units.title: Locally compact abelian groups and Pontryagin duality
objectives: Define Haar measure on a locally compact group and the dual group of characters.
Compute the duals of ℤ, the circle 𝕋, ℝ and ℚ_p.
State Pontryagin duality and the Plancherel theorem for locally compact abelian groups.
State the Poisson summation formula for a closed subgroup and apply it to ℤ ⊂ ℝ.
Explain why compact groups have discrete duals and vice versa.
refs: Folland, A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis (2nd ed.), ch. 2 (Locally Compact Groups) and ch. 4 (Analysis on Locally Compact Abelian Groups), §4.3 (The Pontrjagin Duality Theorem)

modules.title: Spectral theory and operator algebras
modules.summary: Apply the spectral theorem to unbounded operators and work with C*-algebras, von Neumann algebras and the Fredholm index.
refs: Reed–Simon, Methods of Modern Mathematical Physics I: Functional Analysis, ch. VI–VIII
Murphy, C*-Algebras and Operator Theory, ch. 1–5

units.title: Unbounded operators and self-adjointness
objectives: Define closed, closable, symmetric and self-adjoint operators and the domain of the adjoint.
Apply the basic criterion for self-adjointness, Ran(A ± i) = H, and deficiency indices.
Show that −d²/dx² on C_c^∞(0, 1) has many self-adjoint extensions (boundary conditions) while on C_c^∞(ℝ) it is essentially self-adjoint.
State the Kato–Rellich theorem and apply it to −Δ + V with V ∈ L² + L^∞ on ℝ³.
refs: Reed–Simon I, §VIII.1–§VIII.2 (Domains, Graphs, Adjoints, and Spectrum; Symmetric and Self-Adjoint Operators)
Hall, Quantum Theory for Mathematicians, ch. 9 (Unbounded Self-Adjoint Operators)

units.title: The spectral theorem and Stone's theorem
objectives: State the spectral theorem for unbounded self-adjoint operators in multiplication-operator and projection-valued-measure forms.
Build the functional calculus f(A) for bounded Borel functions f.
State Stone's theorem matching strongly continuous unitary groups with self-adjoint generators, and find the generator of translations on L²(ℝ).
Decompose the spectrum into point, absolutely continuous and singular continuous parts, and define the essential spectrum.
State Weyl's theorem that compact perturbations preserve the essential spectrum.
refs: Reed–Simon I, §VII.1–§VII.3 (The Continuous Functional Calculus; The Spectral Measures; Spectral Projections), §VIII.3 (The Spectral Theorem) and §VIII.4 (Stone's Theorem)
Hall, Quantum Theory for Mathematicians, ch. 10 (The Spectral Theorem for Unbounded Self-Adjoint Operators)

units.title: C*-algebras, Gelfand duality and the GNS construction
objectives: Define Banach algebras and C*-algebras and the C*-identity.
State the commutative Gelfand–Naimark theorem (A ≅ C₀(X)) and derive the continuous functional calculus.
Construct the GNS representation from a state and state the Gelfand–Naimark embedding into B(H).
Compute spectra in examples, including the unilateral shift.
Give examples: C(X), the compact operators K(H), B(H) and the Calkin algebra.
refs: Murphy, C*-Algebras and Operator Theory, ch. 1–3 (Elementary Spectral Theory; C*-Algebras and Hilbert Space Operators; Ideals and Positive Functionals) and ch. 5 (Representations of C*-Algebras)

units.title: Von Neumann algebras and the Fredholm index
objectives: Define von Neumann algebras, the weak and strong operator topologies, and state the double commutant theorem.
Describe abelian von Neumann algebras as L^∞(X, μ) and state the type I, II, III classification of factors.
Define Fredholm operators and the index, and prove its invariance under compact perturbations (Atkinson's theorem).
Compute the index of the unilateral shift and state the Toeplitz index theorem (index = minus the winding number).
State the Atiyah–Singer index theorem as the global generalization.
keyTerms: type I, II and III factors
refs: Murphy, ch. 4 (Von Neumann Algebras) and ch. 1–3 (Fredholm and Toeplitz operators)
Atiyah–Singer, The index of elliptic operators I, Annals of Math. 87 (1968)

modules.title: Characteristic classes and homotopy
modules.summary: Compute characteristic classes of vector bundles and use them, together with spectral sequences and K-theory, to answer questions about manifolds and spheres.
refs: Bott–Tu, Differential Forms in Algebraic Topology, §6, §11–§18 and §20–§23
Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory (online), ch. 1–4

units.title: Universal bundles and classifying spaces
objectives: Show that rank-n bundles over a paracompact space X correspond to homotopy classes [X, Gₙ(ℝ^∞)].
Describe Grassmannians with their Schubert cell structures.
Identify BU(1) = ℂP^∞, BO(1) = ℝP^∞ and Bℤ = S¹, and construct K(G, 1) for discrete G.
Classify bundles over spheres by clutching functions in π_(k−1)(O(n)).
Count the complex line bundles on a closed surface.
refs: Milnor–Stasheff, §5 (Grassmann Manifolds and Universal Bundles) and §6 (A Cell Structure for Grassmann Manifolds)
Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory, §1.2 (Classifying Vector Bundles)

units.title: Stiefel–Whitney classes
objectives: State the axioms of Stiefel–Whitney classes and the Whitney product formula.
Compute w(TℝPⁿ) = (1 + a)^(n+1) and decide which ℝPⁿ are parallelizable using it.
State H*(Gₙ(ℝ^∞); ℤ/2) = ℤ/2[w₁, …, wₙ].
Use dual Stiefel–Whitney classes to show ℝP^(2^k) does not immerse in ℝ^(2^(k+1)−2).
Relate w₁ to orientability and w₂ to spin structures, and show TS² has w = 1 but is not trivial.
refs: Milnor–Stasheff, §4 (Stiefel–Whitney Classes), §7 (The Cohomology Ring H*(Gₙ; ℤ/2)) and §8 (Existence of Stiefel–Whitney Classes)
Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory, §3.1 (Stiefel–Whitney and Chern Classes)

units.title: The Thom isomorphism and the Euler class
objectives: State the Thom isomorphism Hᵏ(B) ≅ H^(k+n)(E, E₀) and define the Thom class.
Define the Euler class as an obstruction and show it vanishes when there is a nowhere-zero section.
Derive the Gysin sequence of a sphere bundle and use it to compute H*(ℂPⁿ).
Show that the Euler class of the tangent bundle evaluates to the Euler characteristic.
Show that the Euler class of an odd-rank oriented bundle has order 2.
refs: Milnor–Stasheff, §9–§12 (Oriented Bundles and the Euler Class; The Thom Isomorphism Theorem; Computations in a Smooth Manifold; Obstructions)
Bott–Tu, §6 (The Thom Isomorphism) and §11–§12 (Sphere Bundles; The Thom Isomorphism and Poincaré Duality Revisited)

units.title: Chern and Pontryagin classes
objectives: Define Chern classes through the projective bundle formula (or top Chern class = Euler class) and state their axioms.
Compute c(TℂPⁿ) = (1 + h)^(n+1) and c₁ of O(k) on ℂPⁿ.
Define Pontryagin classes through the complexification and compute p(TℂPⁿ).
Express characteristic classes through curvature (Chern–Weil) and relate c₁ of a line bundle on a surface to its degree.
keyTerms: first Chern class of a line bundle
refs: Milnor–Stasheff, §14 (Chern Classes), §15 (Pontrjagin Classes) and App. C (Connections, Curvature, and Characteristic Classes)
Bott–Tu, §20–§22 (Chern Classes of a Complex Vector Bundle; The Splitting Principle and Flag Manifolds; Pontrjagin Classes)

units.title: Cobordism, characteristic numbers and the signature theorem
objectives: Define unoriented and oriented cobordism and show that characteristic numbers are cobordism invariants.
State Thom's theorem identifying cobordism groups with homotopy groups of Thom spectra, and explain the Pontryagin–Thom construction.
State that the rational oriented cobordism ring is a polynomial ring on the classes of ℂP^(2k).
State Hirzebruch's signature theorem and check σ(ℂP²) = p₁/3 = 1.
Explain how Milnor used it to find exotic 7-spheres.
refs: Milnor–Stasheff, §16–§19 (Chern Numbers and Pontrjagin Numbers; The Oriented Cobordism Ring; Thom Spaces and Transversality; Multiplicative Sequences and the Signature Theorem)

units.title: The Serre spectral sequence
objectives: State the Serre spectral sequence E₂^(p,q) = H^p(B; H^q(F)) ⇒ H^(p+q)(E) for a fibration with simply connected base.
Compute H*(ΩSⁿ) from the path–loop fibration and H*(K(ℤ, 2)) = ℤ[x].
Derive the Gysin and Wang sequences as special cases.
Compute the cohomology of SU(3) or U(n) through fibrations.
State Serre's theorem that πᵢ(Sⁿ) is finite except for i = n and, for even n, i = 2n − 1.
refs: Hatcher, Spectral Sequences (online), ch. 1 (The Serre Spectral Sequence)
Bott–Tu, §14–§18 (The Spectral Sequence of a Filtered Complex; …; The Path Fibration; Review of Homotopy Theory; Applications to Homotopy Theory)

units.title: Topological K-theory and Bott periodicity
objectives: Define K(X) and reduced K-theory through the Grothendieck group of vector bundles.
State complex Bott periodicity, K̃(S^(n+2)) ≅ K̃(Sⁿ) and πᵢ(U) ≅ π_(i+2)(U), and the period-8 real version.
Compute K(S²) = ℤ[H]/(H − 1)² and K̃(S^(2k)) = ℤ.
Show that stably trivial bundles need not be trivial (TS²), so K-theory forgets information.
State Adams' theorem that ℝⁿ is a division algebra only for n = 1, 2, 4, 8 (Hopf invariant one).
refs: Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory, §2.1 (The Functor K(X)), §2.2 (Bott Periodicity) and §2.3 (Division Algebras and Parallelizable Spheres)
Milnor, Morse Theory, Part IV (Applications to Lie Groups and Symmetric Spaces)
Bott, The stable homotopy of the classical groups, Annals of Math. 70 (1959)

units.title: Stable homotopy groups of spheres
objectives: State the Freudenthal suspension theorem and define the stable stems πₖˢ.
Recall the low stems: π₁ˢ = ℤ/2 (η), π₂ˢ = ℤ/2 and π₃ˢ = ℤ/24 (ν).
Describe the J-homomorphism and Adams' determination of its image.
Explain the roles of Steenrod squares and the Adams spectral sequence in computing stems.
Relate stable stems to framed cobordism and state the Kervaire invariant one problem and its near-complete solution (Hill–Hopkins–Ravenel).
refs: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, §4.2 (Elementary Methods of Calculation), 4.F (Spectra and Homology Theories) and 4.L (Steenrod Squares and Powers)
Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory, ch. 4 (The J-Homomorphism)
Hatcher, Spectral Sequences (online), ch. 2 (The Adams Spectral Sequence)
Hill–Hopkins–Ravenel, On the nonexistence of elements of Kervaire invariant one, Annals of Math. 184 (2016)

modules.title: Complex geometry
modules.summary: Use Kähler and Hodge theory to relate the shape of complex manifolds to their holomorphic structure and to decide when they are projective.
refs: Huybrechts, Complex Geometry: An Introduction, ch. 1–5
Griffiths–Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry, ch. 0–2

units.title: Riemann surfaces and uniformization
objectives: State the uniformization theorem: every simply connected Riemann surface is biholomorphic to the Riemann sphere, ℂ or the disc.
Deduce that every Riemann surface is a quotient of one of these three, and classify compact surfaces by genus into spherical, flat and hyperbolic.
Show that compact surfaces of genus at least 2 are quotients of the disc by Fuchsian groups and carry metrics of curvature −1.
State Hurwitz's bound |Aut X| ≤ 84(g − 1) and the Riemann existence theorem.
refs: Donaldson, Riemann Surfaces, ch. 10 (The Uniformisation Theorem)
Forster, Lectures on Riemann Surfaces, ch. 3 (Non-Compact Riemann Surfaces)

units.title: Complex manifolds and Dolbeault cohomology
objectives: Define complex manifolds and almost complex structures, and state the Newlander–Nirenberg integrability theorem.
Define (p, q)-forms, ∂ and ∂̄, and Dolbeault cohomology.
State the Dolbeault–Grothendieck lemma and Dolbeault's theorem identifying H^(p,q) with sheaf cohomology Hᵠ(X, Ωᵖ).
State Hartogs' extension theorem as a several-variables phenomenon with no one-variable analogue.
Give examples: complex tori, projective space and the Hopf surface.
refs: Huybrechts, ch. 1 (Local Theory) and ch. 2 (Complex Manifolds)
Griffiths–Harris, ch. 0 §1–§3 (Rudiments of Several Complex Variables; Complex Manifolds; Sheaves and Cohomology)

units.title: Kähler manifolds
objectives: Define Hermitian and Kähler metrics and the Kähler form.
Show that projective space with the Fubini–Study metric and its complex submanifolds are Kähler.
State the Kähler identities and the ∂∂̄-lemma.
Show that the Hopf surface is not Kähler because b₁ is odd.

units.title: Hodge theory on compact Kähler manifolds
objectives: State the Hodge theorem (each de Rham class has a unique harmonic representative) and explain its elliptic-PDE proof.
Derive Δ_d = 2Δ_∂̄ on Kähler manifolds and the Hodge decomposition Hᵏ(X, ℂ) = ⨁ H^(p,q) with Hodge symmetry.
Deduce that odd Betti numbers of compact Kähler manifolds are even.
Compute the Hodge diamonds of a complex torus and of a curve of genus g.
State the Hodge conjecture.
refs: Huybrechts, §3.2 (Hodge Theory on Kähler Manifolds) and App. A (Hodge Theory on Differentiable Manifolds)
Griffiths–Harris, ch. 0 §6 (Harmonic Theory on Compact Complex Manifolds)

units.title: Lefschetz theorems
objectives: State the hard Lefschetz theorem and the Lefschetz decomposition into primitive cohomology.
State the Hodge–Riemann bilinear relations and derive the Hodge index theorem for surfaces.
State the Lefschetz (1,1) theorem: integral classes of type (1,1) are first Chern classes of line bundles.
State the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem and compute π₁ and low-degree cohomology of smooth hypersurfaces.
refs: Griffiths–Harris, ch. 1 §1–§2 (Divisors and Line Bundles; Some Vanishing Theorems and Corollaries)

units.title: Kodaira vanishing and embedding
objectives: Define positive line bundles through curvature and relate positivity to ampleness.
State Kodaira vanishing Hᵠ(X, K_X ⊗ L) = 0 for q > 0 and L positive, and explain the Bochner–Kodaira–Nakano proof.
State the Kodaira embedding theorem and deduce that a compact Kähler manifold with an integral Kähler class is projective.
State the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem.
State Chow's theorem and GAGA, and explain why every compact Riemann surface is projective.
keyTerms: curvature of a Hermitian line bundle
refs: Huybrechts, §5.1 (Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch Theorem), §5.2 (Kodaira Vanishing Theorem and Applications) and §5.3 (Kodaira Embedding Theorem)
Griffiths–Harris, ch. 1 §2 and §4 (The Kodaira Embedding Theorem)

modules.title: Low-dimensional topology
modules.summary: Tell knots and 3- and 4-dimensional manifolds apart using invariants, geometry and handle decompositions.
refs: Lickorish, An Introduction to Knot Theory, ch. 1–6 and 15–16
Farb–Margalit, A Primer on Mapping Class Groups, ch. 1–4, 8 and 13
Milnor, Lectures on the h-Cobordism Theorem, §1–§9
Thurston, Three-Dimensional Geometry and Topology, Vol. 1, ch. 1–4
Scorpan, The Wild World of 4-Manifolds, ch. 1–5

practice.title: SnapPy: compute hyperbolic structures, volumes and Dehn fillings of knot complements
KnotInfo: look up genus, signature, unknotting number and Alexander and Jones polynomials of small knots

units.title: Knots and classical invariants
objectives: Define knots, links, isotopy and Reidemeister moves.
Construct Seifert surfaces and Seifert matrices and compute the Alexander polynomial and signature of the trefoil.
Define knot genus and unknotting number and show that genus is additive under connected sum.
Show that the trefoil is knotted with Fox 3-colourings and compute its knot group.
Show that the Alexander polynomial does not detect the unknot (a nontrivial knot with Δ = 1).
refs: Rolfsen, ch. 5 (Seifert Surfaces) and ch. 7–8 (Infinite Cyclic Coverings and the Alexander Invariant; Matrix Invariants)
Lickorish, ch. 1–2 and 6 (A Beginning for Knot Theory; Seifert Surfaces and Knot Factorisation; The Alexander Polynomial)

units.title: The Jones polynomial and Khovanov homology
objectives: Define the Kauffman bracket and derive the Jones polynomial through writhe normalization.
Compute the Jones polynomial of the trefoil and deduce that the trefoil is chiral.
State the Tait conjectures on reduced alternating diagrams, proved with the Jones polynomial.
State the HOMFLY-PT skein relation.
Describe Khovanov homology as a categorification of the Jones polynomial that detects the unknot (Kronheimer–Mrowka), and note that unknot detection by the Jones polynomial is open.
refs: Lickorish, ch. 3 (The Jones Polynomial), ch. 5 (The Jones Polynomial of an Alternating Link) and ch. 15–16 (Generalisations of the Jones Polynomial; Exploring the HOMFLY and Kauffman Polynomials)

units.title: Morse theory, handles and the h-cobordism theorem
objectives: Define Morse functions, critical points and their index, and state the Morse lemma.
Show that passing a critical point of index k attaches a k-handle, and derive the Morse inequalities.
State the h-cobordism theorem (simply connected, dimension at least 6) and explain handle cancellation with the Whitney trick.
Deduce Smale's generalized Poincaré conjecture in dimensions at least 5.
Explain why the Whitney trick fails in dimension 4.
refs: Milnor, Morse Theory, Part I (Non-Degenerate Smooth Functions on a Manifold)
Milnor, Lectures on the h-Cobordism Theorem, §1–§9
Smale, Generalized Poincaré's conjecture in dimensions greater than four, Annals of Math. 74 (1961)

units.title: Hyperbolic geometry and geometrization of 3-manifolds
objectives: Describe models of hyperbolic space and its isometries, and state Mostow rigidity (volume is a topological invariant in dimension at least 3).
List Thurston's eight geometries and state the geometrization theorem proved by Perelman.
Describe the prime and JSJ decompositions of 3-manifolds.
Show that the figure-eight knot complement is hyperbolic and that lens spaces are spherical; state Dehn surgery and the Lickorish–Wallace theorem.
Define quasi-isometry and Gromov-hyperbolic groups and state the Švarc–Milnor lemma.
refs: Thurston, Three-Dimensional Geometry and Topology, Vol. 1, ch. 2–4 (Hyperbolic Geometry and Its Friends; Geometric Manifolds; The Structure of Discrete Groups)
Rolfsen, ch. 9 (3-manifolds and Surgery on Links)

units.title: Mapping class groups and 4-manifolds
objectives: Define the mapping class group and Dehn twists, and state that Dehn twists generate it (Dehn–Lickorish).
Compute the mapping class group of the torus as SL₂(ℤ) and state the Dehn–Nielsen–Baer theorem.
State the Nielsen–Thurston classification into periodic, reducible and pseudo-Anosov classes.
Define the intersection form of a closed oriented 4-manifold and compute it for ℂP², S² × S² and the E₈ form.
State Freedman's classification of simply connected topological 4-manifolds and Donaldson's diagonalization theorem, and deduce the existence of exotic ℝ⁴.
refs: Farb–Margalit, ch. 2–4 (Mapping Class Group Basics; Dehn Twists; Generating the Mapping Class Group), ch. 8 (The Dehn–Nielsen–Baer Theorem) and ch. 13 (The Nielsen–Thurston Classification)
Scorpan, ch. 3–5 (Getting Acquainted with Intersection Forms; Intersection Forms and Topology; Classifications and Counterclassifications)

modules.title: Symplectic geometry and mathematical physics
modules.summary: Describe classical mechanics with symplectic geometry, state the main rigidity theorems, and set up quantum mechanics with operators on Hilbert space.
refs: Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics (2nd ed.), ch. 3–4, 7–10 and App. 5
Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry, Parts I–III and VII–XI
McDuff–Salamon, Introduction to Symplectic Topology (3rd ed.), ch. 2–3 and 11–12
Hall, Quantum Theory for Mathematicians, ch. 3, 9–14 and 16–18

units.title: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics
objectives: Derive Lagrange's equations from the principle of least action.
Pass to Hamilton's equations with the Legendre transform.
Define Poisson brackets and show that conserved quantities are exactly the functions that Poisson-commute with the Hamiltonian.
State Liouville's theorem on preservation of phase-space volume.
State the Liouville–Arnold theorem on integrable systems with action-angle coordinates, and the KAM theorem on their perturbations.
refs: Arnold, ch. 3–4 (Variational Principles; Lagrangian Mechanics on Manifolds), ch. 9 (Canonical Formalism) and ch. 10 (Introduction to Perturbation Theory)
Cannas da Silva, Part VII (Hamiltonian Mechanics: Hamiltonian Vector Fields; Variational Principles; Legendre Transform)

units.title: Symplectic manifolds and Darboux's theorem
objectives: Define symplectic vector spaces, symplectic forms and symplectomorphisms.
Show that a cotangent bundle carries a canonical symplectic form.
Prove Darboux's theorem with Moser's trick, so symplectic manifolds have no local invariants.
Show that Kähler manifolds are symplectic while S⁴ admits no symplectic form.
Define Hamiltonian vector fields and flows on a symplectic manifold.
refs: Cannas da Silva, Parts I–III (Symplectic Manifolds; Symplectomorphisms; Local Forms)
McDuff–Salamon, ch. 2–3 (Linear Symplectic Geometry; Symplectic Manifolds)

units.title: Lagrangian submanifolds, moment maps and reduction
objectives: Define Lagrangian submanifolds and show that graphs of closed 1-forms and of symplectomorphisms are Lagrangian.
State the Weinstein neighbourhood theorem.
Define Hamiltonian group actions and moment maps, and compute the moment map of the circle acting on ℂⁿ.
State Marsden–Weinstein–Meyer reduction and obtain ℂP^(n−1) as a reduced space.
State the Atiyah–Guillemin–Sternberg convexity theorem and Delzant's classification of toric manifolds.
refs: Cannas da Silva, Part II (Lagrangian Submanifolds) and Parts VIII–XI (Moment Maps; Symplectic Reduction; Moment Maps Revisited; Symplectic Toric Manifolds)

units.title: Rigidity: Gromov, Arnold and Floer theory (statements)
objectives: State Gromov's non-squeezing theorem and define symplectic capacities.
State the Arnold conjecture lower bound for fixed points of nondegenerate Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms (sum of Betti numbers) and contrast it with the Lefschetz bound.
Describe Hamiltonian Floer homology as Morse homology of the action functional, with a differential counting holomorphic cylinders.
State that Lagrangian Floer homology can prevent a Lagrangian from being displaced, and describe the Fukaya category as a concept.
refs: McDuff–Salamon, ch. 11 (The Arnold Conjecture) and ch. 12 (Symplectic Capacities)
Gromov, Pseudo holomorphic curves in symplectic manifolds, Invent. Math. 82 (1985)

units.title: The mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics
objectives: State the postulates: states are unit vectors up to phase, observables are self-adjoint operators, measurement follows the Born rule, and time evolution is e^(−itH/ħ) by Stone's theorem.
Compute the spectrum of the harmonic oscillator with ladder operators.
Derive the Heisenberg uncertainty principle from commutators.
State the Stone–von Neumann theorem and the Groenewold–van Hove no-go theorem for quantization.
Describe spin through projective representations of SO(3) and state the hydrogen spectrum.
refs: Hall, Quantum Theory for Mathematicians, ch. 3 (A First Approach to Quantum Mechanics), ch. 11–14 (The Harmonic Oscillator; The Uncertainty Principle; Quantization Schemes for Euclidean Space; The Stone–von Neumann Theorem) and ch. 17–18 (Angular Momentum and Spin; Radial Potentials and the Hydrogen Atom)
Reed–Simon I, §VIII.11 (Three Mathematical Problems in Quantum Mechanics)

modules.title: Ergodic theory and dynamics
modules.summary: Prove ergodic theorems and use recurrence, mixing and entropy to study the long-run behaviour of dynamical systems, including applications to number theory.
refs: Einsiedler–Ward, Ergodic Theory with a view towards Number Theory, ch. 2–9 and 11
Katok–Hasselblatt, Introduction to the Modern Theory of Dynamical Systems, ch. 3–4, 6, 11 and 17–20
Walters, An Introduction to Ergodic Theory, ch. 1–2, 4 and 6–8

units.title: Measure-preserving systems and ergodic theorems
objectives: Define measure-preserving transformations and ergodicity (invariant sets are trivial; invariant functions are constant).
Prove Poincaré recurrence.
Prove von Neumann's mean ergodic theorem by splitting L² into invariant functions and coboundaries.
State Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem and explain the maximal ergodic theorem behind it.
Show with Fourier series that irrational rotations and the doubling map are ergodic, and deduce Weyl equidistribution and Borel's normal number theorem.

units.title: Mixing, spectral theory and entropy
objectives: Define weak and strong mixing and show mixing ⇒ weak mixing ⇒ ergodic, with rotations as ergodic but not weakly mixing.
Characterize weak mixing spectrally (no nonconstant eigenfunctions) and define unique ergodicity.
Define Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy and compute the entropy of a Bernoulli shift as −Σ pᵢ log pᵢ.
State the Kolmogorov–Sinai generator theorem and Ornstein's isomorphism theorem for Bernoulli shifts.
Define topological entropy, state the variational principle, and describe the Gauss map and rotation numbers as examples.
refs: Walters, ch. 2 (Isomorphism, Conjugacy, and Spectral Isomorphism), ch. 4 (Entropy), ch. 7 (Topological Entropy) and ch. 8 (Relationship Between Topological Entropy and Measure-Theoretic Entropy)
Einsiedler–Ward, ch. 3 (Continued Fractions) and ch. 4 (Invariant Measures for Continuous Maps)
Katok–Hasselblatt, ch. 3 (Principal Classes of Asymptotic Topological Invariants) and ch. 11 (Homeomorphisms of the Circle)

units.title: Multiple recurrence and Szemerédi's theorem
objectives: State the Furstenberg correspondence principle turning sets of positive upper density into measure-preserving systems.
State Furstenberg's multiple recurrence theorem and derive Szemerédi's theorem from it.
Prove the case of two-term recurrence and sketch three-term recurrence for weakly mixing systems.
State the structure theorem (compact and weak-mixing extensions) and the role of nilsystems as characteristic factors.
State the polynomial Szemerédi theorem and van der Waerden's theorem as topological recurrence.
refs: Einsiedler–Ward, ch. 5–7 (Conditional Measures and Algebras; Factors and Joinings; Furstenberg's Proof of Szemerédi's Theorem) and ch. 10 (Nilrotation)
Furstenberg, Ergodic behavior of diagonal measures and a theorem of Szemerédi on arithmetic progressions, J. Analyse Math. 31 (1977)

units.title: Hyperbolic and homogeneous dynamics
objectives: Define hyperbolic fixed points and Anosov diffeomorphisms, and state the Hartman–Grobman and stable manifold theorems.
Show that the cat map on the 2-torus is Anosov and mixing, and state structural stability.
Explain the ergodicity of the geodesic flow on a compact hyperbolic surface (Hopf argument) and its description as the action of SL₂(ℝ) on Γ∖SL₂(ℝ).
State the Howe–Moore theorem and Ratner's theorems, and their application to the Oppenheim conjecture (Margulis).
State Littlewood's conjecture and the Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss result that the exceptions have Hausdorff dimension 0.
refs: Katok–Hasselblatt, ch. 6 (Local Hyperbolic Theory and Its Applications) and ch. 17–18 (Survey of Examples; Topological Properties of Hyperbolic Sets)
Einsiedler–Ward, ch. 8–9 and 11 (Actions of Locally Compact Groups; Geodesic Flow on Quotients of the Hyperbolic Plane; More Dynamics on Quotients of the Hyperbolic Plane)

modules.title: Graduate combinatorics
modules.summary: Use probabilistic, regularity, Fourier and polynomial methods to prove existence and extremal results in combinatorics and discrete geometry.
refs: Alon–Spencer, The Probabilistic Method (4th ed.), ch. 5–8 and App. A
Zhao, Graph Theory and Additive Combinatorics, ch. 1–9
Guth, Polynomial Methods in Combinatorics (chapters on fundamental examples and polynomial partitioning)
Matoušek, Lectures on Discrete Geometry, ch. 2 and 12–14
Conway–Sloane, Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups, ch. 1 and 4

units.title: The Lovász local lemma and concentration
objectives: State the symmetric and general Lovász local lemma and apply it to hypergraph 2-colouring (property B) and to lower bounds for Ramsey numbers.
State Chernoff and Azuma–Hoeffding bounds and use an edge-exposure martingale to show the chromatic number of G(n, 1/2) is concentrated.
State the FKG and Janson inequalities and describe the Erdős–Rényi phase transition.
Describe the Moser–Tardos algorithmic local lemma.
State concentration of measure on the sphere and the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma.
refs: Alon–Spencer, ch. 5 (The Local Lemma), ch. 6 (Correlation Inequalities), ch. 7 (Martingales and Tight Concentration), §8.1 (The Janson Inequalities), ch. 11 (The Erdős–Rényi Phase Transition) and App. A (Bounding of Large Deviations)
Matoušek, ch. 14 (Measure Concentration and Almost Spherical Sections)

units.title: Szemerédi's regularity lemma and removal
objectives: Define ε-regular pairs and state Szemerédi's regularity lemma, including the tower-type bound that cannot be avoided (Gowers).
Prove the triangle counting lemma and the triangle removal lemma.
Derive Roth's theorem from the triangle removal lemma (Ruzsa–Szemerédi) and the Erdős–Stone–Simonovits theorem from regularity.
Define quasirandom graphs and state the Chung–Graham–Wilson equivalences.
Describe graphons as limits of dense graphs and state Sidorenko's conjecture.
refs: Zhao, ch. 1–5 (Forbidding a Subgraph; Graph Regularity Method; Pseudorandom Graphs; Graph Limits; Graph Homomorphism Inequalities)

units.title: Roth's theorem and Szemerédi's theorem
objectives: Prove Roth's theorem in 𝔽₃ⁿ by the Fourier-analytic density increment method (Meshulam).
Outline Roth's theorem in the integers with its N/log log N bound.
Describe Behrend's construction of 3-AP-free sets of size N·e^(−c√log N).
State Szemerédi's theorem and define the Gowers uniformity norms.
State the Green–Tao theorem and explain the transference principle.
refs: Zhao, ch. 6 (Forbidding 3-Term Arithmetic Progressions) and ch. 9 (Progressions in Sparse Pseudorandom Sets)
Roth, On certain sets of integers, J. London Math. Soc. 28 (1953)
Green–Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Annals of Math. 167 (2008)

units.title: Sumsets and Freiman's theorem
objectives: Define sumsets, the doubling constant and Freiman homomorphisms, and prove the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality and the Ruzsa covering lemma.
State Freiman's theorem (small doubling forces density in a generalized arithmetic progression) and its model version in 𝔽₂ⁿ.
State the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa (Marton) conjecture.
State the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture and prove Elekes' bound with the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem.
Compute |A + A| for an arithmetic progression and for a random set.
refs: Zhao, ch. 7 (Structure of Set Addition) and ch. 8 (Sum-Product Problem)

units.title: The polynomial method
objectives: Prove Dvir's finite-field Kakeya bound with a vanishing lemma and parameter counting.
State Alon's Combinatorial Nullstellensatz and use it to prove the Cauchy–Davenport theorem.
Explain the slice-rank proof that cap sets in 𝔽₃ⁿ have size O(2.756ⁿ) (Ellenberg–Gijswijt).
State the joints theorem and polynomial partitioning, and their use by Guth–Katz on the Erdős distinct distances problem.
refs: Guth, Polynomial Methods in Combinatorics (chapters 'Fundamental examples of the polynomial method' and 'Polynomial partitioning')
Dvir, On the size of Kakeya sets in finite fields, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 22 (2009)
Ellenberg–Gijswijt, On large subsets of 𝔽_qⁿ with no three-term arithmetic progression, Annals of Math. 185 (2017)

units.title: Brunn–Minkowski, lattices and sphere packing
objectives: State the Brunn–Minkowski inequality, prove it via Prékopa–Leindler, and derive the isoperimetric inequality.
State Minkowski's first theorem on lattice points in symmetric convex bodies.
Define packing density and state the Minkowski–Hlawka lower bound of order 2⁻ⁿ.
Describe the E₈ and Leech lattices and state Viazovska's theorem (dimension 8) and its extension to dimension 24, with the Cohn–Elkies linear programming bound.
State the Kabatiansky–Levenshtein upper bound on packing density.
refs: Matoušek, §2.1 (Minkowski's Theorem), §12.2 (The Brunn–Minkowski Inequality) and ch. 13 (Volumes in High Dimension)
Conway–Sloane, ch. 1 (Sphere Packings and Kissing Numbers) and ch. 4 (Certain Important Lattices and Their Properties)
Viazovska, The sphere packing problem in dimension 8, Annals of Math. 185 (2017); Cohn–Kumar–Miller–Radchenko–Viazovska, The sphere packing problem in dimension 24, Annals of Math. 185 (2017)

modules.title: Model theory, set theory, computability
modules.summary: Use quantifier elimination and o-minimality, prove independence results by forcing, and compare degrees of uncomputability, up to Hilbert's tenth problem.
refs: Marker, Model Theory: An Introduction, ch. 3–4 and 6
van den Dries, Tame Topology and o-minimal Structures, ch. 1–3
Kunen, Set Theory: An Introduction to Independence Proofs (1980), ch. VI–VIII
Soare, Turing Computability: Theory and Applications, ch. 3–4 and 7

units.title: Quantifier elimination and model completeness
objectives: Define quantifier elimination and state a test for it.
Prove quantifier elimination for dense linear orders and for algebraically closed fields, and deduce Chevalley's theorem on constructible sets.
Prove the Ax–Grothendieck theorem with the Lefschetz principle.
State Tarski's quantifier elimination for real closed fields and deduce decidability of real algebra.
Explain why the theory of (ℤ, +, ·) admits no such elimination and is undecidable.
refs: Marker, §3.1–§3.3 (Quantifier Elimination; Algebraically Closed Fields; Real Closed Fields)

units.title: Types, saturation and categoricity
objectives: Define types and type spaces, and realizing and omitting types; state the omitting types theorem.
Construct saturated and prime models in examples.
Show that algebraically closed fields of fixed characteristic are uncountably categorical but not countably categorical, and that dense linear orders are countably categorical (back-and-forth).
State the Łoś–Vaught test and Morley's categoricity theorem.
Define strongly minimal sets and their dimension.
refs: Marker, ch. 4 (Realizing and Omitting Types), ch. 6 (ω-Stable Theories) and ch. 8 (Geometry of Strongly Minimal Sets)

units.title: O-minimality and tame geometry
objectives: Define o-minimal structures and show that the real field is o-minimal using Tarski's theorem.
State the monotonicity and cell decomposition theorems and deduce that definable sets have finitely many connected components.
State Wilkie's theorem that ℝ_exp is o-minimal and show that adding sin on all of ℝ destroys o-minimality.
State the Pila–Wilkie counting theorem for rational points on transcendental parts of definable sets and outline the Pila–Zannier strategy.
refs: van den Dries, ch. 1–3 (Some Elementary Results; Semialgebraic Sets; Cell Decomposition)
Wilkie, Model completeness results for expansions of the ordered field of real numbers by restricted Pfaffian functions and the exponential function, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 9 (1996)
Pila–Wilkie, The rational points of a definable set, Duke Math. J. 133 (2006)

units.title: Constructibility, forcing and the independence of CH
objectives: Define the constructible universe L and state Gödel's theorem that L satisfies ZFC + GCH, giving the consistency of CH.
Define forcing posets, generic filters and the generic extension M[G], and state the forcing theorem.
Show that posets with the countable chain condition preserve cardinals.
Outline Cohen forcing that adds ℵ₂ reals to make 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂, giving the independence of CH.
State Martin's axiom and Easton's theorem on the possible values of 2^κ for regular κ.
refs: Kunen, Set Theory: An Introduction to Independence Proofs (1980), ch. V–VII (Defining Definability; The Constructible Sets; Forcing) and ch. VIII (Iterated Forcing)
Cohen, The independence of the continuum hypothesis, Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. USA 50 (1963)

units.title: Turing degrees and the MRDP theorem
objectives: Define Turing reducibility, Turing degrees, the jump and the arithmetical hierarchy, and state Post's theorem.
State Post's problem and the Friedberg–Muchnik theorem, and explain the finite-injury priority method.
Define Diophantine sets and state the MRDP theorem (Diophantine = computably enumerable).
Explain why exponentiation is Diophantine, using solutions of a Pell equation.
Deduce the unsolvability of Hilbert's tenth problem and state that the analogous problem over ℚ is open.
refs: Soare, Turing Computability, ch. 3 (Turing Reducibility), ch. 4 (The Arithmetical Hierarchy) and ch. 7 (The Finite Injury Method)
Matiyasevich, Hilbert's Tenth Problem, ch. 1–5 (Principal Definitions; Exponentiation Is Diophantine; Diophantine Coding; Universal Diophantine Equations; Hilbert's Tenth Problem Is Unsolvable)

modules.title: Applied analysis and optimization
modules.summary: Solve convex and transport problems through duality, and analyse the errors of finite element and polynomial approximations.
refs: Villani, Topics in Optimal Transportation, ch. 1–5 and 7–9
Brenner–Scott, The Mathematical Theory of Finite Element Methods (3rd ed.), ch. 0–5
Trefethen, Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice (Extended ed.), ch. 1–16 and 23–24

POT (Python Optimal Transport): compute Wasserstein distances and transport plans

Chebfun: explore Chebyshev interpolation, the Runge phenomenon and rational approximation

units.title: Convex duality and the KKT conditions
objectives: Define convex sets, convex functions and convex optimization problems.
Form the Lagrangian and dual function and prove weak duality.
State Slater's condition for strong duality and derive the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions.
Compute the duals of a linear program and of a norm-constrained least-squares problem.
Define Fenchel conjugates, and compare first-order methods with Newton and interior-point methods.
refs: Boyd–Vandenberghe, ch. 2–4 (Convex Sets; Convex Functions; Convex Optimization Problems), ch. 5 (Duality), §5.5 (Optimality Conditions) and ch. 9–11 (algorithms)

units.title: Optimal transport
objectives: State Monge's and Kantorovich's formulations and the existence of optimal transport plans.
State Kantorovich duality and the role of c-concave potentials.
State Brenier's theorem (optimal maps for quadratic cost are gradients of convex functions) and derive the Monge–Ampère equation.
Define the Wasserstein distance W_p and compute W₂ on the line with quantile functions and between Gaussians.
Describe displacement convexity, the JKO view of the heat equation as a gradient flow, and Talagrand's transport inequality.
refs: Villani, Topics in Optimal Transportation, ch. 1–5 (The Kantorovich Duality; Geometry of Optimal Transportation; Brenier's Polar Factorization Theorem; The Monge–Ampère Equation; Displacement Interpolation and Displacement Convexity) and ch. 7–9 (The Metric Side; A Differential Point of View; Entropy Production and Transportation Inequalities)
Brenier, Polar factorization and monotone rearrangement of vector-valued functions, Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 44 (1991)

units.title: The finite element method
objectives: Set up the Galerkin method on a finite-dimensional subspace and prove Céa's lemma (quasi-optimality).
Define a finite element as a Ciarlet triple and assemble piecewise-linear elements for −u″ = f.
State the Bramble–Hilbert lemma and derive H¹ error O(h) and L² error O(h²) with the Aubin–Nitsche duality trick.
Explain why the stiffness matrix has condition number of order h⁻² and why multigrid helps.
refs: Brenner–Scott, ch. 0 (Basic Concepts), ch. 2–5 (Variational Formulation of Elliptic Boundary Value Problems; The Construction of a Finite Element Space; Polynomial Approximation Theory in Sobolev Spaces; n-Dimensional Variational Problems) and ch. 6 (Finite Element Multigrid Methods)

units.title: Approximation theory
objectives: State the Weierstrass approximation theorem and Chebyshev's equioscillation characterization of best approximations.
Show that Chebyshev interpolants converge geometrically for analytic functions (Bernstein ellipse) and algebraically for functions with finitely many derivatives.
Explain the Runge phenomenon for equispaced nodes and the growth of Lebesgue constants (logarithmic for Chebyshev points, exponential for equispaced points).
Explain why rational functions beat polynomials near singularities, using Newman's approximation of |x|.
refs: Trefethen, Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice (Extended ed.), ch. 2–3 (Chebyshev Points and Interpolants; Chebyshev Polynomials and Series), ch. 6–8 (Weierstrass Approximation Theorem; Convergence for Differentiable and Analytic Functions), ch. 10 (Best Approximation), ch. 13 (Equispaced Points, Runge Phenomenon), ch. 15 (Lebesgue Constants) and ch. 23–25 (rational approximation)

tiers.name: Research frontier
tiers.summary: You can find your way around current research: place a paper on the map of mathematics, read it efficiently, explain what recent landmark results say, why they matter and whether they are published, and read and write simple machine-checked proofs.

modules.title: Research literacy
modules.summary: Find your way around the research literature by subject, read papers strategically, and know the big open problems.
refs: Gowers (ed.), The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, Parts I, IV, V and VIII
Clay Mathematics Institute, Millennium Prize Problems

practice.title: Skim today's arXiv math listing and classify ten abstracts by MSC2020 class and arXiv category
Browse the MSC2020 classes and find the full code for a topic you know
Read three Princeton generals reports in your two strongest areas and answer their questions aloud

units.title: The map of mathematics: MSC2020 and arXiv
objectives: Place a topic in its MSC2020 top-level class (for example 11 Number theory, 14 Algebraic geometry, 35 Partial differential equations, 53 Differential geometry) and read a full code such as 14H52.
Name the 32 arXiv math categories and their aliases (math.MP = math-ph, math.IT = cs.IT, stat.TH = math.ST), and distinguish primary from cross-listed categories.
Explain how a daily arXiv listing is split into new submissions, cross-lists and replacements.
Use MSC codes and arXiv categories to search the literature in zbMATH Open and MathSciNet.
refs: Gowers (ed.), The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, Part IV (Branches of Mathematics)

units.title: How to read a research paper
objectives: Describe the anatomy of a paper (abstract, introduction with the main theorems, outline of the proof, preliminaries, proofs, references) and choose an order to read it in.
Apply a three-pass strategy: statements first, then key lemmas and proof architecture, then line-by-line checking of what you need.
Distinguish a preprint, a refereed article, a paper 'to appear' and an erratum, and read arXiv version numbers and journal references.
Keep a dependency map of lemmas and decide which cited results to take on trust.
Interpret common conventions: constants C that change from line to line, 'it is well known', room in ε.
refs: Gowers (ed.), The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, VIII.6 (Advice to a Young Mathematician)
Gowers (ed.), The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, Part I (Introduction)

units.title: The Millennium Prize Problems
objectives: State each of the seven Millennium Prize Problems in one precise sentence: Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer, Hodge, Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness, P vs NP, Poincaré, the Riemann hypothesis, and Yang–Mills existence and mass gap.
State that the Poincaré conjecture is the only one solved (Perelman's 2002–2003 preprints; the Clay prize was announced in March 2010) and outline Ricci flow with surgery.
Give one reason each problem matters.
Correct common misstatements, for example that the Navier–Stokes problem asks only for weak solutions.
refs: Clay Mathematics Institute, Millennium Prize Problems (official list and problem descriptions)
Gowers (ed.), The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, V.24 (The P versus NP Problem), V.25 (The Poincaré Conjecture) and V.26 (The Prime Number Theorem and the Riemann Hypothesis)

units.title: Central open conjectures across fields
objectives: State central open conjectures by field: Langlands functoriality, the abc conjecture, the twin prime and Goldbach conjectures, the generalized Riemann hypothesis, Grothendieck's standard conjectures on algebraic cycles, the Jacobian conjecture, the invariant subspace problem, and the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.
Distinguish proved, conditional (for example on GRH) and open statements, and recognize how partial progress is phrased (bounded gaps instead of twin primes; ternary instead of binary Goldbach).
Explain that acceptance of a proof is a community judgement, using the disputed status of Mochizuki's claimed proof of abc and the Scholze–Stix objection.
Explain the role of Grothendieck's standard conjectures, which would have given the Riemann hypothesis part of the Weil conjectures that Deligne proved by other means.
refs: Gowers (ed.), The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, Part V (Theorems and Problems)
Gowers (ed.), The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, IV.2 (Analytic Number Theory) and IV.20 (Computational Complexity)

units.title: How research is organized and judged
objectives: Describe the main prizes and venues: Fields Medals awarded every four years at the International Congress of Mathematicians, the Abel Prize, and the leading general journals (Annals, Acta, Inventiones, JAMS, Publications IHÉS).
Explain what a qualifying (general) exam certifies, using Princeton's format: algebra and real and complex analysis plus two advanced topics from distinct areas.
Explain refereeing, typical publication delays and alphabetical authorship in mathematics.
Describe Polymath-style online collaboration and formal verification as newer ways to produce and check results.
refs: Gowers (ed.), The Princeton Companion to Mathematics, Part VIII (Final Perspectives)
International Mathematical Union, Fields Medal (prize page)
Princeton University Mathematics, graduate program requirements and the Graduate Students' Guide to Generals

modules.title: Arithmetic and Langlands
modules.summary: Explain what recent breakthroughs in number theory, arithmetic geometry and the Langlands program state, why they matter and whether they are published.
refs: Primary sources listed per unit (arXiv preprints, Annals of Mathematics pages, IMU announcements), checked 2026-11
Diamond–Shurman, A First Course in Modular Forms, ch. 9
Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, ch. VI

units.title: The Langlands program: a map
objectives: Explain the Langlands philosophy: automorphic representations correspond to Galois representations, with class field theory as the GL₁ case and modularity of elliptic curves as a GL₂ case.
Distinguish reciprocity from functoriality and define the Langlands dual group (GLₙ is self-dual; SO(2n+1) is dual to Sp(2n)).
Explain where symmetric power functoriality fits, using Newton–Thorne's theorem for Hilbert modular forms (Annals, 2026).
Name the arithmetic, local, geometric and function-field versions of the program and say which parts are theorems.
refs: Neukirch, ch. VI (Global Class Field Theory)
Newton–Thorne, Symmetric power functoriality for Hilbert modular forms, Annals of Math. 203 (2026)

units.title: The geometric Langlands conjecture
objectives: State the geometric Langlands conjecture for a smooth projective curve as an equivalence between D-modules on Bun_G and ind-coherent sheaves with nilpotent singular support on the stack of local systems for the dual group.
Explain Hecke eigensheaves as geometric analogues of Hecke eigenforms.

Describe the proof series 'Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture I–V' (Gaitsgory, Raskin and coauthors; arXiv 2024): construction of the functor, Kac–Moody localization, compatibility with parabolic induction, ambidexterity and multiplicity one; status: preprints as of 2026-11.
Explain why this does not prove the arithmetic Langlands conjectures over number fields.
refs: Gaitsgory–Raskin, Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture I: construction of the functor, arXiv:2405.03599
Arinkin–Beraldo–Campbell–Chen–Faergeman–Gaitsgory–Lin–Raskin–Rozenblyum, Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture II: Kac–Moody localization and the FLE, arXiv:2405.03648
Gaitsgory–Raskin, Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture V: the multiplicity one theorem, arXiv:2409.09856

units.title: Modularity beyond elliptic curves: abelian surfaces
objectives: State the modularity conjecture for abelian surfaces over ℚ: they should match Siegel paramodular forms, with GSp₄ in place of GL₂.

State the Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Pilloni theorem (arXiv, February 2025): a positive proportion of abelian surfaces over ℚ are modular, namely those ordinary at 3 and 3-distinguished, under further conditions; status: preprint as of 2026-11.
Explain the key idea at concept level: modularity lifting for GSp₄ at the prime 3.
Describe Burungale–Tian's rank-zero p-converse (Annals, 2026) as progress toward BSD: algebraic information (a finite p-power Selmer group) forces analytic rank zero, for suitable p.
refs: Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Pilloni, Modularity theorems for abelian surfaces, arXiv:2502.20645
Burungale–Tian, A rank zero p-converse to a theorem of Gross–Zagier, Kolyvagin and Rubin, Annals of Math. 203 (2026)

units.title: Hilbert's tenth problem over rings of integers
objectives: State Hilbert's tenth problem over a ring R and explain why a Diophantine definition of ℤ inside O_K gives a negative answer for O_K.
State the elliptic-curve criterion (Poonen; Shlapentokh): a positive-rank elliptic curve whose rank does not grow in the extension yields such a definition.

State Koymans–Pagano (arXiv, December 2024): the problem has a negative answer over every infinite ring finitely generated over ℤ, in particular every O_K; key idea: elliptic curves with full rational 2-torsion plus additive combinatorics.

State Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman (arXiv, January 2025): for every quadratic extension of number fields there is a positive-rank abelian variety whose rank does not grow, which also settles every O_K; both are preprints as of 2026-11, and the problem over ℚ remains open.
keyTerms: Hilbert's tenth problem over a ring
refs: Koymans–Pagano, Hilbert's tenth problem via additive combinatorics, arXiv:2412.01768
Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman, Rank stability in quadratic extensions and Hilbert's tenth problem for the ring of integers of a number field, arXiv:2501.18774
Matiyasevich, Hilbert's Tenth Problem, ch. 7 (Decision Problems in Number Theory)

units.title: Local–global conjectures in representation theory: McKay
objectives: State the McKay conjecture: for a finite group G and a prime p, the number of irreducible characters of degree prime to p equals the same number for the normalizer of a Sylow p-subgroup.
Explain the Isaacs–Malle–Navarro reduction (2007) to an inductive condition on finite simple groups, and why groups of Lie type are the hard case.
State the Cabanes–Späth theorem completing the proof (arXiv 2024; Annals 2026) and the related Alperin–McKay and Brauer height zero results for p = 2 (Ruhstorfer, Annals 2025).
Explain 'local–global': global invariants of G determined by p-local subgroups.
refs: Cabanes–Späth, The McKay Conjecture on character degrees, Annals of Math. 203 (2026); arXiv:2410.20392
Ruhstorfer, The Alperin–McKay and Brauer's height zero conjecture for the prime 2, Annals of Math. 201 (2025)

units.title: Arithmetic statistics and integer polynomials
objectives: State van der Waerden's 1936 conjecture and Bhargava's theorem (Annals 2025): among monic integer polynomials of degree n with coefficients in [−H, H], those with Galois group other than Sₙ number O(Hⁿ⁻¹).
Explain why this count is sharp (polynomials with constant term 0 already give order Hⁿ⁻¹).

State the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture and Dimitrov's theorem (arXiv 2019; listed as to appear in Annals): an algebraic integer of degree n that is not a root of unity has a conjugate of absolute value at least 2^(1/(4n)).
Contrast this with Lehmer's problem on Mahler measure, which remains open.
keyTerms: Galois group of a random polynomial
refs: Bhargava, Galois groups of random integer polynomials and van der Waerden's Conjecture, Annals of Math. 201 (2025); arXiv:2111.06507
Dimitrov, A proof of the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials, arXiv:1912.12545

units.title: The 2026 Fields Medals and o-minimality in arithmetic
objectives: List the 2026 Fields Medalists (Yu Deng, John Pardon, Jacob Tsimerman, Hong Wang) and the area of each.

Summarize Tsimerman's citation: o-minimality as a central tool in arithmetic and complex algebraic geometry, Griffiths' conjecture on algebraicity of images of period maps, and the André–Oort conjecture for Siegel modular varieties.
State the André–Oort conjecture for the moduli space A_g: the Zariski closure of a set of special (CM) points is a special subvariety.
Explain the o-minimal strategy: definability of uniformization or period maps, Pila–Wilkie counting, and lower bounds for Galois orbits.
refs: International Mathematical Union, Fields Medals 2026 (prize citations)
Pila–Wilkie, The rational points of a definable set, Duke Math. J. 133 (2006)
van den Dries, Tame Topology and o-minimal Structures, ch. 1–3

modules.title: Analysis and PDE
modules.summary: Explain recent landmark results in harmonic analysis, PDE, convex geometry and analytic number theory, why they matter and whether they are published.
refs: Primary sources listed per unit (arXiv preprints, Annals of Mathematics pages, IMU announcements), checked 2026-11
Demeter, Fourier Restriction, Decoupling, and Applications

units.title: The Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions
objectives: State the Kakeya set conjecture (a set in ℝⁿ containing a unit segment in every direction has Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension n) and its links to the Kakeya maximal function and restriction conjectures.

State the Wang–Zahl theorem (arXiv, February 2025): every Kakeya set in ℝ³ has Minkowski and Hausdorff dimension 3; key idea: volume estimates for unions of tubes obeying Wolff-type axioms, proved by multiscale induction.
Place it historically: Besicovitch's measure-zero sets, Wolff's bound 5/2 in ℝ³, and Dvir's finite-field theorem.
State the status (preprint as of 2026-11; cited in Hong Wang's 2026 Fields Medal) and what remains open: dimensions n ≥ 4 and the restriction conjecture.
refs: Wang–Zahl, Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions, arXiv:2502.17655
Demeter, Fourier Restriction, Decoupling, and Applications, ch. 5 (Kakeya and Square Function Estimates)
International Mathematical Union, Fields Medals 2026 (citation for Hong Wang)

units.title: Large values of Dirichlet polynomials and zero density
objectives: Define N(σ, T) and state the density hypothesis N(σ, T) ≪ T^(2(1−σ)+ε).
State Ingham's 1940 bound T^(3(1−σ)/(2−σ)+ε) and the Guth–Maynard bound T^(30(1−σ)/13+o(1)) (arXiv 2024; Annals 2026), which improves Ingham's bound near σ = 3/4, where it had been the best known.
State the application: an asymptotic count of primes in intervals [x, x + x^(17/30+ε)], improving Huxley's exponent 7/12.
Explain the key idea: a new bound on how often a Dirichlet polynomial takes large values, exploiting Fourier-analytic structure of the set where it is large.
keyTerms: mean value theorem for Dirichlet polynomials
refs: Guth–Maynard, New large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials, Annals of Math. 203 (2026); arXiv:2405.20552
Iwaniec–Kowalski, ch. 9 (The Dirichlet Polynomials) and ch. 10 (Zero-Density Estimates)

units.title: High-dimensional convex geometry: slicing and lattice packing
objectives: State Bourgain's slicing problem (every convex body of volume 1 in ℝⁿ has a hyperplane section of volume at least a universal constant) and its equivalent form L_n ≤ C for the isotropic constant.
State Guan's bound L_n ≤ C log log n and the Klartag–Lehec resolution L_n ≤ C (both arXiv, December 2024; preprints as of 2026-11).
State Klartag's lattice packing theorem (arXiv 2025): in every dimension n there is a lattice sphere packing of density at least c·n²·2⁻ⁿ, improving the previous order n log n · 2⁻ⁿ.
Explain the shared toolkit of stochastic localization and stochastically evolving ellipsoids at concept level.
refs: Klartag–Lehec, Affirmative resolution of Bourgain's slicing problem using Guan's bound, arXiv:2412.15044
Guan, A note on Bourgain's slicing problem, arXiv:2412.09075
Klartag, Lattice packing of spheres in high dimensions using a stochastically evolving ellipsoid, arXiv:2504.05042

units.title: From particles to fluids: Boltzmann and Hilbert's sixth problem
objectives: Describe the three levels of description (Newtonian hard spheres, the Boltzmann kinetic equation, fluid equations) and the Boltzmann–Grad scaling limit.

State Lanford's 1975 short-time derivation and the Deng–Hani–Ma long-time derivation of the Boltzmann equation from hard spheres, valid as long as the Boltzmann solution exists (arXiv 2024; listed as to appear in Annals).
State Deng–Hani–Ma's 2025 preprint deriving the compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations from hard-sphere dynamics on 2D and 3D tori.

Explain why calling this a solution of Hilbert's sixth problem is disputed: the problem is a broad program to axiomatize physics, and the result settles Hilbert's question about the passage from atomistic to continuum models in one setting.
refs: Deng–Hani–Ma, Long time derivation of the Boltzmann equation from hard sphere dynamics, arXiv:2408.07818
Deng–Hani–Ma, Hilbert's sixth problem: derivation of fluid equations via Boltzmann's kinetic theory, arXiv:2503.01800
International Mathematical Union, Fields Medals 2026 (citation for Yu Deng)

units.title: Stable minimal hypersurfaces and the Bernstein problem
objectives: State the Bernstein problem and its answer: entire minimal graphs over ℝⁿ are hyperplanes exactly when n ≤ 7, with Bombieri–De Giorgi–Giusti counterexamples for n ≥ 8.
Define stability (nonnegative second variation of area) and state the stable Bernstein problem.

State the Chodosh–Li–Minter–Stryker theorem (arXiv 2024; Annals 2026): a complete two-sided stable minimal hypersurface in ℝ⁵ is flat, following the ℝ³ case (do Carmo–Peng, Fischer-Colbrie–Schoen) and the ℝ⁴ case (Chodosh–Li).
Explain why the problem is open in ℝ⁶ and ℝ⁷ and false from ℝ⁸ on (the Simons cone).
refs: Chodosh–Li–Minter–Stryker, Stable minimal hypersurfaces in ℝ⁵, Annals of Math. 204 (2026); arXiv:2401.01492
Evans, Partial Differential Equations, ch. 8 (The Calculus of Variations)

units.title: The 2026 Fields Medals in analysis: Deng and Wang
objectives: Summarize Hong Wang's citation: multiscale and decoupling methods for the local smoothing conjecture for the planar wave equation, and advances on Fourier restriction, Falconer distance sets, Furstenberg sets in the plane and the 3D Kakeya problem.

Summarize Yu Deng's citation: the derivation of the Boltzmann equation from hard spheres, derivation of wave kinetic equations from nonlinear dispersive systems, and probabilistic methods for nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics.
State the Falconer distance problem, the Furstenberg set problem and the local smoothing conjecture at the level of definitions.
Explain the wave kinetic equation as the analogue of the Boltzmann equation for weakly interacting waves (wave turbulence).
refs: International Mathematical Union, Fields Medals 2026 (citations for Yu Deng and Hong Wang)
Demeter, Fourier Restriction, Decoupling, and Applications, ch. 9–13 (decoupling and its applications)

modules.title: Combinatorics and topology
modules.summary: Explain recent landmark results in combinatorics, homotopy theory, knot theory and symplectic topology, why they matter and whether they are published.
refs: Primary sources listed per unit (arXiv preprints, Annals of Mathematics pages, IMU announcements), checked 2026-11
Zhao, Graph Theory and Additive Combinatorics
McDuff–Salamon, Introduction to Symplectic Topology (3rd ed.)

practice.title: KnotInfo: look up the knot 7₁ and its unknotting number, then compare with the Brittenham–Hermiller bound for 7₁ # mirror(7₁)

units.title: An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey numbers
objectives: State the classical bounds √2^k ≲ R(k) ≤ 4^k: the Erdős–Szekeres upper bound (1935) and Erdős's random-colouring lower bound (1947).
State the Campos–Griffiths–Morris–Sahasrabudhe theorem R(k) ≤ (4 − ε)^k for some fixed ε > 0 (arXiv 2023; Annals 2026), the first exponential improvement.
Explain the key idea at concept level: a 'book algorithm' that builds large monochromatic books and uses them to find a monochromatic clique.
Explain what remains open: the exponential gap between √2 and 4 − ε, with the lower bound essentially still Erdős's.
refs: Campos–Griffiths–Morris–Sahasrabudhe, An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey, Annals of Math. 203 (2026); arXiv:2303.09521
Alon–Spencer, The Probabilistic Method (4th ed.), ch. 1 (The Basic Method)

units.title: Kelley–Meka and Marton's conjecture
objectives: State the Kelley–Meka theorem (arXiv 2023): a subset of {1, …, N} with no nontrivial 3-term progression has size at most N·2^(−c(log N)^β) for some β > 0, close to Behrend's construction.
Explain why this is a jump over the previous bounds of shape N/(log N)^(1+c).

State Marton's conjecture (polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa) over 𝔽₂ⁿ as proved by Gowers–Green–Manners–Tao (arXiv 2023; Annals 2025): if |A + A| ≤ K|A|, then A is covered by at most 2K¹² cosets of a subgroup of size at most |A|.
Explain the entropy method (entropic Ruzsa distance), and that the Lean formalization of the proof was completed within about three weeks of the preprint.
refs: Gowers–Green–Manners–Tao, On a conjecture of Marton, Annals of Math. 201 (2025); arXiv:2311.05762

units.title: Designs, locally testable codes and strong convergence
objectives: State Keevash's existence of designs (arXiv 2014; listed as to appear in Annals): for fixed parameters, designs such as Steiner systems exist whenever the natural divisibility conditions hold and n is large, answering a question going back to Steiner (1853).
State the Dinur–Evra–Livne–Lubotzky–Mozes construction of locally testable codes with constant rate, distance and locality (arXiv 2021; Annals 2026) from left–right Cayley complexes.
State the Chen–Garza-Vargas–Tropp–van Handel approach to strong convergence of random matrices (Annals 2026) and its short proof of Friedman's theorem that random regular graphs are nearly Ramanujan.
Explain the common thread: pseudorandom, expander-like structure made rigorous by algebra or probability.
refs: Keevash, The existence of designs, arXiv:1401.3665
Dinur–Evra–Livne–Lubotzky–Mozes, Good locally testable codes, Annals of Math. 203 (2026); arXiv:2111.04808
Chen–Garza-Vargas–Tropp–van Handel, A new approach to strong convergence, Annals of Math. 203 (2026); arXiv:2405.16026

units.title: Chromatic homotopy theory and the telescope conjecture
objectives: Explain chromatic homotopy theory: stable homotopy organized by height through Morava K-theories K(n) and vₙ-periodic self-maps.
State Ravenel's telescope conjecture (localization at the telescope T(n) agrees with K(n)-localization), which holds at heights 0 and 1.

State the Burklund–Hahn–Levy–Schlank theorem (arXiv 2023): the conjecture fails at every prime and every height ≥ 2, detected through the algebraic K-theory of fixed points of BP⟨n⟩ under ℤ; status: preprint as of 2026-11.
Explain why it matters: two candidate notions of periodic stable homotopy really differ.
refs: Burklund–Hahn–Levy–Schlank, K-theoretic counterexamples to Ravenel's telescope conjecture, arXiv:2310.17459
Hatcher, Spectral Sequences (online), ch. 2 (The Adams Spectral Sequence)

units.title: Unknotting number and exotic 4-manifolds
objectives: State the additivity conjecture u(K₁ # K₂) = u(K₁) + u(K₂) and the Brittenham–Hermiller counterexample (arXiv 2025; Annals 2026): the torus knot 7₁ and its mirror each have unknotting number 3, but their connected sum has unknotting number at most 5.
Explain how the example was found: a computer search with SnapPy over crossing changes in braid diagrams.

State Ren–Willis (arXiv 2024; listed as to appear in Annals): a Khovanov–Rozansky skein lasagna module distinguishes an exotic pair of knot traces, giving an analysis-free proof that exotic compact orientable 4-manifolds exist.
State that some closed aspherical 4-manifolds carry exotic smooth structures (Davis–Hayden–Huang–Ruberman–Sunukjian, Annals 2026).

units.title: Symplectic rigidity: Viterbo's conjecture and Pardon's work
objectives: State Viterbo's volume–capacity conjecture (among convex domains of given volume in ℝ²ⁿ the ball maximizes every normalized symplectic capacity) and the stronger expectation that normalized capacities agree on convex domains.
State the Haim-Kislev–Ostrover counterexample (arXiv 2024; Annals 2026): a convex domain in ℝ⁴ violating the conjecture, so capacities need not coincide on convex domains.
Explain why counting holomorphic curves needs virtual fundamental cycles when moduli spaces are not cut out transversely.

Summarize John Pardon's 2026 Fields Medal citation: virtual fundamental cycles, Fukaya categories and counting holomorphic curves, plus work on group actions on 3-manifolds (the Hilbert–Smith conjecture in dimension 3) and on knot theory.

International Mathematical Union, Fields Medals 2026 (citation for John Pardon)
McDuff–Salamon, Introduction to Symplectic Topology (3rd ed.), ch. 12 (Symplectic Capacities)

units.title: Proof assistants and dependent type theory
objectives: Explain what a proof assistant checks: a small trusted kernel type-checks proof terms (the de Bruijn criterion).
State the propositions-as-types (Curry–Howard) correspondence: a proof of P is a term of type P, and ∀ is a dependent function type.
Distinguish Prop, Type and universe levels, and definitional from propositional equality.
Explain that Lean's library works classically (choice, propositional extensionality, quotients) and what this means for constructive content.
refs: Avigad–Massot, Mathematics in Lean, ch. 1–2 (Introduction; Basics)
Theorem Proving in Lean 4, chapters 'Dependent Type Theory', 'Propositions and Proofs' and 'Axioms and Computation'

objectives: Read the goal view (hypotheses ⊢ target) and use sorry to leave holes.
Use the core tactics intro, exact, apply, rw, simp, constructor, rcases/obtain, use, induction and calc, and the automation linarith, ring and norm_num.
Choose between term-mode and tactic-mode proofs.
Prove small lemmas such as 0 + n = n by induction, as in the Natural Number Game.

units.title: Mathlib: structures, type classes and the library
objectives: Explain how algebraic hierarchies (monoids, groups, rings, fields, modules) are encoded with structures and type classes, and how instance search finds them.
Explain coercions between ℕ, ℤ, ℚ and ℝ and use norm_cast and push_cast.
Find lemmas with Mathlib's naming conventions and the search tactics exact? and apply?.
Explain filters and Tendsto as Mathlib's language for limits, and where topology, calculus and measure theory live in the library.
refs: Avigad–Massot, Mathematics in Lean, ch. 7–13 (Structures; Hierarchies; Groups and Rings; Linear Algebra; Topology; Differential Calculus; Integration and Measure Theory)

units.title: Blueprints and large formalization projects
objectives: Describe the blueprint workflow: an informal proof whose dependency graph records which statements are stated and proved in Lean, so lemmas can be shared among many contributors.
Describe the Liquid Tensor Experiment (Scholze's challenge in condensed mathematics; completed 14 July 2022) and Flyspeck (the Kepler conjecture in HOL Light and Isabelle; completed 10 August 2014).
Describe the PFR project: launched in November 2023, it formalized the proof of Marton's conjecture within about three weeks, followed by phases on improved exponents and bounded-torsion groups.
Explain what formal verification certifies and what it does not (fidelity of definitions and statements).

units.title: Recent landmark formalizations and their status
objectives: Describe the Equational Theories Project: launched in September 2024; on 14 April 2025 all 22,028,942 implications between 4694 equational laws for magmas were settled, each checked in Lean (project report, December 2025).

Describe the sphere-packing formalization: the project announced a sorry-free Lean proof of Viazovska's dimension-8 theorem on 23 February 2026, with the remaining goals completed by Math, Inc.'s Gauss agent; the dimension-24 formalization is vendor-reported and not yet merged (as of 2026-11).
State the status of Fermat's Last Theorem: the Imperial College Lean project is ongoing (funded to September 2029), and no complete formalization has been independently confirmed (as of 2026-11).
Classify a formalization claim as project-confirmed, vendor-reported or independently reviewed, and say what evidence each needs.
refs: The Equational Theories Project: Advancing Collaborative Mathematical Research at Scale (project report, December 2025), teorth.github.io/equational_theories
Sphere Packing in Lean project page (thefundamentaltheor3m.github.io/Sphere-Packing-Lean)

units.title: Automation, AI and the limits of formal proof
objectives: Distinguish automated theorem provers, SMT solvers, tactic-level automation (simp, aesop, omega) and machine-learning provers, and what each contributed to the Equational Theories Project.
Explain autoformalization and why humans must still check that formal statements and definitions mean what the informal ones do.
Explain the de Bruijn factor (formal length over informal length) and why formal proofs are long.
Explain how formalization changes refereeing and large collaborations, and its limits: a formal proof certifies the statement proved, not its importance or its faithfulness to the intended claim.
refs: The Equational Theories Project report (December 2025), sections 'Proof automation' and 'AI and Machine Learning contributions'
